+## 限制
+
+- 原有 `OwnerOnly` 运行来自 debug 构建，代码基线为 `60c20a4`，不能当作干净源码上的正式性能基线；独立 `FirstSuccessor` 补测使用干净的 `6eabea6`，但仍是 debug 构建和繁忙桌面主机。正式性能复测应使用 `--require-clean-source`、release 构建和空闲主机。
+- `fault` 模式的容量背压分成两个计数：以容量错误结束的请求数，和客户端因容量而重试的次数；一次跟随副本丢失仍可能触发复制容量背压，本文按 TODO 要求单独记录，不要求故障期间零阻塞。
+- follower 场景中，被杀死节点对其他 range 仍是 owner；这些键不在本场景的判定范围内，按“附带 owner 故障”单独记录并重新同步模型，不作为 follower 丢失的通过/失败条件。
+- 协调器在故障窗口内把所选 range 标为不可写（`owner lease unavailable`）时，owner 仍会接受写入；该状态是协调器视图，与实际是否拒绝写入不是一回事，本文按状态原样记录。
+- 每个键的已确认历史有上限，由 `--fault-acknowledged-window` 给出（默认 4096 条），超出后丢弃最旧的并计数；被重新确认的状态会移到窗口末尾，因此窗口里是最近确认过的状态。窗口太小会让可解释的回退变成无法判定：一个既不匹配当前状态也不匹配保留历史的读只能记为无法判定，两个场景都判该轮不通过（该读没有被核验过，运行不能算它通过）。默认长度的一次 owner 运行平均每键约 200 次写，默认窗口有二十倍余量；个别键的写入可能高于平均值，更长的运行按实测的 `dropped_acknowledged_states` 调大窗口，否则长跑中“0 次不可解释读”这一结论只在被丢弃状态数为 0 时才完整。
+- `requests.jsonl` 约 580 B/请求且没有上限（10 万请求约 58 MB），按完成顺序写入而不是按请求号排序；长时间运行前要先估算磁盘占用。
+- 回执重试测试把“响应丢失”实现为：mutation 已成功应用，驱动丢弃成功响应后换 epoch 重试。它验证了服务端回执、迁移/提升携带回执和客户端复用 mutation ID，但没有在传输层真实丢弃一个 TCP/HTTP2 响应；客户端内部的每一次 RPC attempt 也没有逐条持久化，`retry-trace.jsonl` 只关联逻辑请求、mutation ID、epoch 和最终结果。
+- 同键历史检查器针对单寄存器，按版本排序 mutation；它覆盖单 owner epoch 和“无故障迁移前后”的交接，不覆盖 owner 故障期间的严格线性一致性（那部分按 `OwnerOnly` 允许回退的契约单独处理）。
+- 故障实验使用 seed 1 的三次重复和 seed 7 的一次两轮运行；更多 seed/受害节点组合仍可继续扩展。

+# Latency acceptance measurements
+
+The `latency` mode offers requests on a fixed schedule and measures from each
+request's scheduled time to completion. These measurements cover an in-memory
+cluster on one shared Linux host, using the native Rust client over loopback.
+They do not measure the Redis gateway or a multi-host deployment.
+
+## Setup and evidence
+
+| Setting | Value |
+| --- | --- |
+| Nodes / replication | 10 / RF=3 |
+| Acknowledgement | `OwnerOnly` (does not wait for follower acknowledgements) |
+| Data | 100,000 keys, 128-byte values |
+| Operations | GET:PUT:DELETE = 90:9:1 |
+| Distributions | uniform and Zipf 0.99 |
+| Virtual nodes | 128, plus comparisons at 16 / 64 / 256 |
+| Main stages | 10 s warmup, 60 s measured, 3 repetitions per point |
+| Overload ladder | 3 s warmup, 10 s measured, 1 repetition per point |
+| In-flight limit | 4,096 requests |
+| Host | 24 logical CPUs, 32 GB RAM, Linux 7.2.11-zen1-1-zen |
+| Campaign | `latency-acceptance-20261022-172621`, about 39 minutes |
+| Source | `52adf85` |
+
+The [host record](data/latency-acceptance/host.txt) identifies the binary and
+machine. The [stage table](data/latency-acceptance/latency-acceptance-20261022-172621/stages.tsv)
+holds all 36 measured stages: 24 main stages, 4 overload stages and 8 virtual-node
+stages, across 11 latency runs. A separate `performance` run measured the
+closed-loop write baseline. The [median table](data/latency-acceptance/latency-acceptance-20261022-172621/medians.tsv)
+contains medians of each field across repetitions; a median p99 is not the
+p99 of pooled request samples. The raw run directories are not checked in;
+see the [data README](data/latency-acceptance/README.md).
+
+The write baseline was **84,054 ops/s**. Main rates are 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and
+0.9 times this baseline. It is a reference for choosing rates, not the
+capacity of the read-heavy mixed workload. Preload write throughput across
+the six main runs ranged from 80,993 to 86,500 ops/s (6.8% spread); the host
+was shared with desktop processes and other work.
+
+## Latency under the main load
+
+GET latency in microseconds, medians over three repetitions:
+
+| Distribution | Offered ops/s | p50 | p95 | p99 | p999 |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| uniform | 21,013 | 56 | 78 | 95 | 209 |
+| uniform | 42,027 | 57 | 82 | 107 | 215 |
+| uniform | 63,040 | 58 | 97 | 190 | 673 |
+| uniform | 75,648 | 62 | 134 | 548 | 1,892 |
+| zipf:0.99 | 21,013 | 57 | 78 | 95 | 234 |
+| zipf:0.99 | 42,027 | 57 | 82 | 109 | 233 |
+| zipf:0.99 | 63,040 | 57 | 93 | 173 | 576 |
+| zipf:0.99 | 75,648 | 62 | 120 | 439 | 2,381 |
+
+All 24 main stages achieved their offered rate without drops, errors or
+client retries. Across individual repetitions, p50 stayed between 56 and
+63 us, while p99 rose from 92–110 us through half the write baseline to
+304–592 us at the highest rate. The largest main-stage GET sample bucket
+was 21,247 us; maxima varied more than the lower percentiles.
+
+Uniform and Zipf latencies overlap in this campaign. Three repetitions on a
+shared host do not establish equal latency or a general advantage for either
+distribution. PUT and DELETE percentiles and every repetition are retained
+in the stage and median tables.
+
+## Load balance
+
+At 75,648 offered ops/s, medians over three repetitions:
+
+| Distribution | Owned keys max/mean | Owned keys CV | Served ops max/mean | Served ops CV | Maximum node CPU |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

+CPU percentages are fractions of one core for the entire node process.
+Key ownership follows the fixed ring; request counts follow the workload's
+key distribution. Zipf traffic therefore concentrates on the owners of hot
+keys even when the key counts are relatively even.

+These are the lower-rate rows; request max/mean differs by at most 0.008

+| Virtual nodes | Owned keys max/mean | Owned keys CV | Served ops max/mean | Served ops CV |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| 16 | 1.200 | 0.177 | 1.206 | 0.183 |
+| 64 | 1.255 | 0.139 | 1.242 | 0.134 |
+| 128 | 1.116 | 0.088 | 1.147 | 0.089 |
+| 256 | 1.087 | 0.048 | 1.066 | 0.049 |

+

+## Accounting and measurement limits

+# Operations
+
+Details that the [README](../README.md) leaves out: how membership changes
+recover from failures, what `replica-status` reports, and the internal timers
+and budgets.
+
+## Membership changes in depth
+
+### Cutover
+
+- The source stays authoritative while a point-in-time snapshot is copied.
+  Independent ranges move concurrently, 16 at a time by default
+  (`coordinator --range-move-concurrency N`, or the same `experiment` flag).
+- Puts and deletes that arrive during the copy are replayed from a bounded
+  changelog.
+- At cutover, affected writes get a retryable `RangeBusy` while reads continue.
+  The coordinator checks the live-record count, the contiguous watermark, and a
+  BLAKE3 digest, then publishes the new epoch.
+- During the read handoff, the frozen source and the committed destination hold
+  the same data. Destination writes stay fenced until every source has
+  installed the new topology.
+- Deleted values are not kept as permanent tombstones.
+
+### Leases and follower admission
+
+- For planned cutovers, the coordinator withholds new-epoch leases until the
+  required target followers are verified and admitted.
+- Automatic failover may publish a degraded placement that still satisfies the
+  write guard, then repair followers in the background.
+
+### Stopping removed nodes
+
+Removed nodes are stopped only after source cleanup, using the process-instance
+identity captured during the migration. The sequence is:
+
+1. The node acknowledges a prepared stop.
+2. The coordinator persists an instance-specific stop confirmation.
+3. The coordinator requests final shutdown.
+
+The confirmation stays durable after the change completes. A node that briefly
+loses contact with the coordinator still shuts down when it reconnects. A lost
+final response can be recovered, and a transient outage is never mistaken for a
+successful stop.
+
+### Failures during a change
+
+- **Coordinator restart.** The persisted transition and repair plan resume
+  automatically.
+- **Failure before publication.** Cleanup has its own deadline. The change
+  stays in a recoverable `Aborting` state until the authoritative sources
+  acknowledge cleanup. If a new joiner stays unavailable for 30 seconds before
+  publication, the attempt aborts after source cleanup.
+- **Failure after publication.** The epoch is never rolled back. If a required
+  target node stays unavailable, the published transition can stay pending.
+- **Single-node join where the new process dies before activation.** This can
+  be recovered by publishing a further epoch with the original members, but
+  only if every original owner is still the same live process and the frozen
+  source ranges still hold their verified watermarks. The superseding change
+  records the previous change ID and re-admits the required followers before it
+  grants leases.
+- **Loss of an original owner, or a more complex second failure.** The change
+  stays blocked because there is no proof that the data is still covered.
+  `change-status` and `replica-status` report why recovery is blocked. Restore
+  the same live process if you can.
+
+Coordinator consensus and failover are not provided.
+
+## `replica-status` fields
+
+Cluster level:
+
+- committed epoch and topology digest
+- desired RF and ACK policy
+- active change phase
+
+Per node:
+
+- process identity
+- lease expiry and last renewal
+- suspicion and fencing state
+- whether the node is joining
+
+Per range:
+
+- `current_rf`: the nominal replica count. **This alone does not prove the
+  replicas are alive.**
+- `live_rf`: the replicas that hold leases
+- owner lease
+- follower admission, lag, and health
+- last known owner ACK sequence
+- `writable`, and the reason when it is false
+- under-replication, repair phase, retry count, next attempt time, and last
+  error
+
+While a cutover fence is in place, affected ranges are conservatively reported
+as possibly blocked. A failed required repair stays visible and is never
+treated as healthy.
+
+## Timers and budgets
+
+These values are fixed in the code. The configurable ones, such as the lease
+duration, receipt retention, node budgets, and worker threads, are listed with
+their defaults in [configuration.md](configuration.md).
+
+| Setting | Value |
+| --- | --- |
+| Failure detection interval | 1 s |
+| Repair and recovery interval | 5 s |
+| Repair groups per pass | 32 |
+| Repair retry backoff cap | 60 s (exponential, per group) |
+| Migration snapshot page | 8 MiB |
+| Control-plane message limit | 64 MiB |
+| Tokio workers: client and admin commands | single-threaded |
+
+The cluster-size limits in the README (1,024 members, 4,096 virtual nodes per
+member, 1,048,576 assignments, 16,384 moved ranges per change) keep topology
+and change snapshots under the 64 MiB control-plane message limit. The
+replica-obligation ceiling is 131,072, which covers the largest legal
+ten-member RF=3 topology (81,920 obligations).
+
+Density is expensive in practice. On a ten-node RF=3 cluster the coordinator's
+resident memory peaked at about 0.13 GB with 128 virtual nodes per member,
+1.4 GB at 1,000, 5.2 GB at 2,000, and 17 GB at 4,096, and a single-node change
+took about 107 s to publish at 1,000 virtual nodes while 2,000 and 4,096 did
+not publish within several minutes. Keep the default 128 unless a denser ring
+is worth that cost; see
+[acceptance-metrics.md](acceptance-metrics.md) for the measurements.
+
+## ACK policies and admission
+
+With the default write guard, owners use stream admissions carried in their
+leases and check the required applied ACKs against the admitted follower
+process identities. Explicit copy or health guards still query live replica
+status. See
+[replica ACK performance](optimizations/replica-ack-performance.md).
+
+Each deduplication receipt identifies one mutation and stores its key,
+operation fingerprint, assigned version, delete flag, and expiry.

+# Prune ACK progress when deduplication receipts expire
+
+## Change and reason
+
+`ack_progress` tracks follower acknowledgments by topology epoch and follower. Entries for an older epoch can be removed once no live deduplication receipt still needs them. Finding those live references requires scanning the receipt store and its required ACK lists.
+
+Previously, every call to `purge_expired_dedup` performed that scan, even when no receipt had expired. The mutation paths call expiry cleanup frequently, so sustained writes repeatedly scanned the same live receipts. [The implementation](../../crates/hashring-node/src/dedup.rs) now marks ACK progress for pruning only when a receipt is removed. It runs the scan at most once per second while that mark is set. Topology refresh still prunes after an epoch change ([replication cleanup](../../crates/hashring-node/src/replication.rs), [topology refresh](../../crates/hashring-node/src/service.rs)).
+
+This changes the usual mutation path from a scan over live receipts to a check of the expiry heap and a flag. It does not change when receipts expire or which acknowledgments are required for a write.
+
+## Evidence and limits
+
+- The [regression test](../../crates/hashring-node/src/tests/replication.rs) verifies that an old epoch's ACK progress remains until the deferred prune and is eventually removed.
+- The 1M-key performance run after this change passed at commit `3c58c54`: [summary](../../results/performance-1m-3c58c54/summary.json). The final run at `e809ce4` also passed: [summary](../../results/performance-1m-e809ce4/summary.json).
+- Neither run isolates the cost saved by this change. The first commit also raised the receipt store capacity, and the final run includes further changes. These results establish workload completion, not an attributable throughput gain from pruning.
+
+## Tradeoff
+
+After receipts expire, ACK progress for an old epoch can remain for up to roughly one second, and until the next expiry-cleanup call after that interval. This retains some small, stale bookkeeping temporarily in exchange for avoiding repeated scans. The current epoch's ACK progress is retained by the pruning rule regardless of this schedule.

-## The epoch atomic
-
-The delivery loop's epoch check, alone, was also reverted after measurement.
-
-**Setup.** This was a paired A/B of `main` against a build carrying the
-completion timing, the epoch atomic and lazy ACK completion. It ran in all
-four cells, with 4 pairs each after a warm-up pair.
-
-**Why `OwnerOnly` isolates it.** Under `OwnerOnly`, no write waits for ACKs, so
-lazy completion and its timing never run. In those cells, the epoch atomic is
-the only change that runs.
-
-| | `OwnerOnly`, 64 | `OwnerOnly`, 256 |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| ACK writeback wait | **+70%** [+42, +105], 4/4 pairs | **+46%** [+43, +50], 4/4 |
-| owner lock wait | −5.3% [−10.2, +0.2] | −3.5% [−7.3, +0.5] |
-| PUT ops/s | −0.1% [−4.0, +4.5] | −4.8% [−10.6, −0.2] |
-| client `Put` RPC mean | +0.1% | +6.7% [+1.2, +13.0] |
-
-**Ruling out batch size.** Replication batches shrank only 1-3%, so batching
-does not explain the ACK writeback increase.
-
-**Hypothesis, not tested.** tokio's `RwLock` is fair, so the removed read
-acquisition queued each delivery attempt behind waiting writers. That spread out
-the ACK writebacks that follow each RPC. Without it, writebacks arrive in step
-with owner write bursts.
-
-**`FirstSuccessor`.** The cumulative build was also worse than `main` in these
-cells: owner wait +11% at concurrency 256 in 4 of 4 pairs.
-
-Raw rows: [epoch-main-vs-lazy-runs.tsv](data/ack-state-lock/epoch-main-vs-lazy-runs.tsv)
-and [epoch-main-vs-lazy-host.txt](data/ack-state-lock/epoch-main-vs-lazy-host.txt).
-
-## Tradeoff and verdict
-
-As built, the split trades a small `OwnerOnly` lock improvement for a
-`FirstSuccessor` regression, with no measurable throughput change in either.
-It also adds a second lock and an ordering rule that every new call site must
-follow.
-
-Two directions followed from the data. The second was tried in
-[lazy-ack-completion.md](lazy-ack-completion.md) and gave no end-to-end gain:
-
-- **Keep owner writes off `AckState` while they hold `NodeState`.** Registering
-  `ack_progress` and the unacked send could move out of the state critical section,
-  but only if dispatch order still matches sequence order. Otherwise, do not split
-  the lock at all.
-- **Remove the second state write lock from ACK-waiting writes.**
-  `complete_required_acks` only clears a receipt's `required_acks` to release its
-  retained bytes. Doing that lazily, at expiry or on the next write to the
-  receipt, would leave one state acquisition per write under `FirstSuccessor`.
-
-The instrumentation part of this change, the timing of the formerly untimed
-completion site, is independent of the split and was kept.
-
-Sharding `records` is not supported by this data. Owner hold is 6-7 µs, and under
-`OwnerOnly` owner wait barely responds to removing a fifth of the acquisitions.

+The window is too short for throughput: loads took 0.26-0.48 s, and pairs swung
+from −24% to +21%.
+
+It agreed on the lock picture:
+- ACK wait fell 13× at concurrency 64 and 23× at 256.
+- Owner wait was unresolved.
+
+Raw rows: [correctness-ab.tsv](data/ack-state-lock/correctness-ab.tsv), with
+[correctness-ab.sh](data/ack-state-lock/correctness-ab.sh) and
+[extract.py](data/ack-state-lock/extract.py).
+
+## The epoch atomic
+
+The delivery loop's epoch check, alone, was also reverted after measurement.
+
+**Setup.** This was a paired A/B of `main` against a build carrying the
+completion timing, the epoch atomic and lazy ACK completion. It ran in all
+four cells, with 4 pairs each after a warm-up pair.
+
+**Why `OwnerOnly` isolates it.** Under `OwnerOnly`, no write waits for ACKs, so
+lazy completion and its timing never run. In those cells, the epoch atomic is
+the only change that runs.
+
+| | `OwnerOnly`, 64 | `OwnerOnly`, 256 |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| ACK writeback wait | **+70%** [+42, +105], 4/4 pairs | **+46%** [+43, +50], 4/4 |
+| owner lock wait | −5.3% [−10.2, +0.2] | −3.5% [−7.3, +0.5] |
+| PUT ops/s | −0.1% [−4.0, +4.5] | −4.8% [−10.6, −0.2] |
+| client `Put` RPC mean | +0.1% | +6.7% [+1.2, +13.0] |
+
+**Ruling out batch size.** Replication batches shrank only 1-3%, so batching
+does not explain the ACK writeback increase.
+
+**Hypothesis, not tested.** tokio's `RwLock` is fair, so the removed read
+acquisition queued each delivery attempt behind waiting writers. That spread out
+the ACK writebacks that follow each RPC. Without it, writebacks arrive in step
+with owner write bursts.
+
+**`FirstSuccessor`.** The cumulative build was also worse than `main` in these
+cells: owner wait +11% at concurrency 256 in 4 of 4 pairs.
+
+Raw rows: [epoch-main-vs-lazy-runs.tsv](data/ack-state-lock/epoch-main-vs-lazy-runs.tsv)
+and [epoch-main-vs-lazy-host.txt](data/ack-state-lock/epoch-main-vs-lazy-host.txt).
+
+## Tradeoff and verdict
+
+As built, the split trades a small `OwnerOnly` lock improvement for a
+`FirstSuccessor` regression, with no measurable throughput change in either.
+It also adds a second lock and an ordering rule that every new call site must
+follow.
+
+Two directions followed from the data. The second was tried in
+[lazy-ack-completion.md](lazy-ack-completion.md) and gave no end-to-end gain:
+
+- **Keep owner writes off `AckState` while they hold `NodeState`.** Registering
+  `ack_progress` and the unacked send could move out of the state critical section,
+  but only if dispatch order still matches sequence order. Otherwise, do not split
+  the lock at all.
+- **Remove the second state write lock from ACK-waiting writes.**
+  `complete_required_acks` only clears a receipt's `required_acks` to release its
+  retained bytes. Doing that lazily, at expiry or on the next write to the
+  receipt, would leave one state acquisition per write under `FirstSuccessor`.
+
+The instrumentation part of this change, the timing of the formerly untimed
+completion site, is independent of the split and was kept.
+
+Sharding `records` is not supported by this data. Owner hold is 6-7 µs, and under
+`OwnerOnly` owner wait barely responds to removing a fifth of the acquisitions.
+
+## Reproducing
+
+```sh
+git archive main | tar -x -C "$S/baseline-src"   # build each side in its own target dir
+mkdir -p "$S/bin"; cp <baseline>/release/hashring-rs "$S/bin/baseline"
+cp target/release/hashring-rs "$S/bin/branch"
+S="$S" REPS=8 caffeinate -i docs/optimizations/data/ack-state-lock/perf-ab.sh
+```

+# Batched replication RPCs
+
+The owner replicates each mutation to its desired followers through separate ordered
+streams. A stream is identified by `(topology epoch, owner, follower)` and has one
+delivery worker. Before this change that worker sent exactly one `ReplicationEntry`
+per `ReplicateMutation` RPC and waited for the follower's ACK before advancing. Each
+mutation therefore cost one round trip per follower, and a burst of N mutations to
+one follower cost N sequential RPCs.
+
+## Change
+
+Delivery now drains a contiguous run of queued entries for the stream and sends them
+in a single `ReplicateMutations(ReplicationBatch)` RPC. The follower applies the
+batch under one state write, in order, and reports the highest applied stream
+sequence. The batch is bounded by both a count (`REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_ENTRIES = 64`)
+and a byte budget (`REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_BYTES = MAX_DATA_MESSAGE_BYTES - 64 KiB`),
+so one batch always fits the data-node message limit.
+
+Entries that would exceed either bound are carried to the next batch instead of being
+dropped, so per-stream ordering — and therefore the follower's existing gap
+detection — is preserved.
+
+## Why it is a system optimization
+
+This is a real change to how the write path spends its RPC budget, not a tunable
+value:
+
+- **Fewer RPCs and round trips.** A run of K queued mutations becomes one RPC instead
+  of K. Round-trip latency no longer accumulates per mutation on a busy stream.
+- **Coalesced follower work.** The follower takes a single state write to apply a
+  whole batch, amortizing lock acquisition, dedup purge, and ACK-progress bookkeeping
+  across many mutations instead of redoing them per entry.
+- **Fewer ACK wakeups.** One response advances the stream's ack progress to the last
+  sequence in the batch, so required-ack waiters wake once per batch.
+
+Ordering, idempotency, and backpressure semantics are unchanged: the per-entry
+validation, fingerprint, dedup, and sequence checks are identical, applied in the
+same order. The single-entry `ReplicateMutation` RPC remains for compatibility with
+the existing tests and any single-entry callers.
+
+## Tradeoffs
+
+- A batch holds up to one batch-worth of entries off the per-stream channel while it
+  is in flight or retrying. The stream's queue depth still bounds queued entries, but
+  the effective in-flight backlog grows from one entry to one batch
+  (`REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_ENTRIES`). The backpressure test now asserts this wider but
+  still bounded limit.
+- A lost response can retry the whole batch. A received partial acknowledgement
+  advances the owner and retries only the suffix. The follower's dedup receipts
+  and fingerprint checks make re-delivery idempotent.
+- A batch is applied under a single write lock. The lock is held for the batch's
+  duration rather than one entry, but the total work per entry is unchanged and the
+  number of acquisitions drops.
+
+## Measured effect
+
+Instrumenting the follower's `ReplicateMutations` handler to count received entries
+and RPCs, over a correctness run of 20,000 keys at concurrency 64, RF=3,
+`OwnerOnly`, 128-byte values, 9 nodes:
+
+| | value |
+| --- | --- |
+| replication entries delivered | 40,000 |
+| `ReplicateMutations` RPCs | 31,357 |
+| **mean batch size** | **1.28** |
+| peak pending per stream | 7–20 (queue capacity 32) |
+
+The bounds are not the limiter: with 128-byte values each entry costs ~450 bytes, so
+64 entries is ~29 KB against a 9 MiB budget. The limiter is that `try_recv` usually
+finds the queue empty.
+
+Mean batch size is governed by `1 + arrival_rate x loop_time`. This workload offers
+~2,300 entries/s per stream and ~274 us per delivery-loop iteration, so ~0.6 entries
+arrive during one iteration. Neither `REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_ENTRIES` nor
+`REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_BYTES` changes that ratio; only a deliberate linger (paid for
+in added latency) or more concurrent producers per stream would.
+
+Consequence: the amortizations claimed above are real in mechanism but small in
+magnitude here. Follower state-write acquisitions fell only from 40,000 to 31,357
+(-21.6%), and ACK writebacks fell by the same 21.6%. At this workload's arrival rate
+the change removes roughly one RPC in five, not one in sixty-four. Throughput here is
+latency-bound per stream, not batch-bound, so this workload cannot show the
+change's ceiling. Re-measure with higher per-stream concurrency before drawing
+conclusions about the bound.
+
+## Source
+
+- `crates/hashring-core/proto/hashring.proto`: `ReplicationBatch`,
+  `ReplicateMutationsResponse`, and the `ReplicateMutations` RPC.
+- `crates/hashring-node/src/rpc.rs`: `apply_replication_entry` (shared per-entry
+  logic) and the `replicate_mutations` handler.
+- `crates/hashring-node/src/replication.rs`: `deliver_replication_stream` batch drain
+  and single-RPC send.
+- `crates/hashring-node/src/lib.rs`: `REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_ENTRIES`,
+  `REPLICATION_BATCH_MAX_BYTES`.
+- Tests: `follower_applies_a_replication_batch_in_order`,
+  `replication_batch_rejects_a_gap_between_entries` in
+  `crates/hashring-node/src/tests/replication.rs`.
+
+See also [replication-backpressure.md](replication-backpressure.md) for the queue and
+retained-byte limits this change builds on, and
+[state-write-lock-profile.md](state-write-lock-profile.md) for the measured wait and
+hold times of the three write paths this change touches.
+
+## Payload accounting and partial progress correction
+
+Batch payloads are materialized only after connecting and acquiring the aggregate
+RPC byte permits. The owned protobuf request is consumed by the RPC instead of
+keeping a second request across retries. Pending entries continue to share their
+original mutation and retained-byte reservation. The request future completes or
+is dropped on timeout before the active permits are released. Transport and
+allocator overhead still make this an accounting bound, not a process RSS cap.
+
+An isolated reproduction on macOS with 32 unreachable follower streams sharing
+one 8 MiB mutation measured 256,240 KiB of RSS growth before this correction,
+while all 64 MiB of active RPC permits remained available. The same reproduction
+afterwards measured 1,664 KiB. These are single-run measurements, not a general
+memory-overhead guarantee. Run the process-wide RSS check alone:
+
+```sh
+cargo test -p hashring-node unreachable_streams_do_not_copy_unbudgeted_payloads -- --ignored --nocapture
+```
+
+A follower now returns the applied prefix if a later entry fails. The owner
+publishes that acknowledgement, releases the corresponding pending entries, and
+retries only the remaining suffix with a recalculated byte reservation. A failure
+on the first remaining entry still follows the normal retryable/permanent status
+handling. A batch must name one stream so its single acknowledgement is unambiguous.
+The integration regression fills follower receipt capacity partway through a
+batch, verifies the prefix reaches owner acknowledgement progress, then frees
+capacity and verifies delivery of the suffix.
+
+## Batch size at moderate load
+
+A stream sends whatever queued during its previous round trip, which is one or
+two entries per batch at moderate load on one host.
+[replication-batch-linger.md](replication-batch-linger.md) lets a stream wait
+briefly to fill batches that no write is waiting on.

+# Wait for receipt store capacity before retrying
+
+## Change and reason
+
+An owner retains deduplication receipts for the 60-second receipt retention period. When the receipt store reaches its byte budget, another write cannot safely acquire a receipt, so the owner rejects it before applying the mutation. Repeating the request immediately cannot create capacity while the oldest receipts are still live.
+
+When the owner's receipt store is full, [the node](../../crates/hashring-node/src/service.rs) returns `retry_after_millis` based on the earliest receipt expiry ([calculation](../../crates/hashring-node/src/dedup.rs)). [The client](../../crates/hashring-client/src/lib.rs) waits for at least that hint on retryable `ResourceExhausted`, subject to its existing logical operation deadline. This aims to avoid requests that are unlikely to succeed before capacity returns. It does not extend the deadline or change the known-not-applied result when the deadline expires.
+
+The hint is sent for **owner receipt store capacity rejection**. Follower receipt store capacity rejection and replication reservation backpressure do not currently supply this timing hint. Other `ResourceExhausted` errors continue to use the client's ordinary backoff when the hint is zero.
+
+## Evidence and limits
+
+- The [owner capacity test](../../crates/hashring-node/src/tests/migration.rs) checks that a rejected write has a positive hint and remains unapplied. The [client test](../../crates/hashring-client/src/lib.rs) checks that a hint longer than the remaining deadline yields a deadline error with `KnownNotApplied`.
+- In the instrumented 1M-key run at `b4f6c41`, one node recorded 73 owner receipt store capacity rejections and the run completed: [summary](../../results/performance-1m-b4f6c41/summary.json). This shows the client can recover from saturation in that workload; the summary does not count hint-driven waits or establish how many retries they saved.
+- The final 1M-key run at `e809ce4` recorded zero owner receipt store capacity rejections: [summary](../../results/performance-1m-e809ce4/summary.json). It therefore does not measure the hint's effect.
+
+## Tradeoff
+
+The hint is an estimate based on the earliest retained expiry, not a reservation of future capacity. Other writes can use capacity first; the client may still retry and be rejected. Waiting longer can reduce request pressure but also consume more of the caller's operation deadline, so a short-deadline operation may fail without another attempt. The separate receipt store capacity increase on this branch is a sizing choice, not this optimization.

+# CPU profile: where the time actually goes
+
+Captured with `scripts/flamegraph.sh` (`perf record -F 99 --call-graph dwarf,8192`).
+Correctness mode, 20,000 keys, concurrency 64, RF=3, `OwnerOnly`, 128-byte values,
+9 data nodes plus a coordinator and a driver on a 24-core AMD Ryzen 9 7845HX.
+46.5 s of wall time, 13,507 samples, 1.78% sample loss.
+
+Self time below is `perf report --no-children`, which reads the sampled IP
+directly and is therefore independent of call-graph quality. Kernel frames are
+grouped by symbol prefix; the two entries marked "unclassified" are spinlocks,
+RCU, and list traversal that fall outside the named buckets.
+
+That independence is not a stylistic choice. This capture predates the
+frame-pointer build and its call graph was truncated: 91.5% of its samples
+carried no Rust frame, so the rendered graph was `comm` -> libc -> kernel and
+could only be read as symbol self time. `scripts/flamegraph.sh` now builds
+`target/fp` with `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` and reads the graph with `fp`. In a
+capture taken that way, 99.0% of user-side samples reach project code and carry
+8-33 frames each. The numbers below are unaffected either way.
+
+## Where the time goes
+
+| | share |
+| --- | --- |
+| user space (`hashring-rs` + libc + vdso) | 65.96% |
+| kernel | 29.17% |
+| *(below the 0.01% report floor)* | ~1.5% |
+
+User space splits further:
+
+| | share of profile |
+| --- | --- |
+| allocator (`alloc`/`free`/`realloc`, incl. libc) | 11.18% |
+| `Vec::from_iter` / `collect` | 5.41% |
+| `Clone::clone` | 2.10% |
+| memcpy / `put_slice` | 0.44% |
+
+Kernel:
+
+| | share of profile |
+| --- | --- |
+| scheduler (wakeup, load balance, runqueue) | 4.17% |
+| SRSO / retpoline mitigation (`srso_*`, `entry_SYSRETQ`, `entry_SYSCALL_64`) | 3.65% |
+| page zeroing (`clear_pages`, `copy_folio_from_iter_atomic`) | 2.44% |
+| futex | 1.26% |
+| interrupts and timer | 1.20% |
+| network stack (TCP/IP/skb) | ~3.1% |
+| epoll | 0.36% |
+| netfilter (conntrack, nftables) | 0.10% |
+
+## Reading
+
+The shape is flat. No single symbol exceeds 2.4% self time, and the top-30 list
+is dominated by allocator and `Vec` machinery rather than any application
+function. That is itself the main finding: **there is no hot spot to fix, only
+a broad allocation and syscall floor.**
+
+Three things follow that are worth acting on.
+
+- **Allocation is the single largest addressable cost at ~19% of the profile**
+  (allocator + `from_iter` + `clone`). `Vec::from_iter` at 5.41% is the largest
+  individual symbol at 3.35%. The allocator pressure traces back to repeated
+  `Vec`/`String` construction on the RPC path rather than to one caller.
+- **`TopologySnapshot::key_token` costs 3.01% self.** It is only
+  `xxh3_64_with_seed`, which is fast, but `put` computes it twice: once inside
+  `owner_error` (`service.rs:503` calls `topology.owner`, which calls
+  `key_token`) and again at `rpc.rs:356`. Computing it once per request and
+  threading it through is a small, local change.
+- **Kernel time is mostly fixed overhead.** Of 29.17%, SRSO/retpoline (3.65%)
+  and page zeroing (2.44%) are environment and allocator costs that no
+  application change removes. Scheduler + futex (5.43%) is the only kernel
+  bucket that responds to reducing work, and it is small.
+
+`btree::search` at 1.61% is the `partition_point` inside
+`replica_node_ids_for_token` and `owner_for_token`. With 128 virtual nodes per
+member the `assignments` slice is short, so this is call volume rather than
+log-depth.
+
+## What this profile cannot answer
+
+The run used only 1.5 cores of 24 (52.7 s user + 19.2 s system over 47.7 s
+wall). The system is latency-bound, not CPU-bound. Per this capture,
+throughput work that removes CPU will not show up as wall-clock improvement;
+only work that removes a **round trip** or a **lock wait** will.
+
+Kernel-side samples carry no user stack (perf records a DWARF user stack only
+when the sampled IP is in user space), so the 29.17% kernel time cannot be
+attributed to a Rust caller from this data. In particular the futex total of
+1.26% here cannot be split between runtime worker wakeups, the node state
+write lock, and gRPC's own parking.
+
+A renderer warning worth repeating: the emitted SVG is an **inverted** flame
+graph. `all` is at the bottom and leaves at the top, so a frame's children are
+at `y-16`. Reading it as a normal flame graph produces self times that sum to
+8x the root.
+
+## Reproducing
+
+```sh
+cat > /tmp/experiment_cpu_profile.yaml <<'YAML'
+mode: correctness
+nodes: 10
+keys: 20000
+concurrency: 64
+policy: owner-only
+YAML
+CONFIG=/tmp/experiment_cpu_profile.yaml ./scripts/flamegraph.sh
+```
+
+The script profiles whatever `experiment` runs, so it needs a settings file;
+`examples/experiment.yaml` is its default. This capture used the flag defaults
+listed above, so it needs its own file. The
+manifest in `<out>/run/` records what was actually resolved.
+
+The script runs `cargo build` for its own frame-pointer `target/fp` binary on
+every run (a no-op when it is current) and never touches `target/release`, so
+no separate build is needed first. Measure
+with one build and profile with the other: frame pointers cost throughput.
+
+Check `perf-record.log` in the output directory for sample loss before trusting
+the graph. Aggregate self time with:
+
+```sh
+perf report -i <out>/perf.data --stdio --no-children --percent-limit 0.01 \
+  --sort dso,symbol -F overhead,dso,symbol
+```
+
+See also [frame-pointer-profiling.md](frame-pointer-profiling.md) for why this
+capture's call graph was truncated and what the script does about it,
+[state-write-lock-profile.md](state-write-lock-profile.md) for the
+`HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES` lock wait/hold counters, which measure the latency
+side that this CPU profile cannot see, and
+[batched-replication-rpc.md](batched-replication-rpc.md) for why the follower
+path takes fewer state writes than there are replicated entries.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Interleaved A/B of baseline (main) vs branch (ack-state-lock) on the
+# correctness run's initial load. Run from the hashring-rs repo root.
+set -uo pipefail
+S="${S:?set S to a directory holding bin/baseline, bin/branch and extract.py}"
+REPS="${REPS:-5}"
+CONCS="${CONCS:-64 256}"
+OUT="$S/ab-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
+mkdir -p "$OUT"
+TSV="$OUT/ab.tsv"
+printf "conc\trep\tvariant\tput_s\tresv_rej\trpc_retry\towner_acq\towner_hold_ns\towner_wait_ns\tfoll_acq\tfoll_hold_ns\tfoll_wait_ns\tack_acq\tack_hold_ns\tack_wait_ns\tackc_acq\tackc_hold_ns\tackc_wait_ns\n" > "$TSV"
+for c in $CONCS; do
+  for r in $(seq 1 "$REPS"); do
+    # ABBA: alternate which variant goes first so drift does not favor one.
+    if (( r % 2 )); then order="baseline branch"; else order="branch baseline"; fi
+    for v in $order; do
+      d="$OUT/$c-$r-$v"
+      HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1 "$S/bin/$v" experiment \
+        --mode correctness --concurrency "$c" --output "$d" > "$d.log" 2>&1
+      status=$?
+      if [[ -f "$d/events.jsonl" ]]; then
+        row=$(python3 -I "$S/extract.py" "$d/events.jsonl")
+        printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n" "$c" "$r" "$v" "$row" >> "$TSV"
+        echo "conc=$c rep=$r $v exit=$status put_s=$(echo "$row" | cut -f1)"
+      else
+        echo "conc=$c rep=$r $v exit=$status NO EVENTS (see $d.log)"
+      fi
+    done
+  done
+done
+echo "raw: $TSV"

+import json, sys
+put_s, nodes = None, {}
+for line in open(sys.argv[1]):
+    e = json.loads(line)
+    if e['event'] == 'initial_put_complete' and put_s is None:
+        put_s = e['fields']['seconds']
+    elif e['event'] == 'node_pressure_sampled' and not nodes:
+        nodes = e['fields']['nodes']  # first sample: right after the initial load
+def tot(k): return sum((n.get(k) or 0) for n in nodes.values())
+def timing(p):
+    g = lambda f: sum(((n.get(p) or {}).get(f) or 0) for n in nodes.values())
+    return [g('acquisitions'), g('hold_nanos'), g('wait_nanos')]
+row = [put_s, tot('replication_reservation_rejections'), tot('replication_rpc_retries')]
+for p in ['owner_write_timing', 'follower_write_timing', 'ack_write_timing', 'ack_completion_write_timing']:
+    row += timing(p)
+print('\t'.join(str(x) for x in row))

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Performance-mode A/B of baseline (main 30b19dc) vs branch (ack-state-lock).
+# Workload matches the 6-node series in docs/optimizations/grpc-io-bottleneck.md
+# and replication-batch-linger.md: performance mode, 6 nodes, seed 1, 300k keys,
+# RF=3, 2 ms linger, default workers. Both profilers on (phase C had RPC, phase E
+# had writes). Rep 0 is a warm-up pair, excluded from analysis.
+# Run from the hashring-rs repo root, under caffeinate.
+set -u
+S="${S:?set S to a directory holding bin/baseline and bin/branch}"
+REPS="${REPS:-8}"
+OUT="${OUT:-$S/perf-ab-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)}"
+mkdir -p "$OUT"
+LOG="$OUT/host.log"
+CELLS=(OO-64 OO-256 FS-64 FS-256)
+flags() {
+  case "$1" in
+    OO-64)  echo "--policy owner-only --concurrency 64" ;;
+    OO-256) echo "--policy owner-only --concurrency 256" ;;
+    FS-64)  echo "--policy first-successor --concurrency 64" ;;
+    FS-256) echo "--policy first-successor --concurrency 256" ;;
+  esac
+}
+start=$(date +%s)
+for rep in $(seq 0 "$REPS"); do
+  # Rotate cell order each rep so drift spreads across cells.
+  n=${#CELLS[@]}
+  for k in $(seq 0 $((n - 1))); do
+    cell=${CELLS[$(( (k + rep) % n ))]}
+    # Alternate which variant runs first, per rep and cell.
+    if (( (rep + k) % 2 )); then order="branch baseline"; else order="baseline branch"; fi
+    for v in $order; do
+      {
+        printf "%s rep=%s cell=%s variant=%s load=%s backupd=%s\n" \
+          "$(date '+%H:%M:%S')" "$rep" "$cell" "$v" \
+          "$(sysctl -n vm.loadavg)" "$(pgrep -x backupd >/dev/null && echo running || echo idle)"
+      } >> "$LOG"
+      BIN="$S/bin/$v" PROFILE_WRITES=1 HASHRING_PROFILE_RPC=1 \
+        scripts/perf/run.sh "$OUT" "$cell-$v" "$rep" --keys 300000 $(flags "$cell")
+    done
+  done
+done
+python3 -I scripts/perf/collect.py "$OUT" > /dev/null
+echo "total wall: $(( $(date +%s) - start ))s"
+echo "runs: $OUT/runs.tsv"
+echo "host log: $LOG"

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Focused A/B: main (30b19dc) vs fix (0c6c9af: timing + lazy required-ACK completion), FirstSuccessor only.
+# Workload matches the 6-node series in docs/optimizations/grpc-io-bottleneck.md
+# and replication-batch-linger.md: performance mode, 6 nodes, seed 1, 300k keys,
+# RF=3, 2 ms linger, default workers. Both profilers on (phase C had RPC, phase E
+# had writes). Rep 0 is a warm-up pair, excluded from analysis.
+# Run from the hashring-rs repo root, under caffeinate.
+set -u
+S="${S:?set S to a directory holding bin/main and bin/fix}"
+REPS="${REPS:-4}"
+OUT="${OUT:-$S/main-fix-ab-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)}"
+mkdir -p "$OUT"
+LOG="$OUT/host.log"
+CELLS=(FS-64 FS-256)
+flags() {
+  case "$1" in
+    OO-64)  echo "--policy owner-only --concurrency 64" ;;
+    OO-256) echo "--policy owner-only --concurrency 256" ;;
+    FS-64)  echo "--policy first-successor --concurrency 64" ;;
+    FS-256) echo "--policy first-successor --concurrency 256" ;;
+  esac
+}
+start=$(date +%s)
+for rep in $(seq 0 "$REPS"); do
+  # Rotate cell order each rep so drift spreads across cells.
+  n=${#CELLS[@]}
+  for k in $(seq 0 $((n - 1))); do
+    cell=${CELLS[$(( (k + rep) % n ))]}
+    # Alternate which variant runs first, per rep and cell.
+    if (( (rep + k) % 2 )); then order="fix main"; else order="main fix"; fi
+    for v in $order; do
+      {
+        printf "%s rep=%s cell=%s variant=%s load=%s backupd=%s\n" \
+          "$(date '+%H:%M:%S')" "$rep" "$cell" "$v" \
+          "$(sysctl -n vm.loadavg)" "$(pgrep -x backupd >/dev/null && echo running || echo idle)"
+      } >> "$LOG"
+      BIN="$S/bin/$v" PROFILE_WRITES=1 HASHRING_PROFILE_RPC=1 \
+        scripts/perf/run.sh "$OUT" "$cell-$v" "$rep" --keys 300000 $(flags "$cell")
+    done
+  done
+done
+python3 -I scripts/perf/collect.py "$OUT" > /dev/null
+echo "total wall: $(( $(date +%s) - start ))s"
+echo "runs: $OUT/runs.tsv"
+echo "host log: $LOG"

+  done
+done
+echo done

--- a/docs/optimizations/dedup-receipt-store-memory.md
+++ b/docs/optimizations/dedup-receipt-store-memory.md
@@ -1,84 +1,84 @@
-# Deduplication receipt store memory layout and accounting
-
-Each node retains deduplication receipts for 60 seconds so retries can reuse the assigned version without applying the mutation again, and migration can carry live receipts to a new owner. The owner and followers each keep their own receipts. The byte budget is admission accounting for these receipts, not a process-wide RSS limit.
-
-## Changes
-
-- A live receipt's mutation ID is now one `Arc<str>` allocation shared by the lookup map and expiration heap. Migration snapshot preparation also clones the shared ID handle instead of allocating another string for every captured receipt. The external mutation ID remains a string; callers do not need to use UUIDs.
-- After the required followers have acknowledged a write and the owner lease is still valid, the owner drops that receipt's follower/sequence requirements and releases their budget charge. An incomplete or timed-out ACK wait keeps them so a retry can wait for the original ACKs. The fingerprint, key, version, delete flag, and expiration remain available for the full receipt retention period.
-- Live receipts and staged migration receipts now have separate byte estimates. The former estimate included the sizes of `DeduplicationRecord` and `StagedDedup`, although neither object is stored in a live receipt. With that double charge removed, the default live receipt budget is 128 MiB again, down from 256 MiB. This accounting correction admits more receipts; by itself it does not reduce physical memory.
-
-See [the live receipt and expiration logic](../../crates/hashring-node/src/dedup.rs), [the ACK completion path](../../crates/hashring-node/src/service.rs), and [the migration snapshot path](../../crates/hashring-node/src/rpc.rs).
-
-On the measured 64-bit target, `String` occupies 24 bytes and `Arc<str>` 16 bytes; the expiration tuple shrinks from 40 to 32 bytes. For a 36-byte client UUID, sharing the ID saves a nominal 36 bytes per live receipt plus one allocation, before allocator rounding and map capacity. This is a per-receipt layout saving, not a promise about whole-process RSS.
-
-## Evidence
-
-The node tests check that the lookup map and expiration heap share the same ID allocation, that successful ACKs release their metadata while preserving the receipt, and that a timed-out ACK leaves its requirements available for a later retry. The existing migration tests exercise snapshot transfer and expiry with the new ID handle.
-
-Two local release runs used the 10-node, RF=3, 1M-key performance profile with owner-only ACKs. The old binary was rebuilt from an isolated archive of `e809ce4`; its source-tree hash matches the earlier `e809ce4` build. Each run sampled child-process RSS with `ps` every 0.5 seconds. The full local artifacts are under `results/memory-baseline-isolated-e809ce4/` and `results/memory-optimized-128m/` (ignored by Git).
-
-| Build | Initial PUT time | Highest receipt-budget charge | Receipt cap | Highest sampled node RSS | Receipt rejections |
-| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
-| `e809ce4` | 74.4 s | 179.5 MiB | 256 MiB | 249.1 MiB | 0 |
-| Optimized working tree | 87.7 s | 71.6 MiB | 128 MiB | 268.8 MiB | 0 |
-

-# Constant-time acknowledgment dedup in the fault window
-
-## Change and reason
-
-`experiment --mode fault` keeps, per key, the states it has acknowledged, so a read that matches one of them but not the key's current state can be classified as a permitted rollback instead of as a value the history never held. A re-acknowledged state moves to the back of the window rather than taking a second slot: a duplicate would push a distinct state out early, and the window exists to keep the recent ones.
-
-`KeyModel::remember` found out whether the state was already there by scanning the window on every write, so the load's write path cost `writes × window` digest comparisons per key. [`--fault-acknowledged-window`](../configuration.md) is sized as a multiple of the writes one key takes, so a long run grows that product quadratically: 10,000 writes per key with a 40,000-state window is about 400 million comparisons per key.
-
-The model now keeps an index of the window's states as 64-bit fingerprints with a count each ([fault.rs](../../crates/hashring-experiment/src/fault.rs)). Acknowledging a state the window has never held is one lookup plus a `push_back`. Only a state the window already holds — a re-acknowledgement, rare in the fault load, whose values are derived from the request — scans for its position and moves it to the back.
-
-## Evidence and limits
-
-- The [unit test](../../crates/hashring-experiment/src/fault.rs) drives new writes, re-acknowledgements of states still in the window, and re-acknowledgements of states the window already dropped. It asserts after every step that the counts add up to the window's length and that every state in the order is indexed.
-- Nothing changes about which reads are verifiable: the window's contents, order, and dropped count are the same, so the classification of a read is unaffected.
-- No throughput difference is measurable at the documented sizes. The window fills only to the writes one key takes (about 200 in the default owner run), and the audit runs on `177387b` measured 6,736 against 6,678 requests per second when the limit rose from 256 to 4,096, inside the run-to-run variation. The gain is asymptotic, for runs that fill a window much larger than a few hundred states.
-- A [white-box test](../../crates/hashring-experiment/src/fault.rs) injects a fingerprint that another state already has and acknowledges a state under it. The state has to enter the window (a read of it is a rollback, not an impossible value) and has to leave the other state's count in place when the window evicts it, which is why the index counts fingerprints instead of storing a set of them.
-
-## Tradeoff
-
-The fingerprint index adds about 25 B per state on top of the 66 B digest pair (an 8-byte key, an 8-byte count, and hash-table overhead), so the driver's bound is roughly 95 B per state and `keys × window × ~95 B` overall (see the [fault document](../fault-under-load.md#历史模型)). Hashing the state per write is cheaper than the scan it replaces but not free; it is the price of not storing a second copy of the state in the index.
-
-A re-acknowledgement still scans the window once. +## Change and reason

+
+`KeyModel::remember` found out whether the state was already there by scanning the window on every write, so the load's write path cost `writes × window` digest comparisons per key. +
+The model now keeps an index of the window's states as 64-bit fingerprints with a count each ([fault.rs](../../crates/hashring-experiment/src/fault.rs)). Acknowledging a state the window has never held is one lookup plus a `push_back`. Only a state the window already holds — a re-acknowledgement, rare in the fault load, whose values are derived from the request — scans for its position and moves it to the back.
+
+## Evidence and limits
+
+- The [unit test](../../crates/hashring-experiment/src/fault.rs) drives new writes, re-acknowledgements of states still in the window, and re-acknowledgements of states the window already dropped. +- A [white-box test](../../crates/hashring-experiment/src/fault.rs) injects a fingerprint that another state already has and acknowledges a state under it. The state has to enter the window (a read of it is a rollback, not an impossible value) and has to leave the other state's count in place when the window evicts it, which is why the index counts fingerprints instead of storing a set of them.
+
+## Tradeoff
+

-# Frame-pointer profiling: why the flame graph was empty
-
-## What was wrong
-
-`scripts/flamegraph.sh` captured `perf record --call-graph dwarf,8192` against
-`target/release/hashring-rs` and rendered the result. The graph looked plausible
-— thousands of folded stacks, 46-58 frames deep — and was unreadable as
-evidence about this project.
-
-A performance-mode capture on a 24-core AMD Ryzen 9 7845HX, 20 nodes, RF=3,
-`FirstSuccessor`, 1M keys, 102.8 s, 57,268 samples, **0 lost**:
-
-| samples with N project frames | share |
-| --- | --- |
-| 0 | 91.5% |
-| 1 | 2.3% |
-| 2 | 1.8% |
-| 3+ | 0.1% |
-
-The graph was `comm` -> `libc` -> kernel. The heaviest single folded stack:
-
-```
-tokio-rt-worker
-writev
-syscall_cancel
-internal_syscall_cancel
-[libc.so.6]
-entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe
-do_syscall_64
-...
-__ip_local_out
-nf_hook_slow
-[[nf_conntrack]]
-```
-
-Unwinding stopped exactly at the libc boundary. The kernel part still unwound
-fine, which is what made the failure easy to miss: the SVG had real depth and no
-project code in it.
-
-## Why
-
-Two assumptions, one of them wrong.
-
-**"Rust omits frame pointers, so `--call-graph fp` truncates; keep DWARF."**
-This was in the script header and is backwards on this host. A default
-`rustc -O` build yields one-frame stacks under *both* methods.
-
-**"The binary has unwind tables, so DWARF can walk it."** It does, and it still
-does not work: `.eh_frame` is 1,070,560 bytes for a 10,220,433-byte `.text`, and
-a 30-line repro has 551 FDEs for 578 functions. The coverage is fine; perf's
-DWARF unwinder does not use it here.
-
-## Measurement
-
-A 30-line busy loop, `rustc 1.93.0 (254b59607 2026-01-19)`, one core, 99 Hz.
-The metric is the share of samples carrying at least two Rust frames, which is
-what a caller needs to attribute CPU to a code path:
-
-| build | `--call-graph fp` | `--call-graph dwarf,8192` |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| `rustc -O` (default) | **0.0%** | **1.1%** |
-| `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` | **94.5%** | **93.8%** |
-| `-C force-unwind-tables=yes` | n/a | **0.0%** |
-
-Three facts follow.
-
-- **Frame pointers are the only thing that works.** They fix both call-graph
-  modes. DWARF is not a workaround for their absence; it fails the same way.
-- **`force-unwind-tables` is not the answer.** It changes nothing measurable
-  here and `.eh_frame` is byte-identical to the default build.
-- **`fp` is then strictly better than `dwarf`.** Once frames are on the stack,
-  the frame-pointer walk is cheaper and sidesteps the ring-buffer limit below.
-
-Raw artifacts: `/tmp/opencode/fptest/` on this host (not kept; rerun the table
-to reproduce).
-
-## Tradeoffs
-
-- **Frame pointers cost throughput.** RBP becomes a callee-saved register.
-  Measurements here are single-digit percent and workload-dependent, so treat
-  the number as unmeasured: measure with `target/release`, profile with
-  `target/fp`, and never ship the profiling build.
-- **A separate build costs disk and a cold rebuild.** `target/fp` is a full
-  dependency tree. `scripts/flamegraph.sh` runs `cargo build` for it on every
-  run (a no-op when it is current) and leaves `target/release` alone.
-- **FP unwinding is unsound through hand-written assembly and some libc
-  frames.** Those frames resolve wrong or stop the walk. That is the same
-  failure the old capture had, at a much smaller scale, and it is why the script
-  now reports the share of samples that reached project code instead of relying
-  on the graph looking reasonable.
-- **`fp` records 16 bytes per frame**, so perf's per-CPU ring buffer
-  (`perf_event_mlock_kb`, 516 KB shared over 24 CPUs, ~22 KB each) stops being
-  the constraint. The DWARF path it replaces lost 12.33% of samples at a
-  64000-byte stack and 0.4% at 8192, for the same run length.
-
-## Result

+# Frame-pointer profiling: why the flame graph was empty
+
+## What was wrong
+
+`scripts/flamegraph.sh` captured `perf record --call-graph dwarf,8192` against
+`target/release/hashring-rs` and rendered the result. The graph looked plausible
+— thousands of folded stacks, 46-58 frames deep — and was unreadable as
+evidence about this project.
+
+A performance-mode capture on a 24-core AMD Ryzen 9 7845HX, 20 nodes, RF=3,
+`FirstSuccessor`, 1M keys, 102.8 s, 57,268 samples, **0 lost**:
+
+| samples with N project frames | share |
+| --- | --- |
+| 0 | 91.5% |
+| 1 | 2.3% |
+| 2 | 1.8% |
+| 3+ | 0.1% |
+
+The graph was `comm` -> `libc` -> kernel. The heaviest single folded stack:
+
+```
+tokio-rt-worker
+writev
+syscall_cancel
+internal_syscall_cancel
+[libc.so.6]
+entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe
+do_syscall_64
+...
+__ip_local_out
+nf_hook_slow
+[[nf_conntrack]]
+```
+
+Unwinding stopped exactly at the libc boundary. The kernel part still unwound
+fine, which is what made the failure easy to miss: the SVG had real depth and no
+project code in it.
+
+## Why
+
+Two assumptions, one of them wrong.
+
+**"Rust omits frame pointers, so `--call-graph fp` truncates; keep DWARF."**
+This was in the script header and is backwards on this host. A default
+`rustc -O` build yields one-frame stacks under *both* methods.
+
+**"The binary has unwind tables, so DWARF can walk it."** It does, and it still
+does not work: `.eh_frame` is 1,070,560 bytes for a 10,220,433-byte `.text`, and
+a 30-line repro has 551 FDEs for 578 functions. The coverage is fine; perf's
+DWARF unwinder does not use it here.
+
+## Measurement
+
+A 30-line busy loop, `rustc 1.93.0 (254b59607 2026-01-19)`, one core, 99 Hz.
+The metric is the share of samples carrying at least two Rust frames, which is
+what a caller needs to attribute CPU to a code path:
+
+| build | `--call-graph fp` | `--call-graph dwarf,8192` |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `rustc -O` (default) | **0.0%** | **1.1%** |
+| `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` | **94.5%** | **93.8%** |
+| `-C force-unwind-tables=yes` | n/a | **0.0%** |
+
+Three facts follow.
+
+- **Frame pointers are the only thing that works.** They fix both call-graph
+  modes. DWARF is not a workaround for their absence; it fails the same way.
+- **`force-unwind-tables` is not the answer.** It changes nothing measurable
+  here and `.eh_frame` is byte-identical to the default build.
+- **`fp` is then strictly better than `dwarf`.** Once frames are on the stack,
+  the frame-pointer walk is cheaper and sidesteps the ring-buffer limit below.
+
+Raw artifacts: `/tmp/opencode/fptest/` on this host (not kept; rerun the table
+to reproduce).
+
+## Tradeoffs
+
+- **Frame pointers cost throughput.** RBP becomes a callee-saved register.
+  Measurements here are single-digit percent and workload-dependent, so treat
+  the number as unmeasured: measure with `target/release`, profile with
+  `target/fp`, and never ship the profiling build.
+- **A separate build costs disk and a cold rebuild.** `target/fp` is a full
+  dependency tree. `scripts/flamegraph.sh` runs `cargo build` for it on every
+  run (a no-op when it is current) and leaves `target/release` alone.
+- **FP unwinding is unsound through hand-written assembly and some libc
+  frames.** Those frames resolve wrong or stop the walk. That is the same
+  failure the old capture had, at a much smaller scale, and it is why the script
+  now reports the share of samples that reached project code instead of relying
+  on the graph looking reasonable.
+- **`fp` records 16 bytes per frame**, so perf's per-CPU ring buffer
+  (`perf_event_mlock_kb`, 516 KB shared over 24 CPUs, ~22 KB each) stops being
+  the constraint. The DWARF path it replaces lost 12.33% of samples at a
+  64000-byte stack and 0.4% at 8192, for the same run length.
+
+## Result
+
+`scripts/flamegraph.sh` now builds `target/fp/release/hashring-rs` with
+`-C force-frame-pointers=yes`, records with `--call-graph fp`, and prints the
+share of folded weight carrying a project frame. A capture taken that way:
+
+- user-side samples: 99.0% carry at least two project frames, 8-33 frames deep;
+- 29.6% of all samples reach project code, the rest being kernel-side IPs, for
+  which perf records no user stack at all;
+- `perf.data` shrank from 500 MB to 952 KB for a comparable run.
+
+The script prints a warning on stderr, without failing, when that share drops
+below 5%, which is where a truncated capture lands (1.8%) and where a working
+one does not.
+
+The 29.6% and 1.8% shares were computed by the first version of that check,
+which tested the process-name field as if it were a frame (so the main thread's
+`hashring-rs` counted as project code), never tested the leaf frame, and read a
+zero weight for any stack whose leaf symbol contains a space. They were not
+recomputed after the parser was fixed and may be off in either direction; the
+1.8% also sits oddly against the 8.5% of samples with at least one project
+frame in the table at the top.
+
+## What the profile then said
+
+The 20261014 performance capture, read as symbol self time since its stacks were
+unusable, is in [cpu-profile-write-path.md](cpu-profile-write-path.md) for the
+correctness profile. Its shape: 52.6% `hashring-rs`, 10.3% libc, 35.3% kernel,
+no symbol above 1.63%. On the performance profile the dominant cost is the
+transport, not the store — HTTP/2, hyper and tonic 26.68%, loopback TCP 9.13%,
+netfilter 1.37%, and redb at 0.01%. A put costs 2.32 Mcycles against 0.35 Mcycles
+for a get, and the nodes hold 83% of it while the coordinator holds about 2%.
+
+## Reproducing
+
+```sh
+./scripts/flamegraph.sh performance
+```
+
+Read the printed `N% of samples carry a hashring frame` line before reading the
+graph. Below ~5%, the capture is unusable and `perf report --no-children` on
+`perf.data` is the only honest readout.

+# The latency mode's sender cannot use a runtime timer
+
+The `latency` mode measures the latency of a load that is offered at a fixed
+rate. Every request's latency starts at the moment it was **due**, not at the
+moment it was sent, so a slow cluster cannot hide its tail behind a delayed
+send. That makes the sender's own timing part of the measurement: if the
+sender wakes up late, every request carries that delay, and the number the
+run reports is the sender's delay plus the cluster's.
+
+The first version of the sender used `tokio::time::sleep_until`, one sleep per
+request. It produced numbers that were plausible and wrong: at 500 operations
+per second it reported a p50 of 1493 us for a `GET`, and the p50 barely moved
+between 200 and 20000 operations per second. The cluster's round trip is
+tens of microseconds, so a p50 of 1493 us was the sender, not the cluster.
+
+## What the timer does
+
+Measured on this host, 200 sleeps per interval, the overshoot of each wake-up
+against the deadline it was given:
+
+| Wait | interval | p50 | p90 | max |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `tokio::time::sleep_until` | 50 us | 847 us | 1297 us | 1604 us |
+| `tokio::time::sleep_until` | 1 ms | 733 us | 1156 us | 2116 us |
+| `tokio::time::sleep_until` | 5 ms | 762 us | 1162 us | 1252 us |
+| `std::thread::sleep` | 50 us | 52 us | 53 us | 57 us |
+| `std::thread::sleep` | 5 ms | 56 us | 64 us | 412 us |
+| `std::thread::sleep` + spin | 50 us | 0 us | 0 us | 67 us |
+| `std::thread::sleep` + spin | 5 ms | 0 us | 0 us | 660 us |
+
+The runtime timer is a millisecond-granularity wheel, so its wake-up is late
+by about three quarters of a millisecond whatever the deadline was. The
+kernel's own timer is late by about 50 us, and a spin for the last few
+microseconds removes even that.
+
+The overshoot does not accumulate: the sender sleeps until the **absolute**
+deadline of the next request, so a late wake-up does not push the schedule
+forward. That is why the offered rate was right and only the latency was
+wrong. At a 50 us interval the rate itself is off by 6%, because there the
+overshoot is a fifth of the interval.
+
+## What the sender does now
+
+The sender runs on a thread of its own, outside the runtime, and waits against
+the wall clock in two parts: a sleep that ends a little before the deadline,
+and a spin for the rest. The margin is the overshoot the last sleep showed,
+plus 20 us, so the spin stays short whatever the host's timer does. A request
+is handed to the runtime only once it is due, and the runtime's own wake-up
+then adds its few microseconds to the request's latency.
+
+The cost of the spin is bounded by the margin, not by the interval, so it is
+about 20 us per request: a fifth of a core at 10000 operations per second.
+
+## What it bought
+
+The same run, 3 nodes, 128-byte values, `GET:PUT:DELETE` of `90:9:1`:
+
+| | p50 `GET` | p99 `GET` | max `GET` |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| runtime timer | 1493 us | 2223 us | 2767 us |
+| dedicated thread | 142 us | 589 us | 1642 us |
+
+The p50 fell by a factor of ten and the number now means something: the
+latencies a cluster is judged by are tens of microseconds, and an instrument
+that is a millisecond late cannot measure them.
+
+The rule this leaves behind: a measurement that resolves microseconds needs a
+clock that is not a millisecond wide, and the cost of that clock is part of
+the measurement budget.
+
+## Trade-offs
+
+- The sender needs a thread of its own, so a phase cannot be driven from a
+  plain async task. The requests themselves still run on the runtime.
+- The spin holds a core for a few microseconds per request. At 10000
+  operations per second that is about a fifth of a core, and it competes with
+  the nodes for the host, which is the same tradeoff every accurate load
+  generator makes.
+- The margin adapts to the host's timer, so the sender behaves the same on a
+  host with a coarse timer and on one with a fine timer, at the cost of a
+  margin that is only right after the first sleep.

+# Completing required ACKs under the read lock: no established speedup
+
+This change was measured and not merged. It turned a second write-lock
+acquisition per ACK-waiting write into a read. At concurrency 256 that
+shortened lock queues by about 10%, but throughput and client latency did not
+move beyond noise. At concurrency 64 it added a small owner-side cost. Since
+it also adds a completion queue and a deferred release, it was not worth
+keeping. The candidate is [candidate.patch](data/lazy-ack-completion/candidate.patch),
+commit `0c6c9af`, applied on the completion timing in `cb71c40`.
+
+Under `FirstSuccessor` and `AllReplicas`, every write took the `NodeState` write
+lock twice: once to apply, and again in `wait_required_acks` after its follower
+ACKs arrived. The second acquisition existed only to clear the receipt's
+`required_acks` and release their retained bytes. It was untimed until
+`ack_completion_write_timing` was added. In the performance matrix of
+[ack-state-lock.md](ack-state-lock.md), it waited 24 µs per write at
+concurrency 64 and 109 µs at 256. That was longer than the write's own first
+acquisition.

+
+`wait_required_acks` made the same final checks under the **read** lock:
+lease, epoch, follower admission, follower process instance, and ACK progress. Instead of clearing the receipt
+itself, it pushed `(mutation_id, version)` onto a new `NodeState::completed_acks`,
+a `std::sync::Mutex<Vec<_>>`.
+

+that are already being taken:
+
+- `purge_expired_dedup`, which runs on every owner `Put`, `Delete` and
+  follower apply
+- the 1-second expiry sweep, for an idle owner

+holder reads the queue through `Mutex::get_mut`.

+

+  `max_dedup_bytes`, until the next write-lock holder ran.

+  already arrived. It returned at once unless the follower restarted in that
+  window, in which case it reported an unknown outcome. The same race existed before, across

+  stream it would have released before.

-# Network RTT sensitivity of the write path
-
-Every CPU profile in `results/flamegraph-*` is a single-host run: the driver, the
-coordinator and every data node talk gRPC over `127.0.0.1`. Those profiles show the
-transport and kernel path is the largest CPU consumer, which invites the conclusion
-that the network is the bottleneck. That conclusion had never been tested, and it
-cannot be tested from those profiles, because they contain no network latency at
-all: the loopback round trip is ~40 us, so every hop looks free.
-
-This note measures what the write path does when the round trip stops being free.
-The result is that on loopback the network is **not** the limiter, that the write
-path serializes exactly the round trips the acknowledgement policy implies, and that
-the two have a crossover which this harness can locate.
-
-## Method
-
-`scripts/netem-sweep.sh` installs one netem qdisc on `lo` and re-runs the correctness
-experiment at a series of delays. Everything is inherited into a
-`unshare --user --map-root-user --net` network namespace, so no privilege is needed
-and only this run's traffic is shaped.
-
-Two facts make a single `lo` qdisc sufficient and its units correct:
-
-- netem delays a packet on egress, and a loopback packet egresses `lo` once per
-  direction, so **RTT is twice the configured delay**. Measured here, not assumed:
-  `delay 0 -> RTT 0.037 ms`, `delay 5ms -> RTT 10.036 ms`.
-- The sweep pings at every point and records the RTT it actually got. Every table
-  below is in measured RTT, never in configured delay.
-
-`DELAYS=off` removes the qdisc and `DELAYS=0` keeps it attached with no delay. The
-gap between them is the instrument's own cost -- a shaped loopback queues packets in
-softirq where an unshaped one does not -- so the slope is fitted from `0` onward and
-never from `off`.
-
-Runs are medians of 2 or 3, which is the limit of what this harness resolves: the
-`--concurrency 64` and `128` loopback points spread 33% and 44% between
-repetitions of one unchanged binary, the same problem `sweep.sh` documents. The
-latency column is far better behaved than the throughput column, for the reason in
-the next section, and the conclusions below lean on it accordingly.
-
-## The latency sample is the load-bearing column
-
-`client_put_latency_us` is the experiment's own sample of 128 puts issued **one at a
-time** after the initial verify, on an otherwise quiet cluster
-(`crates/hashring-experiment/src/lib.rs:613`). It is a single-operation, unloaded
-latency, not the latency under `--concurrency`. The field is now called
-`idle_client_put_latency_us`, because the name says what the sample is; the runs
-below predate the rename.
-
-That is usually a defect and here it is the point. Its slope against RTT is a
-difference, so the queueing that `--concurrency` adds cancels out of it, and what
-remains is the number of round trips the write path serializes on. The throughput
-column carries that queueing and is correspondingly noisy; the latency slope is
-stable to three significant figures across every sweep below.
-
-## What the write path serializes
-
-`first-successor`, 4 nodes, RF=3, 100,000 keys, `--concurrency 64`:
-
-| delay | RTT | put keys/s | p50 us | cores |
-| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
-| off | 64 us | 46,740 | 150 | 2.54 |
-| 0 | 42 us | 39,776 | 161 | 2.83 |
-| 100us | 234 us | 48,843 | 572 | 2.60 |
-| 200us | 420 us | 40,311 | 988 | 2.30 |
-| 400us | 834 us | 24,759 | 1,793 | 1.98 |
-
-```
-p50_us = 91 + 2.06 * RTT_us      (r = 0.999, 4 points)
-```
