+# Network RTT sensitivity of the write path
+
+Every CPU profile in `results/flamegraph-*` is a single-host run: the driver, the
+coordinator and every data node talk gRPC over `127.0.0.1`. Those profiles show the
+transport and kernel path is the largest CPU consumer, which invites the conclusion
+that the network is the bottleneck. That conclusion had never been tested, and it
+cannot be tested from those profiles, because they contain no network latency at
+all: the loopback round trip is ~40 us, so every hop looks free.
+
+This note measures what the write path does when the round trip stops being free.
+The result is that on loopback the network is **not** the limiter, that the write
+path serializes exactly the round trips the acknowledgement policy implies, and that
+the two have a crossover which this harness can locate.
+
+## Method
+
+`scripts/netem-sweep.sh` installs one netem qdisc on `lo` and re-runs the correctness
+experiment at a series of delays. Everything is inherited into a
+`unshare --user --map-root-user --net` network namespace, so no privilege is needed
+and only this run's traffic is shaped.
+
+Two facts make a single `lo` qdisc sufficient and its units correct:
+
+- netem delays a packet on egress, and a loopback packet egresses `lo` once per
+  direction, so **RTT is twice the configured delay**. Measured here, not assumed:
+  `delay 0 -> RTT 0.037 ms`, `delay 5ms -> RTT 10.036 ms`.
+- The sweep pings at every point and records the RTT it actually got. Every table
+  below is in measured RTT, never in configured delay.
+
+`DELAYS=off` removes the qdisc and `DELAYS=0` keeps it attached with no delay. The
+gap between them is the instrument's own cost -- a shaped loopback queues packets in
+softirq where an unshaped one does not -- so the slope is fitted from `0` onward and
+never from `off`.
+
+Runs are medians of 2 or 3, which is the limit of what this harness resolves: the
+`--concurrency 64` and `128` loopback points spread 33% and 44% between
+repetitions of one unchanged binary, the same problem `sweep.sh` documents. The
+latency column is far better behaved than the throughput column, for the reason in
+the next section, and the conclusions below lean on it accordingly.
+
+## The latency sample is the load-bearing column
+
+`client_put_latency_us` is the experiment's own sample of 128 puts issued **one at a
+time** after the initial verify, on an otherwise quiet cluster
+(`crates/hashring-experiment/src/lib.rs:613`). It is a single-operation, unloaded
+latency, not the latency under `--concurrency`. The field is now called
+`idle_client_put_latency_us`, because the name says what the sample is; the runs
+below predate the rename.
+
+That is usually a defect and here it is the point. Its slope against RTT is a
+difference, so the queueing that `--concurrency` adds cancels out of it, and what
+remains is the number of round trips the write path serializes on. The throughput
+column carries that queueing and is correspondingly noisy; the latency slope is
+stable to three significant figures across every sweep below.
+
+## What the write path serializes
+
+`first-successor`, 4 nodes, RF=3, 100,000 keys, `--concurrency 64`:
+
+| delay | RTT | put keys/s | p50 us | cores |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| off | 64 us | 46,740 | 150 | 2.54 |
+| 0 | 42 us | 39,776 | 161 | 2.83 |
+| 100us | 234 us | 48,843 | 572 | 2.60 |
+| 200us | 420 us | 40,311 | 988 | 2.30 |
+| 400us | 834 us | 24,759 | 1,793 | 1.98 |
+
+```
+p50_us = 91 + 2.06 * RTT_us      (r = 0.999, 4 points)
+```
+
+**2.06 round trips per write.** That is the client-to-owner hop plus one
+owner-to-follower hop, which is what `first-successor` should cost: it replicates to
+`replicas[1..2]`, one follower, whose ACK returns in that same response
+(`crates/hashring-node/src/replication.rs:67`). The second follower is never waited
+for.
+
+The prediction is falsifiable, so it was tested against the other policy.
+`owner-only` replicates to no follower at all and should cost one hop. Same sweep:
+
+| delay | RTT | put keys/s | p50 us | cores |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| 0 | 15 us | 60,308 | 76 | 2.34 |
+| 200us | 428 us | 66,555 | 491 | 2.23 |
+| 400us | 839 us | 55,365 | 886 | 2.02 |
+| 800us | 1614 us | 32,980 | 1,698 | 1.38 |
+
+```
+p50_us = 54 + 1.01 * RTT_us      (r = 1.000, 4 points)
+```
+
+**1.01**, as predicted, and a lower intercept, because the owner does not wait for
+replication at all. A method that could not distinguish these two numbers would not
+be measuring round trips. The same run also explains why
+[batched-replication-rpc.md](batched-replication-rpc.md) could not make progress:
+with one hop to remove, and `first-successor` at two, the write path's serialized
+RTT is a small integer, not a term batching can shrink much.
+
+## Throughput: the loopback is not the limiter
+
+Raising RTT tenfold, from 42 us to 420 us, moves single-op latency from 161 us to
+988 us and leaves put throughput unchanged inside the noise (39,776 to 40,311
+keys/s). At 834 us throughput finally falls, to 24,759 keys/s.
+
+Sweeping offered concurrency at both ends of that range separates the two regimes.
+Same binary, same 100,000 keys, medians of 2:
+
+| RTT | conc 64 | conc 128 | conc 256 | conc 512 | cores at 64 |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| ~30 us (loopback) | 48,662 | 55,722 | 74,118 | 37,232 | 2.84 |
+| ~2 ms | 11,746 | 22,272 | 34,111 | 29,508 | 1.07 |
+
+At 2 ms the path behaves exactly as a latency-bound path must: throughput scales
+almost linearly with offered concurrency (11.7k to 34.1k for 64 to 256) at
+*lower* CPU than the loopback runs, landing at 0.56 to 0.77 of the
+`concurrency / p50` ceiling, the shortfall being the queueing the unloaded p50 does
+not contain.
+
+On loopback the same sweep does not scale at all: 48.7k, 55.7k, 74.1k, 37.2k is
+non-monotonic, and the ratio to the concurrency-latency ceiling is 0.01 to 0.13, off
+by one to two orders of magnitude. Whatever caps the loopback write path is not
+offered concurrency divided by network latency. It is local, it lands somewhere in
+the 40,000 to 75,000 keys/s band across this concurrency range, and it uses 2.3 to
+3.0 of the host's 24 cores.
+
+That band is worth being careful about, because it is not a measured ceiling. The
+concurrency sweep is not monotonic and its two lowest points spread 33% and 44%
+between repetitions, so the honest statement is that loopback throughput is
+*insensitive* to offered concurrency over 64 to 512 and lands in that band, not that
+it saturates at any particular number in it. The `first-successor` sweep at
+`--concurrency 64` alone, which repeated well enough to medians, put it at 39,776
+keys/s, and that is the number the crossover below uses. A single sweep cannot
+distinguish "locally limited" from "sharply peaked", and pinning down which is a
+separate question about the local resource, not about the network.
+
+CPU falls monotonically as RTT rises in every sweep above, from 2.84 to 1.07 cores.
+Injected latency becomes waiting, never work. Nothing here converts a slower network
+into more CPU, and the reverse also does not hold: removing CPU from the transport
+path, which is what the flame graphs invite, does not remove this loopback plateau,
+because the plateau is not made of transport CPU.
+
+## Where the two meet
+
+The crossover is where the network's own ceiling falls below the local one:
+
+```
+concurrency / (slope * RTT) = local ceiling
+```
+
+For `first-successor` at `--concurrency 64`, with the slope of 2.06 and the
+39,776 keys/s measured at loopback, that is **RTT ~ 780 us**. Loopback sits at
+~40 us, twenty times below it. A same-datacenter LAN at 0.1 to 0.3 ms RTT is below
+it. A cross-rack or WAN link at 1 ms or more is past it, and there the network path
+is the limiter.
+
+This number inherits the uncertainty above: it is a ratio of a fitted slope and a
+single noisy throughput, so it should be read as an order of magnitude, and it moves
+with `--concurrency` and node count, which are the two axes that set the local
+ceiling. That is the reason the sweep takes `NODE_COUNTS` and `CONCS` as lists
+rather than fixing them: the crossover is the quantity that decides whether this
+project should spend effort on round trips or on the local resource, and it is not
+a property of the network.
+
+## What this does not answer
+
+- **It is not a model of a cluster network.** One shared loopback link is shaped, so
+  every hop is delayed and no bandwidth is charged per hop. There is no per-core link
+  limit, no NIC offload, and no receive cost on another machine. A rate limit can be
+  added with `RATES=`, but it is a shared link in the same way.
+- **It does not name the local ceiling.** That loopback write throughput is insensitive
+  to offered concurrency over 64 to 512, and lands in the 40,000 to 75,000 keys/s
+  band, is measured here; what causes that is not, and neither is whether it is a
+  plateau or a peak. The candidate from
+  [write-path-saturation.md](write-path-saturation.md) is the single
+  `Arc<RwLock<NodeState>>`, whose owner acquisitions were 67% to 69% waiting at
+  concurrency 64 with 1.5 of 24 cores busy, but that note also records that it
+  cannot separate lock contention from client-side saturation. Both are still open,
+  and neither is answered here.
+- **The absolute throughputs are not comparable to `results/flamegraph-*`.** Those
+  runs sit in the host netns, where this host's nftables and conntrack rules are in
+  the path; a fresh namespace has empty netfilter tables. They also use 1,000,000
+  keys against 100,000 here.
+- **One node count, one key count, one concurrency per sweep.** See the crossover
+  discussion above for why that is the binding limitation on what can be concluded.
+- **The driver is on the same host and inside the shaped link.** At 4 nodes a third
+  of the profile is the client, so part of what the RTT shapes is the generator's
+  own round trip.
+

-ties broken by key bytes**. It is the order the source's token index already
-yields (`TokenBucket::Many` is a `BTreeSet`), so the source sorts nothing, and the

-bytes only when two tokens are equal. The digest bytes changed, so the domain
-separator moved from `v2` to `v3`.

-  token alone, so keys whose tokens collide came out in `HashMap` order and a
-  valid range failed verification with `data_loss`.

-  every other range on the node waited for a pass over every value byte of the
-  migrating range. Both handlers now copy cheap handles under the lock (the
-  source's `Arc` keys and records; the destination's records and the seed) and
-  compute tokens, sort and hash after `drop(state)`.

+# Range digest in token order, hashed outside the state lock
+
+A migration or replica seed ends with `finalize_range` comparing the source's
+and the destination's digest of the range. Both sides used to collect the range
+into a `HashMap`, sort it by key bytes and hash it. In a 1,000,000-key migration
+that sort and copy were the two largest items under `source_range_digest` and
+`destination_range_digest` (21.3% and 8.2% of the migration phase in
+`results/flamegraph-correctness-20261015-005607`).
+
+## The change
+
+`range_digest` (`crates/hashring-node/src/migration.rs`) takes records in the
+order the caller supplies, and that order is part of its contract: **token order,
+ties broken by key bytes**. It is the order the source's token index already
+yields (`TokenBucket::Many` is a `BTreeSet`), so the source sorts nothing, and the
+destination sorts `u64` tokens with `sort_into_token_order`, which compares key
+bytes only when two tokens are equal. The digest bytes changed, so the domain
+separator moved from `v2` to `v3`.
+
+Two corrections came out of review:
+
+- **The tie-break is required.** The first version sorted the destination by
+  token alone, so keys whose tokens collide came out in `HashMap` order and a
+  valid range failed verification with `data_loss`.
+  `range_digest_agrees_when_keys_share_a_token`
+  (`crates/hashring-node/src/tests/migration.rs`) migrates constructed XXH3
+  collisions and failed 3 of 3 runs without it.
+- **Hash after releasing the lock.** The first version hashed while holding the
+  `NodeState` read lock. Every `put` takes that lock for writing, so writes to
+  every other range on the node waited for a pass over every value byte of the
+  migrating range. Both handlers now copy cheap handles under the lock (the
+  source's `Arc` keys and records; the destination's records and the seed) and
+  compute tokens, sort and hash after `drop(state)`.
+
+## Evidence
+
+Apple M1 Pro, 8 logical CPUs, release build. 50,000 records in the migrating
+range, 20 digests back to back while a writer puts once per millisecond to keys
+outside the range (`crates/hashring-node/src/tests/digest_stall_bench.rs`).
+*Stall* is the mean of the 20 slowest puts, one per digest. Medians of three
+interleaved runs per tree: `b8deaa1` before the change, `a915f5b` hashing under
+the lock, and the current code.
+
+| value | side | before: stall | hashed under lock: stall | now: stall | writer puts (before / under lock / now) |
+| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
+| 128 B | source | 14.65 ms | 24.10 ms | **7.75 ms** | 242 / 43 / 228 |
+| 128 B | destination | 1.91 ms | 20.13 ms | 2.05 ms | 237 / 43 / 248 |
+| 1 KiB | source | 15.67 ms | 85.82 ms | **8.65 ms** | 814 / 43 / 776 |
+| 1 KiB | destination | 3.02 ms | 85.11 ms | 2.71 ms | 809 / 43 / 817 |
+| 4 KiB | source | 16.28 ms | 287.11 ms | **9.03 ms** | 2589 / 43 / 2601 |
+| 4 KiB | destination | 3.98 ms | 284.06 ms | 3.69 ms | 2583 / 43 / 2588 |
+
+With no digest running, the same writer's stall is 0.09-0.42 ms. Hashing under the
+lock made the stall equal to the whole digest and grow with the value size; the
+writer completed one put per digest. Now the source stalls writers about half as
+long as before the change, because it copies `Arc` handles where the old code
+copied key bytes into a map, and the destination is back to the old clone.
+
+The copy costs CPU the lock-holding version did not pay. `digest_bench.rs`, 20,000
+records, total digest time in one binary:
+
+| | before | hashed under lock | now |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| source | 8.3 ms | 2.12x faster | 5.4 ms, **1.53x** faster |
+| destination | 5.2 ms | 1.35x faster | 5.0 ms, **1.04x** faster |
+
+So the source keeps most of the win, and the destination keeps almost none: its
+saving was the map clone, and taking the records out from under the lock needs a
+copy again. Making `DestinationMigration::records` share keys and values by `Arc`
+would make that copy cheap; it is not done here.
+
+## Reproduce
+
+```sh
+cargo test --release -p hashring-node range_digest_writer_stall -- --ignored --nocapture
+cargo test --release -p hashring-node range_digest_pays -- --ignored --nocapture
+```
+
+`digest_stall_bench.rs` uses only the RPC surface and test helpers, so it can be
+copied into an older tree (and named in `tests/mod.rs`) to repeat the comparison.

-# Range migration: a token index instead of four full key scans
-
-Before this change a data node stored its records in `NodeState.records`, a
-`HashMap<Vec<u8>, Record>` keyed by the raw key bytes. Nothing in that map
-recorded the key's position in the ring, so answering "which of my keys fall in
-this token range?" meant hashing every key with `TopologySnapshot::key_token`
-and testing each one. Four migration RPCs did exactly that, and three of them
-did it while holding a lock.
-
-This was the dominant cost of a topology change. In the capture below it
-accounts for 59% of the cycles the run spends, and it is why concurrent writes
-collapse during scale-out.
-
-## The four scans, before the change
-
-| Handler | Source | Lock | Work over all keys |
-| --- | --- | --- | --- |
-| `prepare_source_range` | `rpc.rs` | **write** | clones every key and every dedup `(id, key)` pair, clones the topology snapshot; then outside the lock hashes every key to filter and sort it, and repeats that for every dedup key |
-| `source_range_digest` | `rpc.rs` | read | hashes every key, clones every record that matches |
-| `commit_destination_range` | `rpc.rs` | **write** | `records.retain(\|key, _\| !range.contains(topology.key_token(key)))`, hashing every key under the write lock |
-| `cleanup_source_range` | `rpc.rs` | **write** | clones the topology, then hashes every key and calls `replica_node_ids_for_token` on each before removing the matches |
-
-A range is one vnode slot wide, so a range query should touch a few dozen keys.
-Instead it touches every key on the node, and the two write-lock scans hold the
-lock for the duration.
-
-`TopologySnapshot::derived_ranges` produces **one range per distinct vnode
-token**, which is `members * virtual_nodes`: 1,024 ranges for the 8-node,
-128-vnode topology in the capture below. Every range whose owner or follower set
-changes when a node joins or leaves goes through all four handlers.

-## The change
-
-Store the token where the key already is, and keep a token-ordered index beside
-each map:
-
-- `records` becomes `HashMap<Arc<[u8]>, Record>`. `Arc<[u8]>` borrows as `[u8]`,
-  so a lookup by bytes keeps working unchanged — the one read in the migration
-  path is `records.get(key.as_ref())` — while a call site that holds a `Vec<u8>`
-  now passes `key.as_slice()` instead of `&key`, because `Arc<[u8]>` borrows as
-  `[u8]` and not as `Vec<u8>`. Cloning a key becomes a refcount bump instead of
-  a `Vec` allocation, and the map, the index and the receipt share one
-  allocation instead of two.
-- `records_by_token: TokenIndex<Arc<[u8]>>` shares those same `Arc`s. It is a
-  `BTreeMap<u64, TokenBucket<T>>`, where a bucket is one inline value or, once
-  tokens collide, a `BTreeSet`: two distinct keys colliding on a 64-bit xxh3
-  token is possible in principle and must not lose a key, but the common case
-  should not pay a `Vec` allocation per record for it. An overwrite leaves the
-  index alone, because `HashMap::insert` keeps the map's original `Arc`, which
-  the index already holds.
-- `dedup_by_token: TokenIndex<Arc<str>>` holds mutation IDs, which are already
-  `Arc<str>` shared with the dedup map, so this index costs no extra key
-  allocation either. Receipts collide routinely: every retained receipt for one
-  key shares that key's token. The `BTreeSet` bucket keeps expiring a hot key's
-  backlog `O(k log k)`; the first version used a `Vec` per token, whose linear
-  search per removal made it quadratic under the write lock (about 736 ms for
-  40,000 receipts of one key in an isolated release harness).
-
-Range extraction becomes a `BTreeMap::range` bounded lookup:
-`O(log n + k)` for the `k` keys actually in the range, instead of `O(n)` hashes
-and clones. `commit_destination_range`'s `retain` and `cleanup_source_range`'s
-scan become removals of the `k` keys the index returns, using the tokens the
-index returns with them rather than hashing each key again. All four handlers stop
-touching keys outside their range, and the two that hold the write lock now hold
-it for `k` operations instead of `n`.
-
-**The load-bearing invariant: a key's token changes only with the seed.**
-`key_token` is `xxh3_64_with_seed(key, hash_seed)` and `hash_seed` is a field of
-the snapshot, so a topology that reseeded the ring would leave the index
-answering range queries with stale positions.
-`crates/hashring-core/src/migration.rs:138` builds every target topology with
-`committed.hash_seed`, so a topology change never reseeds; a recreated
-coordinator does pick a fresh seed, though, and a node can receive it. Members, virtual nodes and epoch change freely and do not affect a key's
-token. `TopologySnapshot::key_token` is not public state a caller can vary
-independently of the snapshot it came from, so the index cannot observe a
-different seed than the snapshot it was built with.
-
-That invariant is what makes an incrementally maintained index safe here rather
-than a correctness hazard. Both places that swap a node's topology —
-`install_topology` and `refresh_topology` — go through
-`NodeState::set_topology`, which rebuilds both indices when the seed differs.
-An earlier version only asserted the seed in debug builds, so a release node
-would have migrated and cleaned up the wrong keys without error.
-`tests/index.rs` pins the behaviour across an epoch bump and a reseed.
-
-Every mutation goes through `NodeState` helpers rather than touching `records`
-or `dedup` directly, because the failure mode of this change is a map and an
-index that disagree — a key invisible to migration, or a migrated key that
-reappears. A test-only consistency check walks both structures and compares
-them (it rehashes every key, so it must not run under the write lock in a
-handler); `tests/index.rs` checks that indexed range answers equal hashing every key
-for wrapping, covering and empty ranges, that replacement, stale-version and
-removal all leave the two structures equal, and that the answers survive an
-epoch bump; and the existing migration and replication tests exercise the same
-paths.
-
-## Tradeoffs
-
-- **The write path gets more expensive.** Every applied mutation now also
-  inserts into a `BTreeMap`: a binary search plus a potential node split, on the
-  hot path, under a lock that was already held. It also adds hashing: the
-  record index hashes a new key under the write lock rather than trusting the
-  token the put path computed before taking it (a reseed in between would
-  misplace the key), and every receipt is hashed once when indexed and once
-  when it expires, on owners and followers alike. This is the cost of moving the scan off the write
-  path and onto the migration path; the measurement below is where it was paid
-  for or not.
-- **Memory grows in the steady state.** Roughly one `BTreeMap` entry per record
-  and per live deduplication receipt: tens of bytes per entry on top of the
-  shared `Arc` payloads. On the 20-node, 1M-key performance profile that is a
-  few hundred thousand entries per node, measured as +23% peak RSS there — while
-  the migration peak it replaces falls 85% in the correctness run.
-  [dedup-receipt-store-memory.md](dedup-receipt-store-memory.md)
-  already bounds the receipt side; this raises the per-node baseline and belongs
-  in the same accounting.
-- **Two structures to keep consistent.** Handled by funneling mutations through
-  helpers and checking the invariant in tests, but it is a real cost and the
-  reason the test-only consistency check exists.
-- **`source_range_digest` loses nothing.** It still clones the records it
-  digests, so its working set for the range is unchanged; only the discovery of
-  which records to clone gets cheaper.
-

+# Range migration: a token index instead of four full key scans
+
+Before this change a data node stored its records in `NodeState.records`, a
+`HashMap<Vec<u8>, Record>` keyed by the raw key bytes. Nothing in that map
+recorded the key's position in the ring, so answering "which of my keys fall in
+this token range?" meant hashing every key with `TopologySnapshot::key_token`
+and testing each one. Four migration RPCs did exactly that, and three of them
+did it while holding a lock.
+
+This was the dominant cost of a topology change. In the capture below it
+accounts for 59% of the cycles the run spends, and it is why concurrent writes
+collapse during scale-out.
+
+## The four scans, before the change
+
+| Handler | Source | Lock | Work over all keys |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `prepare_source_range` | `rpc.rs` | **write** | clones every key and every dedup `(id, key)` pair, clones the topology snapshot; then outside the lock hashes every key to filter and sort it, and repeats that for every dedup key |
+| `source_range_digest` | `rpc.rs` | read | hashes every key, clones every record that matches |
+| `commit_destination_range` | `rpc.rs` | **write** | `records.retain(\|key, _\| !range.contains(topology.key_token(key)))`, hashing every key under the write lock |
+| `cleanup_source_range` | `rpc.rs` | **write** | clones the topology, then hashes every key and calls `replica_node_ids_for_token` on each before removing the matches |
+
+A range is one vnode slot wide, so a range query should touch a few dozen keys.
+Instead it touches every key on the node, and the two write-lock scans hold the
+lock for the duration.
+
+`TopologySnapshot::derived_ranges` produces **one range per distinct vnode
+token**, which is `members * virtual_nodes`: 1,024 ranges for the 8-node,
+128-vnode topology in the capture below. Every range whose owner or follower set
+changes when a node joins or leaves goes through all four handlers.
+
+## Evidence
+
+Captured with `scripts/flamegraph.sh correctness` on a 24-core AMD Ryzen 9
+7845HX, rustc 1.93.0, frame-pointer build (`target/fp`), `--call-graph fp`.
+Config: correctness mode, 8 nodes, 100,000 keys, 128-byte values, RF=3,
+`FirstSuccessor`, concurrency 64, seed 114514. 78.74 s, 15,512 samples,
+672.6 G cycles, 0 lost samples, and 74.1% of cycles carrying a project frame
+(as computed by the script's first coverage check, which mis-parsed some
+stacks; see [frame-pointer-profiling.md](frame-pointer-profiling.md#result)).
+Raw artifacts are under `results/flamegraph-correctness-20261014-111934/`
+(ignored by Git).

+| start, full RF, initial put, get verify | 13.85 s | 97.7 G | 14.5% | 7.1 |
+| scale-out transition to full RF | 31.25 s | 293.6 G | 43.7% | 9.4 |
+| scale-in transition to full RF | 33.42 s | 278.1 G | 41.4% | 8.3 |

+
+Cycle shares over the whole run:

+The same 9,095 mutations are 54x slower while a scan holds the state write lock.
+Scale-in's mutations avoid it because that transition took the `direct_merge`

+run.

+## The change
+
+Store the token where the key already is, and keep a token-ordered index beside
+each map:
+
+- `records` becomes `HashMap<Arc<[u8]>, Record>`. `Arc<[u8]>` borrows as `[u8]`,
+  so a lookup by bytes keeps working unchanged — the one read in the migration
+  path is `records.get(key.as_ref())` — while a call site that holds a `Vec<u8>`
+  now passes `key.as_slice()` instead of `&key`, because `Arc<[u8]>` borrows as
+  `[u8]` and not as `Vec<u8>`. Cloning a key becomes a refcount bump instead of
+  a `Vec` allocation, and the map, the index and the receipt share one
+  allocation instead of two.
+- `records_by_token: TokenIndex<Arc<[u8]>>` shares those same `Arc`s. It is a
+  `BTreeMap<u64, TokenBucket<T>>`, where a bucket is one inline value or, once
+  tokens collide, a `BTreeSet`: two distinct keys colliding on a 64-bit xxh3
+  token is possible in principle and must not lose a key, but the common case
+  should not pay a `Vec` allocation per record for it. An overwrite leaves the
+  index alone, because `HashMap::insert` keeps the map's original `Arc`, which
+  the index already holds.
+- `dedup_by_token: TokenIndex<Arc<str>>` holds mutation IDs, which are already
+  `Arc<str>` shared with the dedup map, so this index costs no extra key
+  allocation either. Receipts collide routinely: every retained receipt for one
+  key shares that key's token. The `BTreeSet` bucket keeps expiring a hot key's
+  backlog `O(k log k)`; the first version used a `Vec` per token, whose linear
+  search per removal made it quadratic under the write lock (about 736 ms for
+  40,000 receipts of one key in an isolated release harness).
+
+Range extraction becomes a `BTreeMap::range` bounded lookup:
+`O(log n + k)` for the `k` keys actually in the range, instead of `O(n)` hashes
+and clones. `commit_destination_range`'s `retain` and `cleanup_source_range`'s
+scan become removals of the `k` keys the index returns, using the tokens the
+index returns with them rather than hashing each key again. All four handlers stop
+touching keys outside their range, and the two that hold the write lock now hold
+it for `k` operations instead of `n`.
+
+**The load-bearing invariant: a key's token changes only with the seed.**
+`key_token` is `xxh3_64_with_seed(key, hash_seed)` and `hash_seed` is a field of
+the snapshot, so a topology that reseeded the ring would leave the index
+answering range queries with stale positions.
+`crates/hashring-core/src/migration.rs:138` builds every target topology with
+`committed.hash_seed`, so a topology change never reseeds; a recreated
+coordinator does pick a fresh seed, though, and a node can receive it. Members, virtual nodes and epoch change freely and do not affect a key's
+token. `TopologySnapshot::key_token` is not public state a caller can vary
+independently of the snapshot it came from, so the index cannot observe a
+different seed than the snapshot it was built with.
+
+That invariant is what makes an incrementally maintained index safe here rather
+than a correctness hazard. Both places that swap a node's topology —
+`install_topology` and `refresh_topology` — go through
+`NodeState::set_topology`, which rebuilds both indices when the seed differs.
+An earlier version only asserted the seed in debug builds, so a release node
+would have migrated and cleaned up the wrong keys without error.
+`tests/index.rs` pins the behaviour across an epoch bump and a reseed.
+
+Every mutation goes through `NodeState` helpers rather than touching `records`
+or `dedup` directly, because the failure mode of this change is a map and an
+index that disagree — a key invisible to migration, or a migrated key that
+reappears. A test-only consistency check walks both structures and compares
+them (it rehashes every key, so it must not run under the write lock in a
+handler); `tests/index.rs` checks that indexed range answers equal hashing every key
+for wrapping, covering and empty ranges, that replacement, stale-version and
+removal all leave the two structures equal, and that the answers survive an
+epoch bump; and the existing migration and replication tests exercise the same
+paths.
+
+## Tradeoffs
+
+- **The write path gets more expensive.** Every applied mutation now also
+  inserts into a `BTreeMap`: a binary search plus a potential node split, on the
+  hot path, under a lock that was already held. It also adds hashing: the
+  record index hashes a new key under the write lock rather than trusting the
+  token the put path computed before taking it (a reseed in between would
+  misplace the key), and every receipt is hashed once when indexed and once
+  when it expires, on owners and followers alike. This is the cost of moving the scan off the write
+  path and onto the migration path; the measurement below is where it was paid
+  for or not.
+- **Memory grows in the steady state.** Roughly one `BTreeMap` entry per record
+  and per live deduplication receipt: tens of bytes per entry on top of the
+  shared `Arc` payloads. On the 20-node, 1M-key performance profile that is a
+  few hundred thousand entries per node, measured as +23% peak RSS there — while
+  the migration peak it replaces falls 85% in the correctness run.
+  [dedup-receipt-store-memory.md](dedup-receipt-store-memory.md)
+  already bounds the receipt side; this raises the per-node baseline and belongs
+  in the same accounting.
+- **Two structures to keep consistent.** Handled by funneling mutations through
+  helpers and checking the invariant in tests, but it is a real cost and the
+  reason the test-only consistency check exists.
+- **`source_range_digest` loses nothing.** It still clones the records it
+  digests, so its working set for the range is unchanged; only the discovery of
+  which records to clone gets cheaper.
+
+## Measurement
+
+Everything below is the same frame-pointer build and capture settings as the
+Evidence section: `--call-graph fp`, `-F 99`, event `cpu/cycles/P`, and **0 lost
+samples in every capture**. Two configurations ran back to back on this shared
+desktop, whose load average was between 3.6 and 17.0 while they ran; the pairs
+were interleaved (before, after, before, after) so neither side always had the
+quiet machine, and the tables give the median with the observed range across
+three correctness pairs and two performance pairs. The before binary is the
+frame-pointer build of `deb5928`, the after one of `3091ddb`. Later commits add
+a guard that de-indexes a replaced receipt id, the seed handling and test
+scaffolding; that guard runs once per committed receipt. The bucketed index,
+the reseed rebuild and the token-carrying range lookups came after these
+captures and were not re-measured; they remove allocations and hashes from the
+measured paths rather than adding work, apart from a rebuild on a reseed. Captures are in
+`results/flamegraph-correctness-{before,after}{,-2,-3}` and
+`results/flamegraph-performance-{before,after}{,-2}`, ignored by Git.

+This mode barely exercises range migration — one topology change after the load
+is placed, so 0.1% of cycles went to the handlers on both sides — and its value
+here is the put and RSS rows. The put path, which now pays a `BTreeMap` insert
+per applied record and per receipt, did not regress: it measured 1.18x faster,
+and that number may be real rather than noise, because the record key is now a
+single `Arc<[u8]>` shared by the map, the index and the receipt where it used to
+be a `Vec` clone plus a separate `Arc` copy. It was measured on the same noisy
+desktop as everything else and is not isolated, so the claim to keep is the
+weaker one: the index insert cost nothing measurable.
+
+Memory moves in both directions, which is the honest shape of this change. The
+migration peak falls 7x because the per-range key and receipt clones are gone:
+sampling inside the scale-out window, peak node RSS was 456, 473 and 463 MiB
+across the three before runs against 68.7, 68.8 and 68.6 MiB across the three
+after runs, and the largest sample anywhere in the before runs, 531 MiB, came
+after the migration had already finished. The steady state rises: at 1M keys
+and RF=3 each node holds about 150k record replicas plus roughly 180k live
+receipts, so about 330k indexed entries, and peak RSS rose 35 MiB for them —
+about 110 bytes an entry, which is what a `BTreeMap` entry and its share of a
+node cost. The `Vec` → `Arc` key change pushes the other way, one shared
+allocation per key instead of two, so the index's own share of that 35 MiB is
+below 110 bytes an entry. The correctness run pays the first effect and the
+performance run pays the second.
+
+### What is left
+
+Cycles of the three after runs pooled together, innermost project frame: gRPC
+dispatch 4.8%, replication stream delivery 2.6%, the per-range
+`TopologySnapshot` clone 2.2%, the client's own `get` 1.9%, and two parts of the
+migration path that still copy rather than look up — `source_range_digest`'s
+records 1.4% and `commit_destination_range` 1.4%. Above project code, the
+coordinator's `seed_replica_group` carries 11.9% and `execute_change` 5.5% of
+weight at any depth, which is where the migration's coordination now shows up,
+and `CoordinatorRepository::store_state` 1.2%.
+
+The snapshot clone is the cheapest of these to remove and the natural
+follow-up. `apply_migration_batch`, `apply_dedup_batch` and
+`cleanup_source_range` each clone `state.topology` once to keep a snapshot
+across the mutations they apply, and they only ever read it —
+`topology.key_token` and `topology.epoch`. Holding it as an
+`Arc<TopologySnapshot>` in `NodeState` would turn those three deep clones into
+reference-count bumps.

+What carries over, and what does not:
+
+**Large: 10 nodes.** Correctness at 10 nodes (9 → 10 → 9) and 100,000 keys,
+the Linux key count; performance at 10 nodes and 1,000,000 keys. Concurrency
+64, as in the settings under [Reproducing both sides](#reproducing-both-sides).
+
+Correctness, median (range) of three runs:
+
+| | before | after | after / before |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| mutations during scale-out | 505 ops/s (497–511) | 858 ops/s (857–863) | **1.70x** |
+| scale-out transition to full RF | 12.81 s (12.67–13.02) | 7.55 s (7.50–7.56) | 0.59x |
+| scale-in transition to full RF | 11.69 s (11.55–16.18) | 11.33 s (11.25–11.38) | 0.97x |

+| initial put | 31,574 ops/s (31,175–31,687) | 31,185 ops/s (30,806–31,411) | 0.99x |
+| scale-in mutations | 9,885 ops/s (6,586–10,762) | 10,572 ops/s (10,561–10,840) | 1.07x |
+
+Performance, median (range) of two runs:
+
+| | before | after | after / before |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| initial put | 29,365 ops/s (29,132–29,598) | 28,559 ops/s (28,465–28,652) | 0.97x |
+| get verify | 77,258 ops/s (75,871–78,644) | 79,046 ops/s (78,669–79,423) | 1.02x |
+| time to full RF after the put | 15.94 s | 15.88 s | 1.00x |
+| peak per-node RSS | 289.9 MiB (286.0–293.8) | 310.9 MiB (309.8–312.0) | 1.07x |
+
+What carries over, and what does not:
+
+- **The migration win reproduces in direction, at a smaller size.** Scale-out
+  mutations are 1.75x faster at 5 nodes and 1.70x at 10, rather than 9.8x,
+  with no overlap between the two sides' ranges in either size. With a quarter as many ranges and fewer keys per node, each
+  scan was shorter to begin with, so there was less to remove.
+- **Scale-in's convergence gets faster at 5 nodes (0.36x) but not at 10
+  (0.97x).** At 5 nodes it is the replica repair after the direct merge, which
+  runs the same handlers, as described under Evidence. At 10 nodes the wait is
+  about 11.3 s on both sides, close to two 5 s repair ticks, and 9 members give
+  up to 72 repair groups against a cap of 32 per pass. That points at the
+  pass timing in
+  [replica-repair-convergence-latency.md](replica-repair-convergence-latency.md)
+  rather than the scans, but these runs did not record per-group timings to
+  confirm it. Scale-in's own mutations do not move, as on Linux.
+- **The migration memory peak falls 9x at 5 nodes and 6x at 10**, in line
+  with Linux's 7x.
+- **The steady-state cost reproduces: +10% and +7% peak RSS** in the two
+  performance runs, about 11 MiB per node at 250k keys and 21 MiB at 1M,
+  against +23% on Linux.

+  four comparisons here, against 1.18x on Linux. The weaker claim above, that the index insert
+  costs nothing measurable, holds; the stronger one, that the put got faster,
+  is not supported by this run.
+

+`results/macos-bench-20261014/` (ignored by Git).

+### Reproducing both sides
+
+Each side is the same script pointed at a different binary. Build the tree under
+test with `RUSTFLAGS='-C force-frame-pointers=yes' cargo build --release
+--target-dir target/fp`, then:
+
+```bash
+mkdir -p experiments
+cat > experiments/range-token-index.yaml <<'YAML'
+mode: correctness
+nodes: 8
+keys: 100000
+value_bytes: 128
+concurrency: 64
+seed: 114514
+virtual_nodes: 128
+operation_timeout_ms: 30000
+migration_timeout_ms: 600000
+range_move_concurrency: 16
+pre_publish_delay_ms: 250
+desired_replication_factor: 3
+minimum_admitted_copies: 1
+minimum_healthy_followers: 0
+policy: first-successor
+YAML
+BINARY=$PWD/target/fp/release/hashring-rs BUILD=0 \
+  CONFIG=experiments/range-token-index.yaml ./scripts/flamegraph.sh
+```
+
+`experiments/` is ignored by Git; this file is the settings the captures used.
+
+The second table needs a copy of that config with `mode: performance`,
+`nodes: 20` and `keys: 1000000`, passed the same way through `CONFIG`, plus the
+`performance` argument. `BUILD=0` keeps the script from building the current
+tree over the binary under test: `BUILD=auto` now runs `cargo build` for its own
+`target/fp` binary on every run (a no-op when it is current), because building
+only when the binary was missing let a stale `target/fp` measure the wrong tree
+without saying so.

+# Coalescing the routing-token read lock: no established speedup
+
+Removing the extra `NodeState` read-lock acquisition from Put and Delete produced
+about 5% higher median PUT throughput on this host, but the paired runs were too
+variable to establish a repeatable improvement. The change is below what this
+benchmark can resolve. It was later applied as a code-clarity cleanup, not as a
+throughput optimization; the measured binaries remain the baseline and the
+benchmark patch described below.
+
+## Comparison
+
+Baseline: `1a586254`, including the memory-accounting, partial-acknowledgement and
+worker-count corrections. The [candidate patch](data/read-lock-ab/candidate.patch)
+only moves the token calculation into the existing initial read-lock block in Put
+and Delete. Both binaries were built with `cargo build --release` using Rust
+1.98.1 on an Apple M1 Pro (8 logical CPUs, 16 GiB RAM).
+
+Each existing performance experiment used 10 nodes, RF=3, OwnerOnly, two Tokio
+workers per process, 100,000 keys, 128-byte values, seed 1 and 128 virtual nodes.
+Lock profiling was disabled. At each concurrency, one warm-up pair was excluded
+in advance, followed by six measured pairs. Baseline/candidate order reversed
+between pairs. All 28 runs completed successfully and verified all keys.
+
+## Results
+
+Throughput is the instrumented initial PUT phase, excluding startup, replica
+admission, GET verification and subsequent sequential latency probes.
+
+| Concurrency | Baseline median PUT/s | Candidate median PUT/s | Change in medians |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| 64 | 28,269 | 29,683 | +5.0% |
+| 256 | 40,570 | 42,542 | +4.9% |
+
+Paired throughput changes, in execution order:
+
+- Concurrency 64: -7.87%, +29.57%, -5.61%, +95.32%, +4.90%, -0.03%.
+- Concurrency 256: -1.48%, -9.21%, +27.85%, +18.70%, -5.42%, +12.10%.
+
+The geometric mean of paired ratios was +15.0% and +6.3%, respectively.
+Exploratory paired-bootstrap 95% intervals (20,000 resamples, seed 5, on log
+ratios) were [-3.4%, +45.1%] and [-3.4%, +17.5%]. Both include no improvement.
+Six pairs on one shared host are limited evidence; these intervals do not remove
+systematic environmental effects. The candidate was faster in three of six pairs
+at each concurrency, so a sign test gives no evidence either way.
+
+At concurrency 64, run order explains more than the variant does. The first run
+of each pair averaged 25,625 PUT/s and the second 29,808 PUT/s. Both large
+candidate gains (+29.57% and +95.32%) came from pairs where the baseline ran
+first; where the candidate ran first the changes were -7.87%, -5.61% and +4.90%.
+The +15.0% geometric mean at 64 is therefore an order and outlier effect, not a
+candidate effect. Concurrency 256 shows no order effect (42,686 versus 42,622
+PUT/s).
+
+The run is also far too small for the effect in question. The standard deviation
+of paired log ratios was 0.287 at 64 and 0.137 at 256; detecting a true 5% change
+with 80% power at a 5% two-sided level would take roughly 270 and 60 pairs. The
+expected effect is much smaller than 5%: the patch removes one uncontended Tokio
+`RwLock` read acquisition per Put or Delete, an estimated sub-microsecond cost
+against requests of about 140 microseconds. The earlier routing-token and
+fingerprint change in [write-path-saturation.md](write-path-saturation.md),
+which removed more work from the same path, moved mean owner hold by only
+0.27 microseconds.
+
+Median sequential direct-owner p50 latency was unchanged at concurrency 64
+(138.5 microseconds for both) and fell from 138 to 134 microseconds at 256.
+These 128-request probes run after the load phase, so they do not measure loaded
+request latency. DELETE performance was not separately measured.
+
+Replication queue backpressure engaged in some runs. Median reservation rejection
+counts were 2.5 versus 0 at concurrency 64 and 90.5 versus 133.5 at 256; all RPC
+retry counters were zero. The comparison measures end-to-end throughput with
+client retries, not isolated read-lock cost.
+
+Two early baseline runs had 613/656-second external wall durations while the
+experiment's monotonic durations were 21/23 seconds. Their rows were retained.
+Idle sleep was inhibited for later runs. This discrepancy and the broad
+throughput spread further limit the conclusion: +5% is an observed median change,
+not a demonstrated optimization benefit.
+
+## Evidence and reproduction
+
+[Per-run measurements](data/read-lock-ab/measurements.csv) include warm-ups,
+latency probes and backpressure counts. [Metadata](data/read-lock-ab/metadata.json)
+records binary SHA-256 hashes. Full local manifests, logs, summaries, binaries,
+build-source copies and the runner/analysis scripts are retained under
+`results/read-lock-ab-20261012/` (ignored by version control).
+
+Build the baseline, save its executable, apply the candidate patch, build and
+save the candidate executable, then restore the baseline source. Run each saved
+binary with the following parameters, alternating order for six measured pairs
+at each concurrency after a warm-up pair:
+
+```sh
+BINARY --worker-threads 2 experiment --mode performance --nodes 10 \
+  --keys 100000 --value-bytes 128 --concurrency 64 --output UNIQUE_OUTPUT
+```
+
+These binaries predate the move of `--worker-threads` onto the subcommands;
+with current builds the equivalent is `experiment --worker-threads 2 ...`.
+
+Repeat with concurrency 256. Each executable spawns its own matching child
+processes. Build/runtime manifests can report dirty or differing source because
+this comparison used saved binaries and restored source; identify the artifacts
+by the recorded hashes, baseline commit and exact candidate patch rather than
+claiming clean-source reproducibility.

+use std::cmp::Reverse;
+use std::collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap};
+use std::sync::Arc;
+use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
+
+pub struct RecordVersion {
+    pub topology_epoch: u64,
+    pub owner_sequence: u64,
+    pub owner_node_id: String,
+}
+pub struct DedupEntry {
+    pub key: Arc<[u8]>,
+    pub fingerprint: [u8; 32],
+    pub version: RecordVersion,
+    pub deleted: bool,
+    pub retained_bytes: usize,
+    pub expires_at: Instant,
+    pub required_acks: Vec<(u64, String, u64)>,
+}
+
+fn entry(i: usize, expires_at: Instant) -> DedupEntry {
+    DedupEntry {
+        key: Arc::from(i.to_be_bytes()),
+        fingerprint: [0; 32],
+        version: RecordVersion {
+            topology_epoch: 1,
+            owner_sequence: i as u64,
+            owner_node_id: "node-1".into(),
+        },
+        deleted: false,
+        retained_bytes: 0,
+        expires_at,
+        required_acks: Vec::new(),
+    }
+}
+
+fn main() {
+    let variant = std::env::args().nth(1).expect("string or arc");
+    let n: usize = std::env::args()
+        .nth(2)
+        .expect("entry count")
+        .parse()
+        .unwrap();
+    let expires_at = Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(60);
+    if variant == "arc" {
+        let mut map: HashMap<Arc<str>, DedupEntry> = HashMap::with_capacity(n);
+        let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(Instant, Arc<str>)>> = BinaryHeap::with_capacity(n);
+        for i in 0..n {
+            let id: Arc<str> = format!("{:08x}-0000-4000-8000-{:012x}", i, i).into();
+            heap.push(Reverse((expires_at, id.clone())));
+            map.insert(id, entry(i, expires_at));
+        }
+        eprintln!("ready arc {} {}", map.len(), heap.len());
+        std::io::stdin().read_line(&mut String::new()).unwrap();
+        std::hint::black_box((map, heap));
+    } else {
+        let mut map: HashMap<String, DedupEntry> = HashMap::with_capacity(n);
+        let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(Instant, String)>> = BinaryHeap::with_capacity(n);
+        for i in 0..n {
+            let id = format!("{:08x}-0000-4000-8000-{:012x}", i, i);
+            heap.push(Reverse((expires_at, id.clone())));
+            map.insert(id, entry(i, expires_at));
+        }
+        eprintln!("ready string {} {}", map.len(), heap.len());
+        std::io::stdin().read_line(&mut String::new()).unwrap();
+        std::hint::black_box((map, heap));
+    }
+}

-# Replica ACK throughput and activation
-
-## Targets and previous bottlenecks
-
-For the local 10-node, RF=3, 128-byte-value workload at concurrency 64, the target is at least 10,000 acknowledged writes/s. The 20k-key correctness workload should normally finish scale-out within 10 seconds, with a 30-second hard cap. A longer logical operation deadline does not satisfy these targets.
-
-Previously, every FirstSuccessor or AllReplicas write called `GetReplicaStatus`. That diagnostic endpoint polls owner/follower streams across the cluster and builds a status record for every range. The 10-node topology has 1,280 ranges and up to 90 directed owner/follower pairs. The FirstSuccessor 20k performance run took 48.25 seconds for initial PUTs; the attempted 1M run was interrupted after roughly 23 minutes without finishing initial writes. OwnerOnly skips this query under the default availability guard.
-
-Activation seeded replica streams using per-range coordinator transactions for Copying, Verifying, and Complete. Each transaction cloned and persisted the complete cluster state. The earlier FirstSuccessor scale-out took 72.6 seconds and caused concurrent operations to exceed their 30-second deadlines.
-
-## Changes and safety boundaries
-
-The owner lease now carries admitted follower identities for the current topology epoch. A follower is included only when every interval requiring that follower under the selected ACK policy has a durable admission matching the registered follower process. Owners discard these identities on epoch changes. This permits default-guard writes to select required followers locally, without calling the diagnostic status endpoint.
-
-Replication responses carry the responding process identity. Before reporting write success, the owner checks that each required sequence has been acknowledged by the admitted process and that its own epoch and lease remain valid. Sequence progress is reset to the response's sequence when the responder identity changes, so an old process's high watermark cannot be attributed to a new process. Missing admissions fail before applying a new mutation. Missing or mismatched ACKs after application preserve an uncertain outcome and the retry receipt. A completed receipt still records success for subsequent retries within the existing window.
-
-The local gate also checks the age of the oldest unacknowledged entry against the configured lag bound. Successful writes require an applied ACK from the selected follower; they do not depend on a separate pre-write probe of that follower's lease. Explicit minimum-copy or minimum-healthy-follower guards retain the existing live status check and are outside the optimized performance claim. The policies still require the exact first successor or every desired follower, respectively; they never substitute an arbitrary responding subset.
-
-Repair phase updates and final admissions are persisted atomically per complete owner/follower stream group. Snapshot transfer, final write fences, digest verification, checkpoint identity checks, and durability before admission remain in place. A failed batch changes neither the in-memory state nor the durable state. Incomplete repairs remain resumable after restart.
-
-Coordinator migration and repair RPCs now share reconnecting HTTP/2 channels by endpoint, including channels for pending members. Each RPC retains its original deadline. This avoids repeatedly opening connections for every range and protocol step. The intermediate build without channel reuse reproduced a transport error during activation twice; connection churn is a suspected contributor, not a proven operating-system diagnosis.
-

+# Replica ACK throughput and activation
+
+## Targets and previous bottlenecks
+
+For the local 10-node, RF=3, 128-byte-value workload at concurrency 64, the target is at least 10,000 acknowledged writes/s. The 20k-key correctness workload should normally finish scale-out within 10 seconds, with a 30-second hard cap. A longer logical operation deadline does not satisfy these targets.
+
+Previously, every FirstSuccessor or AllReplicas write called `GetReplicaStatus`. That diagnostic endpoint polls owner/follower streams across the cluster and builds a status record for every range. The 10-node topology has 1,280 ranges and up to 90 directed owner/follower pairs. The FirstSuccessor 20k performance run took 48.25 seconds for initial PUTs; the attempted 1M run was interrupted after roughly 23 minutes without finishing initial writes. OwnerOnly skips this query under the default availability guard.
+
+Activation seeded replica streams using per-range coordinator transactions for Copying, Verifying, and Complete. Each transaction cloned and persisted the complete cluster state. The earlier FirstSuccessor scale-out took 72.6 seconds and caused concurrent operations to exceed their 30-second deadlines.
+
+## Changes and safety boundaries
+
+The owner lease now carries admitted follower identities for the current topology epoch. A follower is included only when every interval requiring that follower under the selected ACK policy has a durable admission matching the registered follower process. Owners discard these identities on epoch changes. This permits default-guard writes to select required followers locally, without calling the diagnostic status endpoint.
+
+Replication responses carry the responding process identity. Before reporting write success, the owner checks that each required sequence has been acknowledged by the admitted process and that its own epoch and lease remain valid. Sequence progress is reset to the response's sequence when the responder identity changes, so an old process's high watermark cannot be attributed to a new process. Missing admissions fail before applying a new mutation. Missing or mismatched ACKs after application preserve an uncertain outcome and the retry receipt. A completed receipt still records success for subsequent retries within the existing window.
+
+The local gate also checks the age of the oldest unacknowledged entry against the configured lag bound. Successful writes require an applied ACK from the selected follower; they do not depend on a separate pre-write probe of that follower's lease. Explicit minimum-copy or minimum-healthy-follower guards retain the existing live status check and are outside the optimized performance claim. The policies still require the exact first successor or every desired follower, respectively; they never substitute an arbitrary responding subset.
+
+Repair phase updates and final admissions are persisted atomically per complete owner/follower stream group. Snapshot transfer, final write fences, digest verification, checkpoint identity checks, and durability before admission remain in place. A failed batch changes neither the in-memory state nor the durable state. Incomplete repairs remain resumable after restart.
+
+Coordinator migration and repair RPCs now share reconnecting HTTP/2 channels by endpoint, including channels for pending members. Each RPC retains its original deadline. This avoids repeatedly opening connections for every range and protocol step. The intermediate build without channel reuse reproduced a transport error during activation twice; connection churn is a suspected contributor, not a proven operating-system diagnosis.

-## Why convergence takes 10 s on an empty cluster
-
-Seven nodes, 128 virtual nodes each, RF=3, zero keys. Reaching `live_rf == 3` on
-every range should be near-instant work. It takes 10.27 s. Three independent
-limits in the code serialise it, and they compound.
-
-**1. No one seeds the initial replicas. A background poll does.**
-
-`load_or_initialize` calls `reconcile_replica_repairs`
-(`crates/hashring-coordinator/src/lib.rs:497`), which pushes a `Pending`
-`ReplicaRepair` for every follower slot of every derived range. For this
-topology that is **1,792 tasks in 42 `(owner, follower)` groups** (896 ranges x
-2 followers; 7 owners x 6 possible followers), read directly out of
-`run/coordinator.redb`. It only *reconciles*; it seeds nothing. The only seeders
-are `seed_repairs_for_activation`, reached from a topology change
-(`change.rs:449`, `change.rs:909`), and `resume_replica_repairs`, reached only
-from the recovery loop (`src/main.rs:552`).
-
-On a fresh bootstrap there is no topology change. So all 1,792 tasks sit
-`Pending` until the recovery loop's first tick — and the recovery task is
-spawned at `src/main.rs:539`, immediately before the server starts being
-awaited at `src/main.rs:573`. `tokio::time::interval` fires its first tick at
-once, so that tick runs within milliseconds of the coordinator process starting.
-Nodes 1-7 did not call `register_node` until 40 ms later
-(`run/process-logs/node-*.stdout.log`). The first tick is not a race the cluster
-can win; it is a guaranteed no-op.
-
-**2. One pass cannot finish: 42 > 32 — and the sort key degenerates.**
-
-```rust
-// crates/hashring-coordinator/src/lib.rs:53
-const MAX_REPAIR_GROUPS_PER_PASS: usize = 32;
-
-// crates/hashring-coordinator/src/repair.rs:276-284
-let mut due = groups.into_values().collect::<Vec<_>>();
-due.sort_by_key(|group| group.iter().map(|r| r.retry_count).max().unwrap_or(0));
-due.truncate(MAX_REPAIR_GROUPS_PER_PASS);
-```
-
-This is **a rate limiter, not a defect on its own**, and the code says so:
-`repair.rs:274-275` states that remaining groups "stay durable and are
-considered on the next periodic pass". Nothing is lost — the 10 excluded groups
-keep their `Pending` phase in redb and are selected on the following tick.

-What makes it a problem is the interaction, and the sort key makes it worse than
-it first looks. `slice::sort_by_key` is **stable**, and on a fresh topology every
-group's `retry_count` is **0** (read straight out of `run/coordinator.redb`:
-42 groups, one distinct `retry_count` value). With all keys equal the sort is a

-| `node-7 ->` | `node-1`, `node-2`, `node-3`, `node-4`, `node-5`, `node-6` |

-## Cost model
-
-Convergence is bounded below by
-
-```
-ceil(groups / MAX_REPAIR_GROUPS_PER_PASS) x 5 s      (the tick quantisation)
-  + ceil(groups / width) x per-group latency          (the seeding pipeline)
-```
-
-where `width` is `replica_repair_concurrency` — 4 in this run, and now
-configurable. With 42 groups the first term alone is
-`ceil(42/32) x 5 s = 10 s`, regardless of cluster size, key count, or available
-CPU. The floor is a property of the constants, not of the load.
-
-Scaling up makes it worse rather than better. At 8 members the group count grows
-toward 8 x 7 = 56, so `ceil(56/32)` is still 2 ticks but the second tick carries
-24 groups instead of 10, and the truncation is worse in absolute terms. Only
-small clusters escape it: with 6 or fewer members there are at most 6 x 5 = 30
-groups, which fit in one pass. From 7 members up the cap is binding.

+## Why convergence takes 10 s on an empty cluster
+
+Seven nodes, 128 virtual nodes each, RF=3, zero keys. Reaching `live_rf == 3` on
+every range should be near-instant work. It takes 10.27 s. Three independent
+limits in the code serialise it, and they compound.
+
+**1. No one seeds the initial replicas. A background poll does.**
+
+`load_or_initialize` calls `reconcile_replica_repairs`
+(`crates/hashring-coordinator/src/lib.rs:497`), which pushes a `Pending`
+`ReplicaRepair` for every follower slot of every derived range. For this
+topology that is **1,792 tasks in 42 `(owner, follower)` groups** (896 ranges x
+2 followers; 7 owners x 6 possible followers), read directly out of
+`run/coordinator.redb`. It only *reconciles*; it seeds nothing. The only seeders
+are `seed_repairs_for_activation`, reached from a topology change
+(`change.rs:449`, `change.rs:909`), and `resume_replica_repairs`, reached only
+from the recovery loop (`src/main.rs:552`).
+
+On a fresh bootstrap there is no topology change. So all 1,792 tasks sit
+`Pending` until the recovery loop's first tick — and the recovery task is
+spawned at `src/main.rs:539`, immediately before the server starts being
+awaited at `src/main.rs:573`. `tokio::time::interval` fires its first tick at
+once, so that tick runs within milliseconds of the coordinator process starting.
+Nodes 1-7 did not call `register_node` until 40 ms later
+(`run/process-logs/node-*.stdout.log`). The first tick is not a race the cluster
+can win; it is a guaranteed no-op.
+
+**2. One pass cannot finish: 42 > 32 — and the sort key degenerates.**
+
+```rust
+// crates/hashring-coordinator/src/lib.rs:53
+const MAX_REPAIR_GROUPS_PER_PASS: usize = 32;
+
+// crates/hashring-coordinator/src/repair.rs:276-284
+let mut due = groups.into_values().collect::<Vec<_>>();
+due.sort_by_key(|group| group.iter().map(|r| r.retry_count).max().unwrap_or(0));
+due.truncate(MAX_REPAIR_GROUPS_PER_PASS);
+```
+
+This is **a rate limiter, not a defect on its own**, and the code says so:
+`repair.rs:274-275` states that remaining groups "stay durable and are
+considered on the next periodic pass". Nothing is lost — the 10 excluded groups
+keep their `Pending` phase in redb and are selected on the following tick.
+
+What makes it a problem is the interaction, and the sort key makes it worse than
+it first looks. `slice::sort_by_key` is **stable**, and on a fresh topology every
+group's `retry_count` is **0** (read straight out of `run/coordinator.redb`:
+42 groups, one distinct `retry_count` value). With all keys equal the sort is a
+no-op and the order is whatever `BTreeMap<(String, String), _>` yielded —
+lexicographic by node id. So the 32-group quota becomes a **quota by node name**:
+
+| deferred on the first pass | groups |
+| --- | --- |
+| `node-6 ->` | `node-3`, `node-4`, `node-5`, `node-7` |
+| `node-7 ->` | `node-1`, `node-2`, `node-3`, `node-4`, `node-5`, `node-6` |
+
+**Every obligation owned by `node-7` is served last, on every convergence.** In a
+quiescent cluster this costs one extra 5 s tick and nothing more, because pass 2
+has only 10 pending groups and all fit under the cap. Under sustained load —
+anything that keeps 32 or more groups pending — the tail is starved
+indefinitely, because the throttle has a position, not a fairness rule. The
+natural tie-breakers (`oldest obligation first`, `largest group first`) are
+absent, and `retry_count` only becomes a meaningful key once something has
+actually failed.
+
+**3. Passes only happen every 5 s.**
+
+```rust
+// src/main.rs:540
+let mut interval = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_secs(5));
+```
+
+`run_failure_pass`, which runs on its own 1 s loop, cannot cover the gap: it
+returns early for the first lease duration (`repair.rs:81`, `self.lease_duration`
+read from the committed topology, 5 s by default), and it does not seed replicas
+at all — the only three callers of `seed_replica_group` are `merge.rs:221`,
+`repair.rs:289` and `repair.rs:504`. Ticks land at t = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 s.
+
+The arithmetic matches the measurement to within the driver's own poll
+granularity:

+- t=0 tick: no-op, as above.
+- t=5 tick: `resume_replica_repairs` now has both endpoints registered for all
+  42 groups (`repair.rs:256-257`), takes the first 32 in the degenerate
+  lexicographic order, leaves the 10 `node-6`/`node-7`-owned ones.

+The same arithmetic explains the scale-in wait. `scale_in_with_mutations` takes

+**4. And each pass is a narrow RPC pipeline.**
+
+```rust

+try_map_bounded(groups, self.replica_repair_concurrency, ...)

+So a pass that *could* finish still ran 42 groups 4 at a time. This is the limit

+The driver's own poll is a fifth, smaller quantiser: `wait_for_full_rf` sleeps

+## Cost model
+
+Convergence is bounded below by
+
+```
+ceil(groups / MAX_REPAIR_GROUPS_PER_PASS) x 5 s      (the tick quantisation)
+  + ceil(groups / width) x per-group latency          (the seeding pipeline)
+```
+
+where `width` is `replica_repair_concurrency` — 4 in this run, and now
+configurable. With 42 groups the first term alone is
+`ceil(42/32) x 5 s = 10 s`, regardless of cluster size, key count, or available
+CPU. The floor is a property of the constants, not of the load.
+
+Scaling up makes it worse rather than better. At 8 members the group count grows
+toward 8 x 7 = 56, so `ceil(56/32)` is still 2 ticks but the second tick carries
+24 groups instead of 10, and the truncation is worse in absolute terms. Only
+small clusters escape it: with 6 or fewer members there are at most 6 x 5 = 30
+groups, which fit in one pass. From 7 members up the cap is binding.

+# Replication backpressure: entry count and byte budget
+
+The owner replicates each mutation to its desired followers through separate ordered streams. A stream is identified by `(topology epoch, owner, follower)` and has one delivery worker. That worker sends one entry at a time and retries retryable failures before advancing to the next entry. This ordering lets the follower reject gaps and apply mutations in the owner's stream order.
+
+## What is the backlog?
+
+A follower's **backlog** is the work the owner has accepted for that follower but has not yet confirmed as applied. It includes entries waiting in the stream queue and the entry currently being sent or retried. The in-flight entry has already left the queue, so a stream can have 32 queued entries plus one in flight. If a follower is slow, unreachable, or repeatedly rejects an RPC with a retryable error, later entries wait behind the stalled entry. The backlog grows when the owner's arrival rate exceeds that stream's delivery rate.
+
+This matters to writes because the owner must reserve replication capacity *before* applying a new PUT or DELETE. It reserves space in every target follower's stream and in the owner's retained-byte budget. If any reservation fails, the owner rolls back the tentative stream sequence and returns retryable replication backpressure without applying the mutation. An ACK still requires the followers specified by the write policy to apply the mutation; placing it in a queue is never an ACK.
+
+## The two limits
+
+| Limit | Scope | What it bounds |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| 32 queued entries | One `(epoch, owner, follower)` stream | The number of entries waiting behind that stream's active delivery. |
+| 64 MiB of retained mutation data | All replication streams on one owner node | The estimated bytes retained for mutations awaiting follower delivery. |
+
+The owner charges a mutation's key, value, identifiers, and a fixed overhead estimate against the byte budget. Entries sent to multiple followers share that one byte reservation. It stays held until every follower entry using it is delivered or dropped. The byte limit is an accounting bound for this replication work, not an exact cap on the process's total memory. A separate 64 MiB semaphore limits bytes in active replication RPCs; it does not replace the retained-byte or queue limits.
+
+Both reservations must succeed. Many small mutations can fill one stream's 32 slots while the 64 MiB budget remains mostly free. Conversely, large mutations across several streams can exhaust 64 MiB while no individual queue reaches 32. A stalled entry also consumes retained bytes while it is being retried, even though it no longer occupies a queue slot.
+
+## Why keep a per-stream count limit?
+
+Using only the aggregate byte budget would still bound retained data, but it would allow one slow stream to accumulate many small entries. Those entries would increase the amount of ordered work waiting behind its first stalled entry. The per-stream limit bounds that waiting count and applies backpressure to writes targeting that follower sooner. It also limits how much queueing a short follower slowdown can create before the owner asks clients to retry.
+
+The count limit is **not** a fairness guarantee. A stream with large entries can still occupy most or all of the shared byte budget and affect other streams. Nor does a larger queue increase delivery parallelism: the worker still processes its stream in order. Raising the limit from 8 to 32 trades more burst tolerance for a larger possible backlog and more retained work. +# Replication batch linger

+[batched-replication-rpc.md](batched-replication-rpc.md) let one
+`ReplicateMutations` RPC carry up to 64 entries, but a stream only batches what
+queued while its previous RPC was in flight. On one host with 6 nodes,
+replication batches averaged **2.2 entries**, so at RF=3 every client write cost
+about 1.9 RPCs for the nodes to serve. Almost all of an RPC's cost is in the
+transport, not the handler ([grpc-io-bottleneck.md](grpc-io-bottleneck.md)), so
+that RPC count, not the hashring code, set the RF=3 write ceiling.
+
+## Change
+
+A follower stream that has entries to send now waits up to
+`replication_batch_linger_ms` (default **2 ms**) for more before it sends the
+batch, unless some write is waiting for that follower's ACK:
+
+- Each queued entry records whether its write waits for this follower's ACK
+  (`PreparedReplication::ack_awaited`, set from the owner's ready followers when
+  the mutation is prepared). Under `OwnerOnly` no entry does. Under
+  `FirstSuccessor` only the first follower's do.

+  the batch is not full and no entry in it is awaited, it keeps receiving until
+  the linger deadline. An awaited entry ends the wait at once, so a write that
+  waits for ACKs is never delayed by lingering.

+1 ms resolution, so a 1 ms linger waits 1-2 ms.

+| RF=1, 64 (no replication) | | 71,466 | | | | 704 µs | 21 µs |
+
+- **Fewer RPCs.** A 2 ms linger cuts replication RPCs 4-5x under `OwnerOnly`.
+- **More throughput, lower client latency.** Followers wait, yet the client's
+  `Put` RPC gets faster (1,586 -> 1,089 µs at concurrency 64). With fewer
+  replication RPCs, the nodes' two workers spend less time on replication
+  traffic and owner handlers finish sooner (203 -> 87 µs). This confirms that
+  per-RPC transport cost was the limit.
+- **ACK-waiting writes get faster too.** Under `FirstSuccessor` the first
+  follower's stream never lingers, but the second follower's does. That removes
+  a third of all replication RPCs, and the owner handler, which includes
+  waiting for the ACK, drops from 1,039 to 704 µs.
+- **Fewer rejections.** Stream-queue reservation rejections fall about 8x
+  (706 -> 89 at concurrency 64), because lingering moves entries
+  out of the queue sooner.
+- **Time to full RF does not change.** It is 6.2 s in every configuration
+  (`initial_full_rf_seconds`), since milliseconds of linger are small against
+  it.
+
+The default is 2 ms rather than 5. In this sweep 5 ms was no better at
+concurrency 64 and 10% better at concurrency 256. Repeats at 256 (below) put the
+typical gain at about 6%, so the smaller value, which keeps the added
+`OwnerOnly` loss window (below) short, gives up little.
+
+## Why a longer linger adds little
+
+Going from 2 ms to 5 ms halves the replication RPCs again, so a follow-up
+tested whether the driver was hiding the gain. Concurrency 256, three runs
+each, under heavier background load (one disk-image service and `logd` busy,
+so the first repetition was slow in every configuration). A temporary build
+gave only the driver 4 workers and spawned writer tasks, while nodes kept
+2 workers. Raw data:
+[phase-d-driver-runs.tsv](data/grpc-io-bottleneck/phase-d-driver-runs.tsv).
+
+| PUT ops/s, median | linger 0 | 2 ms | 5 ms | RF=1 |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| driver 2 workers (default) | 47,398 | 64,202 | 56,062 | 92,005 |
+| driver 4 workers, spawned tasks | 46,383 | 69,793 | 65,918 | 116,363 |
+
+Comparing within each repetition, 5 ms against 2 ms was -4%, -29% and +3% with
+the default driver, and -27%, +3% and +8% with the faster one: no gain that
+stands out from the noise either way. 0 to 2 ms was +29% to +41% with the
+default driver. Across all nine paired comparisons of 5 ms against 2 ms at
+concurrency 256 with the default driver (this run, the sweep above, and the lock
+profile below), the median gain is **+6.5%**, with a range of -29% to +30%.
+
+- **The driver is not the RF=3 limit.** It does cap RF=1: at concurrency 256 the
+  default driver runs both workers at 1.94 cores, and giving it more lifts RF=1
+  from 92k to 116k. RF=3 stays well below either ceiling, and a faster driver
+  does not widen the 2 to 5 ms gap. (Comparing RF=3 at concurrency 256 with RF=1
+  at concurrency 64, as an earlier version of this note did, uses a ceiling that
+  is itself latency-bound. At equal concurrency and the default 2 ms, RF=3 is
+  about 30% below RF=1.)
+- **Halving a small share of RPCs gains little.** With about 300k client `Put`
+  RPCs per run, replication was 35% of the RPCs that nodes serve at linger 0,
+  12% at 2 ms and 6% at 5 ms. By Amdahl's law, halving the replication RPCs at
+  2 ms can speed the RPC load up by at most about 6%. Removing them entirely
+  would give at most about 14%.
+- **The write lock is not the remaining limit.** A third run added
+  `HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1`. Same workload and default driver, Time Machine
+  busy throughout, so throughput is noisy but the lock counters agree across
+  repetitions. Raw data:
+  [phase-e-lock-runs.tsv](data/grpc-io-bottleneck/phase-e-lock-runs.tsv).
+
+  | linger | PUT ops/s | owner lock wait per write | follower lock hold, total | per batch | per entry | owner `Put` handler |
+  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+  | 0 | 52,777 | 73 µs | 3.13 s | 22 µs | 5.2 µs | 456 µs |
+  | 2 ms | 64,565 | 43 µs | 2.75 s | 72 µs | 4.6 µs | 280 µs |
+  | 5 ms | 74,943 | 35 µs | 2.34 s | 127 µs | 3.9 µs | 230 µs |
+  | RF=1 | 91,704 | 12 µs | | | | 72 µs |
+
+  Each follower batch holds the lock longer as batches grow, but total hold
+  time falls, because per-entry cost shrinks with batching, and owner writes
+  wait *less* for the lock. At 5 ms the lock accounts for about 23 µs of the
+  158 µs gap between the RF=3 and RF=1 owner handlers. The rest is time the
+  handler spends outside the write lock, most likely waiting for one of the
+  node's two workers, which also serve replication sends and follower applies,
+  or for the state read lock. Pinning that down needs a scheduling profile.
+
+## Tradeoffs
+
+- **`OwnerOnly` loss window.** A write acknowledged by the owner alone may now
+  wait up to the linger before its first follower copy is sent. An owner crash
+  in that interval can lose writes that would otherwise already have been on
+  their way to a follower.
+  Policies that wait for follower ACKs are unaffected for the followers they
+  wait on.
+- **Follower freshness.** Followers may lag by up to the linger more, which
+  is far below the `max_replica_lag_ms` default of 5,000.
+- **A timer per lingering batch.** That is cheap next to the RPCs it saves.
+
+## Verification
+
+- Unit tests `batch_linger_collects_entries_that_arrive_while_waiting` and
+  `batch_linger_never_delays_an_acknowledged_write`
+  (`crates/hashring-node/src/tests/replication.rs`) run `collect_replication_batch`
+  on tokio's paused clock: linger collects late entries and ends at its
+  deadline, and an awaited entry, first or arriving late, ends the wait
+  immediately.
+- The full workspace suite passes, and with the 2 ms default one correctness-mode
+  and one availability-mode run each completed successfully.
+
+## Reproducing
+
+```sh
+cargo build --release
+for linger in 0 2; do for rep in 1 2 3; do
+  HASHRING_PROFILE_RPC=1 scripts/perf/run.sh results/linger L$linger-c64 $rep \
+    --keys 300000 --concurrency 64 --replication-batch-linger-ms $linger
+done; done
+python3 scripts/perf/collect.py results/linger
+```
