+# Request id generation without a syscall per operation
+
+Every client `get`, `put` and `delete` carries a request id that the owner uses
+as the mutation's deduplication key. The client made it with
+`uuid::Uuid::new_v4().to_string()`, which reads the OS random source on every
+call. On macOS that is a `getentropy` syscall, and CPU profiles of the
+experiment driver put it at 4.5-7% of the driver's on-CPU time
+([grpc-io-bottleneck.md](grpc-io-bottleneck.md)). The driver is the bottleneck
+for RF=1 writes and for all reads on one host.
+
+## Change
+
+`new_request_id()` in `crates/hashring-client/src/lib.rs` formats a random
+`u128` from `rand`'s thread-local generator as 32 hex characters. That
+generator is a ChaCha CSPRNG seeded from the OS, reseeding after every 64 KiB
+of output (about 4,000 ids), so almost no call makes a syscall.
+
+- **Uniqueness:** 128 random bits against a v4 UUID's 122.
+- **Format:** nothing parses request ids as UUIDs. Nodes only check that an id
+  has 1-128 bytes.
+- **Size:** ids shrink from 36 to 32 bytes, which slightly reduces the
+  deduplication receipt and journal bytes each mutation is charged.
+- **Dependency:** the client no longer depends on `uuid`. Nodes still use it for
+  process instance ids, once per process.
+
+## Measurement
+
+**Isolated cost** ([bench.rs](data/request-id-generation/bench.rs), single
+thread, Apple M1 Pro, 2 million ids per round, three rounds): `Uuid::new_v4()`
+plus `to_string()` takes 855-891 ns per id, and the `rand` hex id takes 65 ns,
+13x less.
+
+**End to end:** performance mode, 6 nodes, 300,000 keys, 128-byte values, base
+commit `4ec7a0c` against this change. Five repetitions, each running the before
+and after binaries back to back, on an otherwise idle host. Medians. Driver
+CPU per operation is the driver's sampled user and system time during the
+phase divided by its operations (`scripts/perf/run.sh`). Raw data:
+[runs.tsv](data/request-id-generation/runs.tsv).
+
+| configuration | PUT ops/s | GET ops/s | driver CPU per PUT | driver CPU per GET |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| RF=1, concurrency 64 | 75,196 -> 76,595 (+1.9%) | 77,595 -> 80,289 (+3.5%) | 26.7 -> 26.2 µs (-2.0%) | 30.2 -> 26.9 µs (-11%) |
+| RF=1, concurrency 256 | 87,651 -> 94,764 (+8.1%) | 90,625 -> 102,380 (+13%) | 22.6 -> 21.1 µs (-6.8%) | 24.5 -> 21.8 µs (-11%) |
+| RF=3, concurrency 64 | 58,448 -> 59,587 (+1.9%) | 75,519 -> 77,059 (+2.0%) | 26.7 -> 26.1 µs (-2.5%) | 28.7 -> 27.0 µs (-6.1%) |
+
+The RF=1, concurrency 64 PUT ranges do not overlap: 74,433-75,417 before
+against 76,357-78,437 after. The system-time share of all PUT-phase CPU fell
+by 1-3 points in every configuration, for example from 39% to 36% at RF=1,
+concurrency 256.
+
+Under load the saving exceeds the isolated cost: about 3 µs of driver CPU per
+`GET` against 0.8 µs measured alone. A syscall is costlier when every core is
+busy, which matches the profile's 4.5-7% share. The gain is largest where the
+driver is the bottleneck (RF=1 and reads, especially at concurrency 256). At
+RF=3 the write path is limited by node-side RPC latency instead, so it gains
+least.
+
+## Notes
+
+A first attempt at this measurement ran while an Xcode build used 60-77% of a
+core per process, and paired runs moved by up to 2x in either direction. It is
+not used here.

+# State write-lock profile
+
+`HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1` makes every node time its `Arc<RwLock<NodeState>>`
+acquisitions. `diagnostics::write` records, per write path, the count of
+acquisitions, cumulative wait and hold nanos, and the maximum of each. The
+counters are cumulative per process, reset on restart, and surfaced through
+`GetProcessInfo` into the experiment's `node_pressure_sampled` event. Timed paths
+skip clock reads entirely when the variable is unset, so an unprofiled run pays
+only the two extra atomics guarding the `OnceLock` read.
+
+## Measurement
+
+Correctness run, 20,000 keys, concurrency 64, RF=3, `OwnerOnly`, 128-byte values,
+9 nodes. Sample taken 2 ms after `initial_put_complete`; the initial load itself
+took 478 ms (41.8k keys/s). Aggregated over all 9 nodes:
+
+| write path | acquisitions | mean wait | mean hold | wait/hold | total wait | total hold |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| owner (`Put`/`Delete`) | 20,000 | 24.98 us | 11.88 us | 2.10 | 0.500 s | 0.238 s |
+| follower (`ReplicateMutations`) | 31,140 | 36.53 us | 10.87 us | 3.36 | 1.138 s | 0.338 s |
+| replication ACK writeback | 31,140 | 31.17 us | 1.95 us | **15.95** | 0.971 s | 0.061 s |
+
+Worst single waits were 5.71 ms (owner) and 9.91 ms (follower/ACK), all on the
+same node, consistent with a FIFO writer queue draining behind one long hold.
+
+## Reading
+
+Three things follow, and they do not all point the same way.
+
+- **The lock is busy, not saturated.** Owner and follower holds total 0.576 s
+  across 9 nodes over a 478 ms window. Per node that is ~13,100 acquisitions at a
+  ~7.7 us mean hold, a duty cycle near 31%. Real contention, real headroom, but
+  no queue collapse. Little's law on the observed means puts the mean writer
+  queue at ~0.6 deep.
+- **The ACK writeback is the worst ratio and the cheapest payload.** It holds the
+  lock for 1.95 us to mutate three maps — a few dozen instructions of real work —
+  yet waits 31.17 us, because it queues behind owner and follower writers it does
+  not share any invariant with. It also fires more often than the owner path
+  (31,140 acquisitions to 20,000). This is the clearest case in the profile for
+  moving state off the shared lock.
+- **Summing wait overstates it.** The README's warning that wait totals overlap
+  across tasks and nodes is load-bearing: 0.971 s of summed ACK wait is ~0.108 s
+  per node against a 478 ms window, and those waits queue rather than run
+  concurrently. Per-operation means are the trustworthy quantity here.
+
+## Consequences
+
+`ack_process_instances`, `ack_progress`, and `owner_stream_unacked` have no
+invariant shared with `records` or `dedup`, which is what makes them candidates
+to relocate. Two caveats found while reading the call sites:
+
+- `prune_ack_progress` reads `dedup` to build the live-receipt set and mutates
+  `ack_progress` and `ack_process_instances` together. It is reached from
+  `purge_expired_dedup`, which runs under the `NodeState` write lock on the put
+  and follower-apply paths. If the ACK maps move behind their own lock, the
+  acquisition order there is `NodeState` -> `AckState`, and that order must hold
+  everywhere or the two locks can deadlock.
+- `prepare_replication_entries` also registers `ack_progress` entries, under the
+  same `NodeState` write lock, so it inherits that same order.
+
+Directions 1 and 2 were later implemented, measured and rejected in
+[ack-state-lock.md](ack-state-lock.md). The ACK split regressed `FirstSuccessor`.
+The epoch atomic made ACK writebacks wait longer. That work also timed a second
+write lock per ACK-waiting write. Turning it into a read
+([lazy-ack-completion.md](lazy-ack-completion.md)) shortened lock queues but
+did not change throughput.
+
+Direction 2 (cache the topology epoch in an `Arc<AtomicU64>` so the delivery loop
+stops taking a read lock per retry) is consistent with this order and strictly
+removes work; it is worth doing first because it cannot deadlock.
+
+Direction 4 (sharding `records` by token) was not attempted. At a 31% duty cycle
+the ceiling on any lock change is bounded, and sharding additionally forces
+`next_sequence` per shard and cross-shard consistent reads for migration
+snapshots. Revisit only if a profile after directions 1-3 still shows owner
+holds dominating.
+
+## Reproducing
+
+```sh

+  --mode correctness --output results/<dir>
+```
+
+Read `node_pressure_sampled` from `events.jsonl` and aggregate
+`owner_write_timing`, `follower_write_timing`, and `ack_write_timing` across
+nodes. Run against a clean tree (`--require-clean-source`) so the manifest
+records a reproducible revision.

-# Worker pool sizing on a shared host
-
-The `experiment` command starts a driver, a coordinator and every data node as
-separate processes on one host. Each process built its tokio runtime through
-`#[tokio::main]`, which defaults to one worker per logical CPU. On a 24-core host
-that is 24 workers in each of 11 processes: **275 threads on 24 cores**.
-
-This records what that cost, and the fix.
-
-## Measurement
-
-Correctness mode, 20,000 keys, concurrency 64, RF=3, `OwnerOnly`, 128-byte values,
-9 data nodes on a 24-core AMD Ryzen 9 7845HX. Five runs per variant, medians, with

+The `experiment` command starts a driver, a coordinator and every data node as
+separate processes on one host. Each process built its tokio runtime through
+`#[tokio::main]`, which defaults to one worker per logical CPU. On a 24-core host
+that is 24 workers in each of 11 processes: **275 threads on 24 cores**.

+This records what that cost, and the fix.
+

+9 data nodes on a 24-core AMD Ryzen 9 7845HX. Five runs per variant, medians, with
+`HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1`:

+| `--worker-threads 4` | 0.391 s | 0.371 s | 51,132 | 9.6 us | 20.0 us | 31.2 us |

-# Receipt cleanup and request routing
-
-## Problem and changes
-
-The repeated one-million-key runs varied across ACK policies. Two concrete sources of avoidable work were identified while investigating that variation.
-
-Receipt expiry invokes ACK-progress pruning up to once per second per node. The old implementation scanned every live receipt to find old-epoch ACK references even when every tracked stream belonged to the current epoch. Current-epoch streams must always survive pruning. The new fast path checks the much smaller ACK-progress and process-identity maps first and skips the receipt scan when no older stream exists. When an older stream exists, pruning still scans receipt requirements and preserves any stream needed by a retry. Receipt lifetime, expiry order, byte accounting, and retry results are unchanged.
-
-Each client GET, PUT, and DELETE attempt previously called `topology()`, cloning the complete snapshot, including all token assignments and their node-ID strings, before selecting an owner. At 10 nodes with 128 virtual nodes each, this copies 1,280 assignments per attempt. Routing now reads the epoch and selected endpoint under one topology read lock, then releases that lock before network I/O. Explicit callers of the public `topology()` API still receive an owned snapshot. Retry handling continues to use the epoch that selected the endpoint. There is no change to ACK policy or stream ordering.
-
-Source: [ACK pruning](../../crates/hashring-node/src/replication.rs), [client routing](../../crates/hashring-client/src/lib.rs), and [receipt expiry](../../crates/hashring-node/src/dedup.rs).
-

-
-`HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1` enables per-process cumulative wall-time counters, returned by node info and saved in the experiment's post-write pressure sample. With profiling disabled, these optional timing messages are absent and the experiment records null values; hot paths skip clock reads and timing-counter updates. Unit tests enable diagnostics automatically.
-
-The counters cover the state write lock for owner PUT/DELETE application, follower replication application, and sender-side ACK processing. They do not cover read-lock waits, the separate final required-ACK completion lock, client CPU, transport queues, or all migration locks. Counts include successful lock acquisitions, and early-return paths still record hold duration. Wait sums can overlap across tasks and nodes. Hold and cleanup durations include descheduling; they are not CPU-time measurements.
-
-Cleanup time includes expiry-heap work, receipt destruction, and any nested ACK-pruning scan. Report pruning as a component of cleanup, not additional time. These counters reveal avoidable work but cannot alone assign the entire throughput gap to locks or expiry.

+# Receipt cleanup and request routing
+
+## Problem and changes
+
+The repeated one-million-key runs varied across ACK policies. Two concrete sources of avoidable work were identified while investigating that variation.
+
+Receipt expiry invokes ACK-progress pruning up to once per second per node. The old implementation scanned every live receipt to find old-epoch ACK references even when every tracked stream belonged to the current epoch. Current-epoch streams must always survive pruning. The new fast path checks the much smaller ACK-progress and process-identity maps first and skips the receipt scan when no older stream exists. When an older stream exists, pruning still scans receipt requirements and preserves any stream needed by a retry. Receipt lifetime, expiry order, byte accounting, and retry results are unchanged.
+
+Each client GET, PUT, and DELETE attempt previously called `topology()`, cloning the complete snapshot, including all token assignments and their node-ID strings, before selecting an owner. At 10 nodes with 128 virtual nodes each, this copies 1,280 assignments per attempt. Routing now reads the epoch and selected endpoint under one topology read lock, then releases that lock before network I/O. Explicit callers of the public `topology()` API still receive an owned snapshot. Retry handling continues to use the epoch that selected the endpoint. There is no change to ACK policy or stream ordering.
+
+Source: [ACK pruning](../../crates/hashring-node/src/replication.rs), [client routing](../../crates/hashring-client/src/lib.rs), and [receipt expiry](../../crates/hashring-node/src/dedup.rs).
+
+## Profiling
+
+`HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1` enables per-process cumulative wall-time counters, returned by node info and saved in the experiment's post-write pressure sample. With profiling disabled, these optional timing messages are absent and the experiment records null values; hot paths skip clock reads and timing-counter updates. Unit tests enable diagnostics automatically.
+
+The counters cover the state write lock for owner PUT/DELETE application, follower replication application, and sender-side ACK processing. They do not cover read-lock waits, the separate final required-ACK completion lock, client CPU, transport queues, or all migration locks. Counts include successful lock acquisitions, and early-return paths still record hold duration. Wait sums can overlap across tasks and nodes. Hold and cleanup durations include descheduling; they are not CPU-time measurements.
+
+Cleanup time includes expiry-heap work, receipt destruction, and any nested ACK-pruning scan. Report pruning as a component of cleanup, not additional time. These counters reveal avoidable work but cannot alone assign the entire throughput gap to locks or expiry.
+

+# Where the write path saturates
+
+Sweeping `--concurrency` over the correctness run's initial load, with
+`HASHRING_PROFILE_WRITES=1` on every node so the state write lock reports its own
+wait and hold times. Medians of 3 runs per point, 20,000 keys, RF=3,
+`OwnerOnly`, 128-byte values, 9 data nodes.
+
+Reproduce with `./scripts/sweep.sh`; raw rows land in `results/sweep-<ts>/sweep.tsv`.
+
+## Measurement discipline
+
+A single run of this benchmark is not a measurement. Five runs of one unchanged
+binary at concurrency 128 spanned 0.362 s to 0.551 s, a **41.7% spread**, which is
+wider than any effect worth chasing. Every point below is therefore a median over
+three runs, and the conclusion below rests on the one column that is stable
+across repeats rather than on the throughput column, which is not.
+
+That distinction matters: throughput does **not** show a clean peak. The medians
+are 34.9k, 44.8k, 40.7k, 44.3k, 35.3k keys/s for concurrency 16, 64, 128, 256,
+512. The 64 and 256 points are indistinguishable given the spread, and 128 looks
+like a dip only because one of its three reps was slow. **This profile does not
+support the earlier claim that throughput inflects at concurrency 128.**
+
+## What is stable: the write lock is wait-dominated
+
+Cumulative across all nodes, microseconds, from `StateWriteTiming`:
+
+| conc | owner hold | owner wait | wait share |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| 16 | 205,646 | 89,838 | 30% |
+| 64 | 211,366 | 428,292 | 67% |
+| 128 | 238,365 | 537,382 | 69% |
+| 256 | 221,938 | 406,112 | 65% |
+| 512 | 256,213 | 401,794 | 61% |
+
+Owner **hold** is nearly flat at ~0.21-0.26 s regardless of offered load: the work
+per put does not change. Owner **wait** climbs 6x from concurrency 16 to 128 and
+then flattens. A queue that grows and then plateaus is a saturated lock, and the
+plateau is the signal.
+
+At concurrency 16 the lock is still mostly uncontended (30% of lock time is
+waiting). By 64 it is two-thirds waiting. Past that, more concurrency only adds
+queue depth. This is consistent with the CPU profile showing 1.5 of 24 cores busy:
+there is spare CPU, and the serialized resource is the single `NodeState` write
+lock, not compute.
+
+## What is not the cause
+
+Three counters that would each explain a knee are **zero at every concurrency**:
+
+| counter | value at all points |
+| --- | --- |
+| `replication_reservation_rejections` | 0 |
+| `replication_rpc_retries` | 0 |
+| `owner_dedup_rejections` | 0 |
+
+So the replication queue never filled, no RPC was ever retried, and the
+deduplication store never rejected an insert. Peak pending per replication stream
+stayed at 8-19 against a queue capacity of 32. Backpressure is not engaged, which
+also means the batching change in
+[batched-replication-rpc.md](batched-replication-rpc.md) is not limited by queue
+depth here -- it is limited by arrival rate, as that note records.
+

+
+The serialized resource is one `Arc<RwLock<NodeState>>` guarding records, dedup,
+topology, stream state and migration state together. Owner hold is ~11 us per
+acquisition and every other write path queues behind it, so the only lever that
+moves throughput is reducing the number of write-lock acquisitions or the time
+each holds it.
+
+Shrinking per-request work inside the critical section does not help much. The
+`683b337c` change removed three of four routing-token hashes and one of two
+mutation-fingerprint hashes from the owner path, and mean owner hold moved 11.88 us
+to 11.61 us: real, but under the noise floor. The 11 us is dominated by the dedup
+probe, the record insert and the replication reservation, all of which are real
+work rather than waste.
+
+That leaves reducing acquisition count, which is the ACK-relocation direction in

+riskier change: 90 access sites across 8 files, and `prune_ack_progress` reads
+`dedup` while writing the ACK maps, so the lock order has to stay
+`NodeState` -> `AckState` or the two can deadlock.

+
+The wait curve plateaus rather than rising without bound, and hold stays flat.
+That is what a saturated mutex looks like, but it is equally consistent with the
+driver itself becoming the bottleneck: past some concurrency the client side
+cannot keep 9 nodes fed and the offered load stops rising. Distinguishing the two
+needs a per-node arrival rate, which this run does not record. Treat the

-# Redis Cluster comparison
-
-This page answers one question: **how fast is hashring-rs when a Redis client
-talks to it, compared with a real Redis Cluster of the same shape?**
-
-The answer measured here: with one Redis gateway in front, the cluster serves
-about a fifth of the throughput of a Redis Cluster with the same number of
-owners, and the latency of a command is three to nine times higher. The gap is
-not in the ring, the storage or the replication: it is in the transport, and
-the gateway process is the limit in the single-gateway setup. Three gateways
-instead of one recover a sixth of the difference on reads and less on writes.
-
-The numbers come from a real Redis 8.10.2 built from source, driven by
-Redis' own `redis-benchmark`, against a hashring-rs cluster of the same shape
-driven by the same binary with the same commands. Everything ran on one host,
-one system at a time.
-
-- The scripts are in [`scripts/redis-cluster/`](../scripts/redis-cluster).
-- The raw measurements are in `results/redis-cluster-20261020/` (ignored by
-  Git): [`measurements.csv`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/measurements.csv),
-  [`summary.json`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/summary.json),
-  [`metadata.json`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/metadata.json) and
-  [`run.log`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/run.log).
-
-## The two systems
-
-| | Redis Cluster | hashring-rs |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| Version | Redis 8.10.2, built from `download.redis.io` | commit `8771351`, release build |
-| Nodes | `redis-server` processes with `cluster-enabled yes` | one coordinator, N data nodes, one Redis gateway |
-| Routing | by slot, computed by the client | by the ring, computed by the client library |
-| Replication | one replica per master, asynchronous | RF copies per range, asynchronous followers |
-| Client | `redis-benchmark` 8.10.2 | `redis-benchmark` 8.10.2, the same binary |
-
-The host had 24 logical CPUs and 30 GiB of RAM, and every process of both
-systems ran on it, as did the benchmark client.

-## Method
-
-### The cases
-
-| Case | Redis | hashring-rs |
-| --- | --- | --- |
-| `3m` | 3 masters | 3 nodes, RF=1, 1 gateway |
-| `3m1r` | 3 masters, 1 replica each | 3 nodes, RF=2, 1 gateway |
-| `3m-gw3` | 3 masters | 3 nodes, RF=1, 3 gateways |
-| `6m` | 6 masters | 6 nodes, RF=1, 1 gateway |
-
-RF=2 with three nodes holds the same number of copies as three masters with
-one replica each: one owner and one follower per range, against one master and
-one replica per slot range.
-
-### How each side is driven
-
-Redis Cluster routes by slot, and `redis-benchmark` cannot route by itself, so
-the harness runs one benchmark process per master. Each process uses a key
-template whose hash tag falls inside that master's slot range, so every key
-belongs to the master it is sent to and no client is redirected. The aggregate
-of those processes is the cluster's number.

-## What the numbers say
-
-1. **The cluster is several times slower than a Redis Cluster.** Through the
-   gateway the cluster reaches 80,000 to 170,000 operations per second,
-   against 440,000 to 707,000 for a Redis Cluster of the same shape. The
-   native client path is in the same range as the gateway (73,000 to 102,000
-   operations per second in the reference run), so switching clients does not
-   close the gap.
-2. **The cost is transport, not the cluster.** The node spends 1.8 µs on a
-   read and a median of 12.3 µs on a write, while the client waits half a
-   millisecond. The ring, the storage and the follower copy are not what the
-   time is spent on.
-3. **The gateway is a single point of contention.** One gateway caps the
-   cluster at about 100,000 operations per second, and more gateways lift that
-   cap. The cluster behind it has more to give: in `3m` the three nodes
-   together use 4.6 of their 12 workers.
-4. **The default deduplication budget limits sustained writes.** A node keeps
-   one receipt per write for 60 seconds, and 128 MiB fills after about ten
-   seconds of sustained writes at these rates. A deployment that writes
-   continuously needs a larger `--max-dedup-bytes` or a shorter receipt
-   retention.
-5. **Replication costs both systems.** RF=2 costs the hashring-rs side about
-   20% of its write throughput and the Redis side about 9%, and the CPU per
-   operation goes up by 30% on both sides.
-
-## Limits
-
-- One host, with the benchmark client on the same host as both systems. The
-  client takes CPU that the servers do not get, and it is the same client for
-  both sides, but the absolute numbers would be lower on a quieter machine.
-- The Redis side gets one key space per master, each inside its own slots,
-  because that is what a slot-routed client does. The hashring-rs side has
-  one key space over the ring. The key count per owner is the same.
-- The Redis side is measured with `redis-benchmark` talking to masters
-  directly, which is what a cluster-aware client does after it learns the slot
-  map. The hashring-rs side is measured with `redis-benchmark` talking to a
-  gateway, because the gateway is what a Redis client has to talk to.
-- The node budgets listed above were raised, so these numbers describe the
-  data path and not the deduplication store.
-- Three repetitions of 15 seconds per phase on a shared host. The spread
-  between the three repetitions of one configuration was 0.7% to 7.5% of the
-  median for the Redis side, except one mixed phase at 20.7%, and 1.3% to
-  19.8% for the hashring-rs side.
-- The measurements are of this build of this project on this host. The
-  project's own numbers in
-  [optimizations/](optimizations/) were taken on other machines and are not
-  comparable with these.
-- Valkey 9.1.2 is installed on the host as `redis-server`, and is a Redis
-  fork with the same protocol and the same cluster commands. The measurements
-  here used Redis 8.10.2 built from source.

+# Redis Cluster comparison
+
+This page answers one question: **how fast is hashring-rs when a Redis client
+talks to it, compared with a real Redis Cluster of the same shape?**
+
+The answer measured here: with one Redis gateway in front, the cluster serves
+about a fifth of the throughput of a Redis Cluster with the same number of
+owners, and the latency of a command is three to nine times higher. The gap is
+not in the ring, the storage or the replication: it is in the transport, and
+the gateway process is the limit in the single-gateway setup. Three gateways
+instead of one recover a sixth of the difference on reads and less on writes.
+
+The numbers come from a real Redis 8.10.2 built from source, driven by
+Redis' own `redis-benchmark`, against a hashring-rs cluster of the same shape
+driven by the same binary with the same commands. Everything ran on one host,
+one system at a time.
+
+- The scripts are in [`scripts/redis-cluster/`](../scripts/redis-cluster).
+- The raw measurements are in `results/redis-cluster-20261020/` (ignored by
+  Git): [`measurements.csv`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/measurements.csv),
+  [`summary.json`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/summary.json),
+  [`metadata.json`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/metadata.json) and
+  [`run.log`](../results/redis-cluster-20261020/run.log).
+
+## The two systems
+
+| | Redis Cluster | hashring-rs |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Version | Redis 8.10.2, built from `download.redis.io` | commit `8771351`, release build |
+| Nodes | `redis-server` processes with `cluster-enabled yes` | one coordinator, N data nodes, one Redis gateway |
+| Routing | by slot, computed by the client | by the ring, computed by the client library |
+| Replication | one replica per master, asynchronous | RF copies per range, asynchronous followers |
+| Client | `redis-benchmark` 8.10.2 | `redis-benchmark` 8.10.2, the same binary |
+
+The host had 24 logical CPUs and 30 GiB of RAM, and every process of both
+systems ran on it, as did the benchmark client.
+
+## Method
+
+### The cases
+
+| Case | Redis | hashring-rs |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `3m` | 3 masters | 3 nodes, RF=1, 1 gateway |
+| `3m1r` | 3 masters, 1 replica each | 3 nodes, RF=2, 1 gateway |
+| `3m-gw3` | 3 masters | 3 nodes, RF=1, 3 gateways |
+| `6m` | 6 masters | 6 nodes, RF=1, 1 gateway |
+
+RF=2 with three nodes holds the same number of copies as three masters with
+one replica each: one owner and one follower per range, against one master and
+one replica per slot range.
+
+### How each side is driven
+
+Redis Cluster routes by slot, and `redis-benchmark` cannot route by itself, so
+the harness runs one benchmark process per master. Each process uses a key
+template whose hash tag falls inside that master's slot range, so every key
+belongs to the master it is sent to and no client is redirected. The aggregate
+of those processes is the cluster's number.
+
+The gateway routes by the ring, so the harness runs one benchmark process per
+gateway with the same key template, and the aggregate of those processes is the
+cluster's number.
+
+Three workloads over a 300,000-key key space, with values of `--value-bytes`
+(128 by default):
+
+| Workload | Command | Meaning |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| write | `set k:{tag}:__rand_int__ <value>` | a stream of writes over random keys |
+| read | `get k:{tag}:__rand_int__` | a stream of reads of keys the write phase wrote |
+| mixed | a writer and a reader at the same time | half the clients write, half read |
+
+Reads run after the writes of the same repetition, so they hit keys that
+exist. The harness checks the key count in the cluster after every write phase
+(`DBSIZE`): 300,000 keys on the Redis side and 298,531 to 300,000 on the
+hashring-rs side, so the reads are reads, not misses.
+
+### The client
+
+`redis-benchmark` has no time limit, only a request count, so every phase runs
+a pilot first and the measured phase is then long enough to cover the same
+wall-clock time on both systems. The pilot doubles as the warmup.
+
+One `redis-benchmark` process tops out around 130,000 requests per second on
+this host, which is below what the Redis side reaches. The harness therefore
+runs two processes per endpoint, 64 client connections in total on both sides.
+Without that, the measurement would be of the client.
+
+The client is never the limit on the hashring-rs side: two, three and four
+client processes against one gateway produce the same total throughput
+(92.6k, 87.9k and 79.2k requests per second in a check before the run), while
+the Redis side gains 34% when a second process is added per master.

+| `--max-dedup-bytes` | 128 MiB per node | 2 GiB | A node keeps one deduplication receipt per write for the receipt retention period (60 s). At the write rate measured here the default store fills after about ten seconds, the node then rejects writes, and the phase ends in `TRYAGAIN` before the deadline. The default is a real limit on sustained writes, not a detail of the benchmark; see [dedup-receipt-store-memory.md](optimizations/dedup-receipt-store-memory.md#the-budget-is-also-a-sustained-write-rate-limit). |
+| `--deadline-ms` of the gateway | 5000 | 60000 | Redis has no deadline. A saturated gateway should be slow, not `TRYAGAIN`. |
+| `--max-pending-replication-bytes` | 64 MiB per node | 512 MiB | The queue of mutations waiting for a follower, for the same reason. |

+the Redis gateway (`hashring-rs experiment --mode performance`, 3 nodes,
+300,000 keys, 128-byte values, concurrency 64):
+
+| Cluster | PUT | GET (with verification) |
+| --- | ---: | ---: |
+| 3 nodes, RF=1 | 86,858 ops/s | 101,982 ops/s |
+| 3 nodes, RF=2 | 72,799 ops/s | 98,499 ops/s |
+
+These come from a different client and a different workload, so they are a
+reference and not a controlled comparison. They do show the size of the
+effect: the native client path is in the same range as the gateway path, so a
+client that skips the gateway does not close the gap to Redis. Both paths
+share the gRPC hop to a node; this reference does not measure what the
+gateway adds on top of it.
+
+## What the numbers say
+
+1. **The cluster is several times slower than a Redis Cluster.** Through the
+   gateway the cluster reaches 80,000 to 170,000 operations per second,
+   against 440,000 to 707,000 for a Redis Cluster of the same shape. The
+   native client path is in the same range as the gateway (73,000 to 102,000
+   operations per second in the reference run), so switching clients does not
+   close the gap.
+2. **The cost is transport, not the cluster.** The node spends 1.8 µs on a
+   read and a median of 12.3 µs on a write, while the client waits half a
+   millisecond. The ring, the storage and the follower copy are not what the
+   time is spent on.
+3. **The gateway is a single point of contention.** One gateway caps the
+   cluster at about 100,000 operations per second, and more gateways lift that
+   cap. The cluster behind it has more to give: in `3m` the three nodes
+   together use 4.6 of their 12 workers.
+4. **The default deduplication budget limits sustained writes.** A node keeps
+   one receipt per write for 60 seconds, and 128 MiB fills after about ten
+   seconds of sustained writes at these rates. A deployment that writes
+   continuously needs a larger `--max-dedup-bytes` or a shorter receipt
+   retention.
+5. **Replication costs both systems.** RF=2 costs the hashring-rs side about
+   20% of its write throughput and the Redis side about 9%, and the CPU per
+   operation goes up by 30% on both sides.
+
+## Limits
+
+- One host, with the benchmark client on the same host as both systems. The
+  client takes CPU that the servers do not get, and it is the same client for
+  both sides, but the absolute numbers would be lower on a quieter machine.
+- The Redis side gets one key space per master, each inside its own slots,
+  because that is what a slot-routed client does. The hashring-rs side has
+  one key space over the ring. The key count per owner is the same.
+- The Redis side is measured with `redis-benchmark` talking to masters
+  directly, which is what a cluster-aware client does after it learns the slot
+  map. The hashring-rs side is measured with `redis-benchmark` talking to a
+  gateway, because the gateway is what a Redis client has to talk to.
+- The node budgets listed above were raised, so these numbers describe the
+  data path and not the deduplication store.
+- Three repetitions of 15 seconds per phase on a shared host. The spread
+  between the three repetitions of one configuration was 0.7% to 7.5% of the
+  median for the Redis side, except one mixed phase at 20.7%, and 1.3% to
+  19.8% for the hashring-rs side.
+- The measurements are of this build of this project on this host. The
+  project's own numbers in
+  [optimizations/](optimizations/) were taken on other machines and are not
+  comparable with these.
+- Valkey 9.1.2 is installed on the host as `redis-server`, and is a Redis
+  fork with the same protocol and the same cluster commands. The measurements
+  here used Redis 8.10.2 built from source.
+
+## Reproducing
+
+```sh
+cargo build --release --bin hashring-rs
+make -C /path/to/redis MALLOC=jemalloc
+
+python3 scripts/redis-cluster/compare.py \
+  --output results/redis-cluster \
+  --cases 3m,3m1r,3m-gw3,6m \
+  --reps 3 --seconds 15 \
+  --redis-bin /path/to/redis/src
+```
+
+The harness writes `measurements.csv` with one row per phase, `summary.json`
+with the medians, and `metadata.json` with the versions, the checkout's
+revision, the digest of the binary that ran, and every resolved setting,
+including what `hashring-cluster.sh` resolved for each case. The node-side profile comes from:
+
+```sh
+python3 scripts/redis-cluster/gateway-profile.py \
+  --output results/node-profile --redis-bin /path/to/redis/src
+```

-# Redis compatibility
-
-This page describes the ordinary `redis-gateway` command. The separate
-[experimental Lua gateway](experimental-redis.md) adds scripting through the shared
-gateway's extension API; it requires an explicit feature and command selection.
-
-`redis-gateway` serves the Redis protocol on a TCP port over a hashring-rs
-cluster. A Redis client connects to it the way it would to a Redis server, so
-`redis-cli`, redis-py, Jedis, Lettuce and go-redis all work against it in
-single-node mode without knowing that the data lives on several nodes behind a
-consistent hash ring.
-
-This page is the honest description of what that buys and what it does not.
-Read the [limits](#limits-here) before pointing anything at it that matters.
-
-## Quick start
-
-```sh
-# With a cluster already running:
-cargo run -- redis-gateway --listen 127.0.0.1:6379 \
-  --coordinator http://127.0.0.1:50050
-
-redis-cli -p 6379 set greeting hello
-redis-cli -p 6379 get greeting
-```
-
-The coordinator is contacted on the **first command**, not at startup, so a
-gateway may be started before, alongside, or instead of the coordinator.
-Clients get `-TRYAGAIN` until the cluster answers. Several gateways may be run
-at once; see [how read-modify-write stays atomic](#read-modify-write-is-a-conditional-write).
-
-Settings are in [configuration.md](configuration.md#redis-gateway), and the
-gateway itself lives in [`crates/hashring-redis`](../crates/hashring-redis).
-
-## What it is not
-
-It is **not Redis Cluster**. There is no slot table, no `MOVED`, no `ASK`, and
-no gossip. Those exist in Redis because a client cannot compute Redis' hash
-ring; this cluster already hands out its whole topology through the
-coordinator, and `hashring_client` routes every key to its owner. So the gateway
-adds the protocol, not the routing.
-
-The consequence to weigh: the project deliberately chose client routing so that
-normal reads and writes take no extra hop
-([`docs/report/related-work.md`](report/related-work.md)). A Redis-speaking
-client cannot be given the topology, so the gateway puts a proxy back in the
-path. Every request becomes client → gateway → node: two hops, two
-serializations of the value, and a central process that did not previously
-exist. That is the price of not changing the client.
-
-That price has been measured against a real Redis Cluster of the same shape:
-see [redis-cluster-comparison.md](redis-cluster-comparison.md).
-
-## Supported commands
-
-`COMMAND` reports exactly this list, so a client that asks what the server
-supports sees what is actually implemented.
-
-### Connection and administration
-
-| Command | Notes |
-| --- | --- |
-| `PING`, `ECHO` | |
-| `HELLO` | RESP2 and RESP3. The reply is a map under RESP3 and a flat array under RESP2. `HELLO <ver> AUTH <user> <pass>` and `SETNAME` are accepted; the request is checked whole before any of it applies, so a wrong password changes neither the protocol nor the name. |
-| `AUTH` | Only when `--requirepass` is set. Otherwise it answers the error Redis gives when no password is configured. |
-| `SELECT` | Accepts database 0 only; one flat namespace, so any other index is refused. |
-| `CLIENT` | `ID`, `SETNAME`, `GETNAME`, `SETINFO`, `INFO`, `LIST`, `NO-EVICT`, `NO-TOUCH`, `UNPAUSE`, `GETREDIR`, and `REPLY ON\|OFF\|SKIP`. As in Redis, `REPLY ON` answers `OK` and `OFF` and `SKIP` answer nothing. |
-| `RESET` | Returns `+RESET` and restores RESP2, even on a RESP2 connection where Redis errors. Being liberal here is what keeps clients that send it on reconnect working. |
-| `QUIT` | Answers, then closes. |
-| `COMMAND` | `COMMAND`, `COMMAND COUNT`, `COMMAND INFO`, `COMMAND DOCS`. `GETKEYS` is declined. |
-| `INFO` | Server, clients, memory, persistence, stats, replication, cluster and keyspace sections. |
-| `CONFIG` | `GET` with globs, `SET` for the listed parameters, `RESETSTAT`, `REWRITE`. |
-
-`INFO` and `CONFIG` are honest but minimal. `CONFIG GET` and `CONFIG SET` cover
-`maxmemory`, `maxmemory-policy`, `appendonly`, `appendfsync`, `save`, `dir`,
-`dbfilename`, `timeout`, `notify-keyspace-events` and `lazyfree-lazy-user-del`.
-`CONFIG SET` accepts them and changes nothing, which is what Redis does for a
-parameter it has no other value for; any other parameter is an error.
-`notify-keyspace-events` reports empty because no events are emitted.
-
-### Keys
-
-| Command | Notes |
-| --- | --- |
-| `DEL`, `UNLINK` | Both are the same delete. `UNLINK` is not asynchronous here. |
-| `EXISTS` | Counts duplicates, as Redis does. |
-| `TOUCH` | |
-| `TYPE` | Always `string` or `none`. |
-| `RENAME`, `RENAMENX` | The value and its deadline move together. `RENAMENX` on an existing destination errors, as Redis does. |
-
-### Keyspace
-
-| Command | Notes |
-| --- | --- |
-| `KEYS` | Redis' glob, matched over bytes; only `^` negates a class, and range ends compare as signed bytes, as in Redis on x86-64. Errors rather than answer with more than 64 MiB of keys, each key counted with 64 bytes of overhead, or spend more than 100 million pattern steps matching. |
-| `SCAN` | `MATCH`, `COUNT` (default 10) and `TYPE`. Returns each key that is live for the whole scan exactly once, where Redis promises at least once. A cursor may be continued through any gateway and across membership changes. `MATCH` and the reply size have `KEYS`' limits. |
-| `DBSIZE` | Live keys only: each owner counts its own ranges, without its follower copies or keys past their deadline. |
-| `RANDOMKEY` | The first key at or after a random point on the ring, or nil when there are none. Not uniform: a key after a wide gap is likelier, as Redis' choice is not uniform either. |
-
-`KEYS`, `DBSIZE` and `RANDOMKEY` walk every owner, all at once, page by page;
-each node pages only through the ranges it owns at the topology epoch the walk
-started from. If
-ranges change hands mid-walk, a node at the newer epoch refuses the page and the
-walk starts over. So an answer counts every key that was live for the whole
-command exactly once; a key written or deleted while it ran may or may not be
-in it. Under constant topology churn a walk can run out of its deadline and
-answer `TRYAGAIN`.
-
-`SCAN` goes round the ring in hash order instead, one owner's stretch at a
-time, asking whichever node owns the next stretch when it gets there. Its
-cursor is the ring position to continue from, printed as the decimal integer
-clients expect, so the gateway keeps no state between calls. A position means
-the same thing in every topology: a range that moved between two calls is read
-from its new owner, which holds all of it before it owns it, and a range the
-scan already passed is not read again. That is why a key that is live
-throughout comes back exactly once. As in Redis, a key written or deleted
-during the scan may or may not come back, a step may return fewer keys than
-`COUNT`, or none, before the scan is done, and with `TYPE` naming anything but
-`string`, a type Redis knows or not, the scan is over at once, since every key
-is a string.
-
-A page of keys always ends between two ring positions, so that the cursor can
-be one number. That needs a bound on how many keys one position holds: by
-chance two keys share a 64-bit position almost never, but keys can be built to
-collide by anyone who knows the cluster's hash seed. So a node refuses to
-create a seventeenth key at one position, with an error, while writes to the
-keys already there go on working. A coordinator
-recreated from scratch picks a new hash seed, which moves every key and so
-invalidates every cursor; nothing else does.
-
-Unlike Redis, `DBSIZE` is not a stored counter: it costs a walk over every key,
-on every node. `KEYS` costs the same plus the matching keys' bytes, buffered at
-the gateway before the reply is sent, hence its limit.
-
-### Strings
-
-| Command | Notes |
-| --- | --- |
-| `GET`, `GETDEL` | |
-| `GETEX` | Takes `EX`, `PX`, `EXAT`, `PXAT`, `PERSIST`. Without an option it keeps the deadline. Changing the deadline does not rewrite the value. |
-| `GETRANGE` | Redis' index rules, including negative indices. |
-| `SET` | `NX`, `XX`, `GET`, `EX`, `PX`, `EXAT`, `PXAT`, `KEEPTTL`. |
-| `SETEX`, `PSETEX` | |
-| `SETNX`, `GETSET` | |
-| `SETRANGE` | Pads with zero bytes. An empty patch reports the length and creates nothing. |
-| `APPEND`, `STRLEN` | |
-| `MSET`, `MGET` | Not atomic across owners. A key named twice takes its later value. See [cross-key atomicity](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all). |
-| `MSETNX` | One key only, where it is `SETNX`. With more than one key it is declined, since it cannot set them atomically; see [cross-key atomicity](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all). |
-| `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`, `DECRBY` | Atomic against every writer. A value that is not an integer is an error and the value is left alone. |
-| `INCRBYFLOAT` | Atomic against every writer. The result is printed in the shortest form that reads back as the same double. |
-
-### Expiry
-
-| Command | Notes |
-| --- | --- |
-| `TTL`, `PTTL` | `-1` is a key with no deadline, `-2` no key at all. `TTL` rounds up to whole seconds. |
-| `EXPIRE`, `PEXPIRE`, `EXPIREAT`, `PEXPIREAT` | Accepts one of `NX`, `XX`, `GT`, `LT`. A key with no deadline counts as never expiring, so `LT` sets one and `GT` does not. A deadline that is not in the future, including a negative timeout, deletes the key. |
-| `PERSIST` | Clears the deadline without rewriting the value. |

-
-These are answered with a clear error rather than a wrong answer:
-
-```
-127.0.0.1:6379> flushall
-(error) ERR FLUSHALL is not supported by the hashring-rs Redis gateway; see docs/redis-compatibility.md
-```
-
-| Command | Why |
-| --- | --- |
-| `FLUSHALL`, `FLUSHDB` | A write to every key on every owner, which no node can apply atomically across owners: a flush that failed part-way would leave some ranges emptied and others not. |
-| `MSETNX` with more than one key | Cannot set its keys atomically; see [cross-key atomicity](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all). |
-
-Anything not in this document is answered with Redis' own unknown-command error.
-A data structure command (`HSET`, `ZADD`, `LPUSH`, …) is unknown here, because
-this gateway stores byte strings and nothing else, and will go on doing so; see
-[out of scope](#out-of-scope-data-structures). So are `MULTI`, `EXEC`,
-`WATCH`, `EVAL`, `SCRIPT`, and the `SUBSCRIBE` family.
-
-If a workload needs any of those, this is not a Redis substitute.
-
-## Semantics that differ from Redis
-
-These are the places where an application that works against Redis would notice
-a difference.
-
-### Read-modify-write is a conditional write
-
-Redis makes `INCR` atomic because one thread owns the key. A gateway has no such
-owner: the key lives on a data node. So `INCR`, `APPEND`, `SETRANGE`, `SETNX`,
-`GETSET`, `GETDEL`, `GETEX`, `SET ... NX|XX|GET`, `INCRBYFLOAT`, `DEL`, `EXPIRE`
-and `PERSIST` read the key, compute, and write.
-
-The write carries a precondition: the version the read returned, or that the key
-was absent. The owning node checks it under the same lock that applies the
-write, and refuses the write if anything else wrote the key in between. The
-gateway then reads again and recomputes. So these commands are atomic against
-**every** writer: clients of the same gateway, clients of other gateways behind
-the same load balancer, and programs using `hashring-client` directly.
-
-The costs are a read before every such write, as before, and a retry when two
-writers collide on one key. Within one gateway, a striped per-key lock makes its
-own clients take turns, so collisions are with writers elsewhere. A command that
-keeps colliding is bounded by the [command deadline](#limits-here).
-
-A plain `SET`, `SETEX`, `PSETEX` or `MSET` has nothing to compute and is one
-unconditional write. A read-modify-write that raced it simply reads again.
-
-### Cross-key atomicity is not available at all
-
-`MSET`, `DEL`, `EXISTS`, `MGET` and `RENAME` fan out to whichever
-owners hold their keys, and each key is applied on its own. There is no
-operation that spans two nodes atomically, and none can be added at this layer:
-the keys are on different machines.
-
-If any key fails, the whole command answers with an error rather than a count
-or a list built from the keys that happened to answer. When a writing command
-such as `DEL` or `MSET` failed on one key after writing another, that error is
-`ERR` and says its writes may have been applied, never `TRYAGAIN`: sending the
-command again could undo someone else's write in between.
-
-`RENAME` makes the best of it and reports what it could not do. It writes the
-destination, then deletes the source on condition that it is still the version
-it copied. A source rewritten in between is left in place and the command
-answers with an error, since the destination holds the earlier value.
-
-`MSETNX` is declined when it names more than one key. Its whole purpose is to
-set several keys as one, typically to claim them together, and a version that
-can leave some of them set would break exactly that use: two clients racing on
-overlapping keys could each set part of them and neither hold the set. With one
-key it is `SETNX` and atomic.
-
-This is the same trade Redis Cluster makes, where such commands fail with
-`CROSSSLOT`. Here they succeed but are not atomic. The honest comparison for
-this gateway is Redis Cluster, not Redis single-instance.
-
-If a write must not be observed half-applied, it must be one key.
-
-### `DEL` reads before it deletes
-
-Redis counts the keys that existed and were removed. This cluster's delete is
-idempotent and reports success whether or not the key was there, so the gateway
-reads each key first and deletes it on condition that it is still the version
-read, which keeps the count exact. The cost is one extra request per key, issued
-concurrently. `DEL` of a large keyspace is therefore roughly twice the requests
-of a Redis `DEL`.
-
-### `EXPIRE` with a past deadline deletes the key
-
-As in Redis, `EXPIRE key 0`, or an `EXPIREAT` in the past, removes the key
-rather than setting a deadline that has already passed.
-
-### `SET` without an expiry drops the deadline
-
-As in Redis. `SET key value` clears any TTL the key had; `SET key value KEEPTTL`
-keeps it; `SET key value EX 60` sets a new one. `NX` and `XX` may not be
-combined, nor two expiry options, nor `KEEPTTL` with one.
-
-### `INFO` reports an empty keyspace section
-
-`# Keyspace` has no `db0:keys=` line, because counting means walking every key
-on every owner, which `INFO` should not cost. `DBSIZE` does that walk. A tool
-that reads key counts from `INFO` will see nothing rather than a wrong number.
-
-## How expiry works
-
-A deadline is a field on the record, absolute, in Unix milliseconds. It is
-enforced by whichever replica is asked: a record past its deadline reads as
-absent, wherever it lives. That is what makes it survive the things a
-gateway-local expiry could not:
-
-- **Failover.** A promoted replica holds the same record with the same deadline.
-- **Migration.** The deadline travels with the record through the snapshot and
-  the changelog, and both sides of a range include it in the verification
-  digest, so a source and a destination that disagree about a deadline fail
-  verification instead of handing over a key that stops being readable at two
-  different times.
-- **Restart.** A gateway restart, a coordinator restart, or a node restart does
-  not lose it.
-
-Records past their deadline are hidden on read and reclaimed by a sweep every
-500 ms, bounded per pass so the sweep cannot stall writers. A key nobody asks
-about stays resident until its next sweep. While a range is migrating off a
-node, its expired records wait for the migration to end before they are
-reclaimed, because both sides of the migration verify the same records.
-
-Two consequences worth knowing:
-
-- **Clock skew shifts deadlines.** The gateway's clock decides when a relative
-  TTL such as `EX 60` becomes an absolute deadline, and the node's clock decides
-  when that deadline passes. A gateway whose clock is a minute fast sets a
-  deadline a minute early. Cluster nodes should be on NTP.
-- **Expiry is not a deletion.** Nothing is deleted at the deadline, so an
-  expired key is invisible but still occupies memory until the sweep. This is
-  what avoids a delete having to travel through replication, and why `KEYS`
-  and `DBSIZE` check each key's deadline rather than count what is stored.
-
-## Errors
-
-| Condition | Code |
-| --- | --- |
-| Key or value too large | `OOM` |
-| Bad argument, syntax, unknown command | `ERR` |
-| Retryable cluster condition: a range is moving, a follower is not ready, replication is backed up, the coordinator is unreachable, a read passed its deadline | `TRYAGAIN` |
-| Command sent before `AUTH` | `NOAUTH` |
-| Wrong password | `WRONGPASS` |
-| A write whose outcome is unknown, including a write command that passed its deadline | `ERR`, saying the writes may or may not have been applied |
-| More than `--maxclients` connections | `ERR max number of clients reached`, and the connection is closed |
-
-`TRYAGAIN` is the code clients already back off on, so a client that honours it
-behaves sensibly across a migration. A missing key is never an error: `GET`
-returns nil, `EXISTS` returns 0, `TTL` returns -2.
-
-## Client notes
-
-- The handshake every client performs works: `HELLO`, `AUTH`, `SELECT`,
-  `CLIENT SETINFO` are all answered.
-- **RESP3 is supported** and negotiated through `HELLO 3`. A missing value is
-  `$-1` under RESP2 and `_` under RESP3, maps are flat arrays under RESP2 and
-  real maps under RESP3. go-redis defaults to RESP3 and works.
-- Every value is a byte string, binary-safe, and keys are not restricted to
-  UTF-8.
-- `CLIENT SETINFO` is accepted and ignored.
-- The connection is not closed for a bad command, a declined command, or a
-  protocol error in a command; only an unparseable frame ends it, because the
-  stream cannot be resynchronized.
-- Before a connection authenticates it may send at most 10 arguments of at most
-  16 KiB each, as in Redis, so a client without the password cannot make the
-  gateway hold memory for it. Any connection may have at most 1 GiB received
-  and not yet run, and a line without a newline (an inline command, or a RESP
-  header) may be at most 64 KiB.
-
-## Limits here
-
-- One process, one extra hop. See [what it is not](#what-it-is-not).
-- No atomicity across keys, ever.
-- No `FLUSHALL`. `KEYS` and `DBSIZE` walk every key on every owner,
-  so they cost as much as the keyspace is large.
-- No data structures, by decision; see
-  [out of scope](#out-of-scope-data-structures). No transactions, scripting or
-  Pub/Sub.
-- The gateway keeps nothing, so it holds no expiry state, no keys and no
-  replication state. Losing it loses no data; losing the *cluster* loses every
-  value on every node, as the cluster's own guarantees describe.
-- Command deadlines come from `--deadline-ms`, default 5 s, and cover the whole
-  command: lock waits, every request it makes, and the retries of a conditional
-  write. Redis has no such deadline; a proxy in front of a migrating cluster
-  needs one. A read that passes it answers `TRYAGAIN`, so a long migration turns
-  into client retries rather than silent timeouts. A write that passes it
-  answers `ERR` instead, because it may already have been applied.
-

-## Out of scope: data structures
-
-Hashes, sets, sorted sets, lists and streams will not be added. The gateway
-aims to be a drop-in for caching and key-value use, the Rails, Django and Spring

+# Redis compatibility
+
+This page describes the ordinary `redis-gateway` command. The separate
+[experimental Lua gateway](experimental-redis.md) adds scripting through the shared
+gateway's extension API; it requires an explicit feature and command selection.
+
+`redis-gateway` serves the Redis protocol on a TCP port over a hashring-rs
+cluster. A Redis client connects to it the way it would to a Redis server, so
+`redis-cli`, redis-py, Jedis, Lettuce and go-redis all work against it in
+single-node mode without knowing that the data lives on several nodes behind a
+consistent hash ring.
+
+This page is the honest description of what that buys and what it does not.
+Read the [limits](#limits-here) before pointing anything at it that matters.
+
+## Quick start
+
+```sh
+# With a cluster already running:
+cargo run -- redis-gateway --listen 127.0.0.1:6379 \
+  --coordinator http://127.0.0.1:50050
+
+redis-cli -p 6379 set greeting hello
+redis-cli -p 6379 get greeting
+```
+
+The coordinator is contacted on the **first command**, not at startup, so a
+gateway may be started before, alongside, or instead of the coordinator.
+Clients get `-TRYAGAIN` until the cluster answers. Several gateways may be run
+at once; see [how read-modify-write stays atomic](#read-modify-write-is-a-conditional-write).
+
+Settings are in [configuration.md](configuration.md#redis-gateway), and the
+gateway itself lives in [`crates/hashring-redis`](../crates/hashring-redis).
+
+## What it is not
+
+It is **not Redis Cluster**. There is no slot table, no `MOVED`, no `ASK`, and
+no gossip. Those exist in Redis because a client cannot compute Redis' hash
+ring; this cluster already hands out its whole topology through the
+coordinator, and `hashring_client` routes every key to its owner. So the gateway
+adds the protocol, not the routing.
+
+The consequence to weigh: the project deliberately chose client routing so that
+normal reads and writes take no extra hop
+([`docs/report/related-work.md`](report/related-work.md)). A Redis-speaking
+client cannot be given the topology, so the gateway puts a proxy back in the
+path. Every request becomes client → gateway → node: two hops, two
+serializations of the value, and a central process that did not previously
+exist. That is the price of not changing the client.
+
+That price has been measured against a real Redis Cluster of the same shape:
+see [redis-cluster-comparison.md](redis-cluster-comparison.md).
+
+## Supported commands
+
+`COMMAND` reports exactly this list, so a client that asks what the server
+supports sees what is actually implemented.
+
+### Connection and administration
+
+| Command | Notes |
+| --- | --- |
+| `PING`, `ECHO` | |
+| `HELLO` | RESP2 and RESP3. The reply is a map under RESP3 and a flat array under RESP2. `HELLO <ver> AUTH <user> <pass>` and `SETNAME` are accepted; the request is checked whole before any of it applies, so a wrong password changes neither the protocol nor the name. |
+| `AUTH` | Only when `--requirepass` is set. Otherwise it answers the error Redis gives when no password is configured. |
+| `SELECT` | Accepts database 0 only; one flat namespace, so any other index is refused. |
+| `CLIENT` | `ID`, `SETNAME`, `GETNAME`, `SETINFO`, `INFO`, `LIST`, `NO-EVICT`, `NO-TOUCH`, `UNPAUSE`, `GETREDIR`, and `REPLY ON\|OFF\|SKIP`. As in Redis, `REPLY ON` answers `OK` and `OFF` and `SKIP` answer nothing. |
+| `RESET` | Returns `+RESET` and restores RESP2, even on a RESP2 connection where Redis errors. Being liberal here is what keeps clients that send it on reconnect working. |
+| `QUIT` | Answers, then closes. |
+| `COMMAND` | `COMMAND`, `COMMAND COUNT`, `COMMAND INFO`, `COMMAND DOCS`. `GETKEYS` is declined. |
+| `INFO` | Server, clients, memory, persistence, stats, replication, cluster and keyspace sections. |
+| `CONFIG` | `GET` with globs, `SET` for the listed parameters, `RESETSTAT`, `REWRITE`. |
+
+`INFO` and `CONFIG` are honest but minimal. `CONFIG GET` and `CONFIG SET` cover
+`maxmemory`, `maxmemory-policy`, `appendonly`, `appendfsync`, `save`, `dir`,
+`dbfilename`, `timeout`, `notify-keyspace-events` and `lazyfree-lazy-user-del`.
+`CONFIG SET` accepts them and changes nothing, which is what Redis does for a
+parameter it has no other value for; any other parameter is an error.
+`notify-keyspace-events` reports empty because no events are emitted.
+
+### Keys
+
+| Command | Notes |
+| --- | --- |
+| `DEL`, `UNLINK` | Both are the same delete. `UNLINK` is not asynchronous here. |
+| `EXISTS` | Counts duplicates, as Redis does. |
+| `TOUCH` | |
+| `TYPE` | Always `string` or `none`. |
+| `RENAME`, `RENAMENX` | The value and its deadline move together. `RENAMENX` on an existing destination errors, as Redis does. |
+
+### Keyspace
+
+| Command | Notes |
+| --- | --- |
+| `KEYS` | Redis' glob, matched over bytes; only `^` negates a class, and range ends compare as signed bytes, as in Redis on x86-64. Errors rather than answer with more than 64 MiB of keys, each key counted with 64 bytes of overhead, or spend more than 100 million pattern steps matching. |
+| `SCAN` | `MATCH`, `COUNT` (default 10) and `TYPE`. Returns each key that is live for the whole scan exactly once, where Redis promises at least once. A cursor may be continued through any gateway and across membership changes. `MATCH` and the reply size have `KEYS`' limits. |
+| `DBSIZE` | Live keys only: each owner counts its own ranges, without its follower copies or keys past their deadline. |
+| `RANDOMKEY` | The first key at or after a random point on the ring, or nil when there are none. Not uniform: a key after a wide gap is likelier, as Redis' choice is not uniform either. |
+
+`KEYS`, `DBSIZE` and `RANDOMKEY` walk every owner, all at once, page by page;
+each node pages only through the ranges it owns at the topology epoch the walk
+started from. If
+ranges change hands mid-walk, a node at the newer epoch refuses the page and the
+walk starts over. So an answer counts every key that was live for the whole
+command exactly once; a key written or deleted while it ran may or may not be
+in it. Under constant topology churn a walk can run out of its deadline and
+answer `TRYAGAIN`.
+
+`SCAN` goes round the ring in hash order instead, one owner's stretch at a
+time, asking whichever node owns the next stretch when it gets there. Its
+cursor is the ring position to continue from, printed as the decimal integer
+clients expect, so the gateway keeps no state between calls. A position means
+the same thing in every topology: a range that moved between two calls is read
+from its new owner, which holds all of it before it owns it, and a range the
+scan already passed is not read again. That is why a key that is live
+throughout comes back exactly once. As in Redis, a key written or deleted
+during the scan may or may not come back, a step may return fewer keys than
+`COUNT`, or none, before the scan is done, and with `TYPE` naming anything but
+`string`, a type Redis knows or not, the scan is over at once, since every key
+is a string.
+
+A page of keys always ends between two ring positions, so that the cursor can
+be one number. That needs a bound on how many keys one position holds: by
+chance two keys share a 64-bit position almost never, but keys can be built to
+collide by anyone who knows the cluster's hash seed. So a node refuses to
+create a seventeenth key at one position, with an error, while writes to the
+keys already there go on working. A coordinator
+recreated from scratch picks a new hash seed, which moves every key and so
+invalidates every cursor; nothing else does.
+
+Unlike Redis, `DBSIZE` is not a stored counter: it costs a walk over every key,
+on every node. `KEYS` costs the same plus the matching keys' bytes, buffered at
+the gateway before the reply is sent, hence its limit.
+
+### Strings
+
+| Command | Notes |
+| --- | --- |
+| `GET`, `GETDEL` | |
+| `GETEX` | Takes `EX`, `PX`, `EXAT`, `PXAT`, `PERSIST`. Without an option it keeps the deadline. Changing the deadline does not rewrite the value. |
+| `GETRANGE` | Redis' index rules, including negative indices. |
+| `SET` | `NX`, `XX`, `GET`, `EX`, `PX`, `EXAT`, `PXAT`, `KEEPTTL`. |
+| `SETEX`, `PSETEX` | |
+| `SETNX`, `GETSET` | |
+| `SETRANGE` | Pads with zero bytes. An empty patch reports the length and creates nothing. |
+| `APPEND`, `STRLEN` | |
+| `MSET`, `MGET` | Not atomic across owners. A key named twice takes its later value. See [cross-key atomicity](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all). |
+| `MSETNX` | One key only, where it is `SETNX`. With more than one key it is declined, since it cannot set them atomically; see [cross-key atomicity](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all). |
+| `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`, `DECRBY` | Atomic against every writer. A value that is not an integer is an error and the value is left alone. |
+| `INCRBYFLOAT` | Atomic against every writer. The result is printed in the shortest form that reads back as the same double. |
+
+### Expiry
+
+| Command | Notes |
+| --- | --- |
+| `TTL`, `PTTL` | `-1` is a key with no deadline, `-2` no key at all. `TTL` rounds up to whole seconds. |
+| `EXPIRE`, `PEXPIRE`, `EXPIREAT`, `PEXPIREAT` | Accepts one of `NX`, `XX`, `GT`, `LT`. A key with no deadline counts as never expiring, so `LT` sets one and `GT` does not. A deadline that is not in the future, including a negative timeout, deletes the key. |
+| `PERSIST` | Clears the deadline without rewriting the value. |
+
+## Declined commands
+
+These are answered with a clear error rather than a wrong answer:
+
+```
+127.0.0.1:6379> flushall
+(error) ERR FLUSHALL is not supported by the hashring-rs Redis gateway; see docs/redis-compatibility.md
+```
+
+| Command | Why |
+| --- | --- |
+| `FLUSHALL`, `FLUSHDB` | A write to every key on every owner, which no node can apply atomically across owners: a flush that failed part-way would leave some ranges emptied and others not. |
+| `MSETNX` with more than one key | Cannot set its keys atomically; see [cross-key atomicity](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all). |
+
+Anything not in this document is answered with Redis' own unknown-command error.
+A data structure command (`HSET`, `ZADD`, `LPUSH`, …) is unknown here, because
+this gateway stores byte strings and nothing else, and will go on doing so; see
+[out of scope](#out-of-scope-data-structures). So are `MULTI`, `EXEC`,
+`WATCH`, `EVAL`, `SCRIPT`, and the `SUBSCRIBE` family.
+
+If a workload needs any of those, this is not a Redis substitute.
+
+## Semantics that differ from Redis
+
+These are the places where an application that works against Redis would notice
+a difference.
+
+### Read-modify-write is a conditional write
+
+Redis makes `INCR` atomic because one thread owns the key. A gateway has no such
+owner: the key lives on a data node. So `INCR`, `APPEND`, `SETRANGE`, `SETNX`,
+`GETSET`, `GETDEL`, `GETEX`, `SET ... NX|XX|GET`, `INCRBYFLOAT`, `DEL`, `EXPIRE`
+and `PERSIST` read the key, compute, and write.
+
+The write carries a precondition: the version the read returned, or that the key
+was absent. The owning node checks it under the same lock that applies the
+write, and refuses the write if anything else wrote the key in between. The
+gateway then reads again and recomputes. So these commands are atomic against
+**every** writer: clients of the same gateway, clients of other gateways behind
+the same load balancer, and programs using `hashring-client` directly.
+
+The costs are a read before every such write, as before, and a retry when two
+writers collide on one key. Within one gateway, a striped per-key lock makes its
+own clients take turns, so collisions are with writers elsewhere. A command that
+keeps colliding is bounded by the [command deadline](#limits-here).
+
+A plain `SET`, `SETEX`, `PSETEX` or `MSET` has nothing to compute and is one
+unconditional write. A read-modify-write that raced it simply reads again.
+
+### Cross-key atomicity is not available at all
+
+`MSET`, `DEL`, `EXISTS`, `MGET` and `RENAME` fan out to whichever
+owners hold their keys, and each key is applied on its own. There is no
+operation that spans two nodes atomically, and none can be added at this layer:
+the keys are on different machines.
+
+If any key fails, the whole command answers with an error rather than a count
+or a list built from the keys that happened to answer. When a writing command
+such as `DEL` or `MSET` failed on one key after writing another, that error is
+`ERR` and says its writes may have been applied, never `TRYAGAIN`: sending the
+command again could undo someone else's write in between.
+
+`RENAME` makes the best of it and reports what it could not do. It writes the
+destination, then deletes the source on condition that it is still the version
+it copied. A source rewritten in between is left in place and the command
+answers with an error, since the destination holds the earlier value.
+
+`MSETNX` is declined when it names more than one key. Its whole purpose is to
+set several keys as one, typically to claim them together, and a version that
+can leave some of them set would break exactly that use: two clients racing on
+overlapping keys could each set part of them and neither hold the set. With one
+key it is `SETNX` and atomic.
+
+This is the same trade Redis Cluster makes, where such commands fail with
+`CROSSSLOT`. Here they succeed but are not atomic. The honest comparison for
+this gateway is Redis Cluster, not Redis single-instance.
+
+If a write must not be observed half-applied, it must be one key.
+
+### `DEL` reads before it deletes
+
+Redis counts the keys that existed and were removed. This cluster's delete is
+idempotent and reports success whether or not the key was there, so the gateway
+reads each key first and deletes it on condition that it is still the version
+read, which keeps the count exact. The cost is one extra request per key, issued
+concurrently. `DEL` of a large keyspace is therefore roughly twice the requests
+of a Redis `DEL`.
+
+### `EXPIRE` with a past deadline deletes the key
+
+As in Redis, `EXPIRE key 0`, or an `EXPIREAT` in the past, removes the key
+rather than setting a deadline that has already passed.
+
+### `SET` without an expiry drops the deadline
+
+As in Redis. `SET key value` clears any TTL the key had; `SET key value KEEPTTL`
+keeps it; `SET key value EX 60` sets a new one. `NX` and `XX` may not be
+combined, nor two expiry options, nor `KEEPTTL` with one.
+
+### `INFO` reports an empty keyspace section
+
+`# Keyspace` has no `db0:keys=` line, because counting means walking every key
+on every owner, which `INFO` should not cost. `DBSIZE` does that walk. A tool
+that reads key counts from `INFO` will see nothing rather than a wrong number.
+
+## How expiry works
+
+A deadline is a field on the record, absolute, in Unix milliseconds. It is
+enforced by whichever replica is asked: a record past its deadline reads as
+absent, wherever it lives. That is what makes it survive the things a
+gateway-local expiry could not:
+
+- **Failover.** A promoted replica holds the same record with the same deadline.
+- **Migration.** The deadline travels with the record through the snapshot and
+  the changelog, and both sides of a range include it in the verification
+  digest, so a source and a destination that disagree about a deadline fail
+  verification instead of handing over a key that stops being readable at two
+  different times.
+- **Restart.** A gateway restart, a coordinator restart, or a node restart does
+  not lose it.
+
+Records past their deadline are hidden on read and reclaimed by a sweep every
+500 ms, bounded per pass so the sweep cannot stall writers. A key nobody asks
+about stays resident until its next sweep. While a range is migrating off a
+node, its expired records wait for the migration to end before they are
+reclaimed, because both sides of the migration verify the same records.
+
+Two consequences worth knowing:
+
+- **Clock skew shifts deadlines.** The gateway's clock decides when a relative
+  TTL such as `EX 60` becomes an absolute deadline, and the node's clock decides
+  when that deadline passes. A gateway whose clock is a minute fast sets a
+  deadline a minute early. Cluster nodes should be on NTP.
+- **Expiry is not a deletion.** Nothing is deleted at the deadline, so an
+  expired key is invisible but still occupies memory until the sweep. This is
+  what avoids a delete having to travel through replication, and why `KEYS`
+  and `DBSIZE` check each key's deadline rather than count what is stored.
+
+## Errors
+
+| Condition | Code |
+| --- | --- |
+| Key or value too large | `OOM` |
+| Bad argument, syntax, unknown command | `ERR` |
+| Retryable cluster condition: a range is moving, a follower is not ready, replication is backed up, the coordinator is unreachable, a read passed its deadline | `TRYAGAIN` |
+| Command sent before `AUTH` | `NOAUTH` |
+| Wrong password | `WRONGPASS` |
+| A write whose outcome is unknown, including a write command that passed its deadline | `ERR`, saying the writes may or may not have been applied |
+| More than `--maxclients` connections | `ERR max number of clients reached`, and the connection is closed |
+
+`TRYAGAIN` is the code clients already back off on, so a client that honours it
+behaves sensibly across a migration. A missing key is never an error: `GET`
+returns nil, `EXISTS` returns 0, `TTL` returns -2.
+
+## Client notes
+
+- The handshake every client performs works: `HELLO`, `AUTH`, `SELECT`,
+  `CLIENT SETINFO` are all answered.
+- **RESP3 is supported** and negotiated through `HELLO 3`. A missing value is
+  `$-1` under RESP2 and `_` under RESP3, maps are flat arrays under RESP2 and
+  real maps under RESP3. go-redis defaults to RESP3 and works.
+- Every value is a byte string, binary-safe, and keys are not restricted to
+  UTF-8.
+- `CLIENT SETINFO` is accepted and ignored.
+- The connection is not closed for a bad command, a declined command, or a
+  protocol error in a command; only an unparseable frame ends it, because the
+  stream cannot be resynchronized.
+- Before a connection authenticates it may send at most 10 arguments of at most
+  16 KiB each, as in Redis, so a client without the password cannot make the
+  gateway hold memory for it. Any connection may have at most 1 GiB received
+  and not yet run, and a line without a newline (an inline command, or a RESP
+  header) may be at most 64 KiB.
+
+## Limits here
+
+- One process, one extra hop. See [what it is not](#what-it-is-not).
+- No atomicity across keys, ever.
+- No `FLUSHALL`. `KEYS` and `DBSIZE` walk every key on every owner,
+  so they cost as much as the keyspace is large.
+- No data structures, by decision; see
+  [out of scope](#out-of-scope-data-structures). No transactions, scripting or
+  Pub/Sub.
+- The gateway keeps nothing, so it holds no expiry state, no keys and no
+  replication state. Losing it loses no data; losing the *cluster* loses every
+  value on every node, as the cluster's own guarantees describe.
+- Command deadlines come from `--deadline-ms`, default 5 s, and cover the whole
+  command: lock waits, every request it makes, and the retries of a conditional
+  write. Redis has no such deadline; a proxy in front of a migrating cluster
+  needs one. A read that passes it answers `TRYAGAIN`, so a long migration turns
+  into client retries rather than silent timeouts. A write that passes it
+  answers `ERR` instead, because it may already have been applied.
+

+## Out of scope: data structures
+
+Hashes, sets, sorted sets, lists and streams will not be added. The gateway
+aims to be a drop-in for caching and key-value use, the Rails, Django and Spring
+cache stores and `INCR`-and-`EXPIRE` counters, which need only what is
+[supported](#supported-commands) now.
+
+The way this cluster could hold a structure is as one record under one key. That
+would make each structure atomic, since it would inherit the cluster's per-key
+linearizability, but:
+
+- **Every mutation rewrites the whole structure.** An `HSET` of one field sends
+  the whole hash to the owner and then to every follower, and a write that loses
+  a [conditional-write](#read-modify-write-is-a-conditional-write) race sends
+  it again.
+- **A structure is capped at 8 MiB**, the value limit. How many members that
+  holds depends on their size: about 50 000 of 150 bytes each, about 8 000 of
+  1 KiB. The rewrite cost bites well before that.
+- **It would not buy the libraries that need structures.** Job queues and locks
+  such as Sidekiq, Celery, BullMQ and Redlock also need blocking pops and Lua,
+  and honest scripting needs atomicity across keys, which is
+  [not available](#cross-key-atomicity-is-not-available-at-all).
+
+Lists and streams fit worst of all: `LPOP` and consumer groups want element
+access without a rewrite, and blocking reads across the cluster.
+
+Storing each member as its own record, placed by its parent key so a structure
+stays on one owner, would remove the size limit and the rewrite. It needs
+atomic multi-record writes on the node and changes to migration and range
+digests, which is a storage redesign rather than gateway work.
+
+## Not attempted
+
+Recorded so the gap is deliberate rather than an oversight. In rough order of
+how much each would cost:
+
+| | What it would take |
+| --- | --- |
+| `MULTI`, `EXEC`, `WATCH` | Would need server-side execution, and cross-key atomicity is unavailable underneath, so `EXEC` could not honestly promise atomicity across keys. |
+| Durability | The cluster is in-memory by design; the gateway adds no storage. |
